meta.title: Viva final boss: examiner question bank
meta.thesis: Shared Space, Separate Freight (University of Wolverhampton)
notes: Each item has four spoken answers; answer_index points to the strong one. Positions are balanced across 0 to 3 with a fixed seed.
'why' describes the flawed answers by what they do wrong, not by letter, so options can be reshuffled at run time.

Questions about the full coding files 1 and 2, the transcript-by-transcript coding of files 3 to 6, the full claim register (O), the search log (M.2 apart from its rules) and most of E.3.2 to E.3.5 expect the answer that they are held by the author and available on request.
Participants appear by interview code only; authors only as cited sources.

v3 (3 Nov 2026): options rewritten so that no strong answer is a length giveaway: none is more than 1.25 times the mean of its item's other answers, in words or in characters; the strong answer is the longest (ties included) in 27 per cent of items, and its length rank is spread across first to fourth. Wrong-answer openings varied so no opening word marks right or wrong. Nine examiner items added on what would falsify P2, P3 and P4 (pro-26 to pro-34; three of them killers). fin-33's strong answer now says the 2023 plan announces the end of the privilege, as 5.2 does. Every earlier id, answer position and fact is unchanged. Log: bank_fixes.md.

questions.question: So what is new here? Everyone in this field already knows carriers don't like sharing with their rivals.
options: Much of it confirms what the field suspected, and I say so. The value is the breadth of evidence, twenty-six interviews across eleven countries and a survey, so I'd call it a careful synthesis that documents the reluctance better than anyone before.

What's new is the emphasis on trust. The field treats distrust as one barrier among thirty-one, and my record is consistent with it being the central one: build trust through staged relationships and fair gain-sharing, and most of the reluctance falls away. That reframing is the contribution.

What's new is that I show carriers will collaborate once a neutral holder runs the shared point. The locker networks establish that causally, at p = .008; so the field's pessimism about rivals sharing was mistaken, and cities can now rely on the rule.

The reluctance is established, and I say so. What wasn't shown is that it tracks overlap rather than size, that sharing stops at the freight unless something outside binds it, that most arrangements are bound from outside, and that no rule re-checks a point's holder.
questions.why: Strong concedes the known reluctance and names what 1.5 says had not been shown. The others claim a causal proof the thesis disclaims, undersell the work as synthesis, or reverse the thesis, which replaces trust with overlap and binding.
questions.follow_up: Which of those four would survive if I took your locker data away entirely?

questions.question: Name the four forms your contribution takes.
options: A framework of four pillars tested in the field; the understanding that trust is the decisive condition; a survey of 119 organisations; and the extension of Ostrom's design principles to carriers governing their own commons.

A corrected systematic review, twenty-six interviews in eleven countries, a document analysis of Ghent and a savings scenario. Those four stages of the design are the four contributions, each answering one of the field's gaps in turn.

A new understanding of an existing issue, refusal explained by overlap and binding rather than trust; a combination of concepts from four literatures; the extension of others' work at three named points; and a new issue, who holds the shared point.

A tested causal model of carrier behaviour; a new dataset of 117 arrangements; a validated survey of trust; and a policy instrument, the red-cell rule, already adopted in Ghent's 2023 plan, which shows the contribution reaching practice in a working city as well as knowledge.
questions.why: Strong gives the four forms 7.2 names. The others claim a tested causal model and a city adoption that the thesis denies, confuse the design's stages with forms of contribution, or offer the four pillars the data replaced.
questions.follow_up: Which of the four is the weakest, and why do you still claim it?

questions.question: Isn't your 'binder' just trust by another name? You've relabelled trust as contracts and grants.
options: No, because I measured trust directly in the survey. Respondents rate it highly, 89 of 119 at four or five, yet the arrangements they described still failed, which proves trust is irrelevant to whether a collaboration lasts. Saying trust matters while failing anyway shows it isn't the variable.

No, the record separates them. Participants named trust as a wish, as something that grew after years, and as trust placed in a trustee; only one named it as what held an arrangement. By row, 95 of 117 were bound from outside, 6 by their own trust.

No, because trust is a psychological state and a binder is an economic device. They belong to different disciplines; so I keep them apart by definition at the start of Chapter 2, and that separation is what stops the binder collapsing back into ordinary trust.

In a sense, yes: a contract or a grant is institutionalised trust; so I'd accept that the binder is trust made formal. The contribution is to show which formal devices carry trust best between rivals, from the neutral third party down to reputation. That keeps trust at the centre while explaining what carries it.
questions.why: Strong rests the distinction on what participants said trust did and on the row counts. The others concede the relabelling, misuse the survey (it tests no link and says nothing about failure), or defend the line by definition rather than evidence.
questions.follow_up: Then what is trust, in your account, if it isn't what starts an arrangement?

questions.question: You claim to extend three pieces of others' work. Which three, and how?
options: Sternberg and colleagues' commons reading, by separating the facilitator who convenes from the binder who enforces; Holguín-Veras's conditions, from the off-hours to the whole receiver's clock; and van Duin's initiators, counted across the 241 papers.

Sternberg's commons reading, by showing outside facilitators succeed after all; Holguín-Veras, by showing tolls aimed at carriers work best; and van Duin's initiators, by counting who began each arrangement in my interviews rather than in the published literature.

Berger and Bierwirth, by measuring their 155 per cent in real networks; Yang, Dai and Ma, by testing their core condition in rural logistics; and Allen and colleagues, by tracking London's parcel vans again and finding them parked for most of the round.

Ostrom's design principles, by showing all eight are met inside the parties; Barney's resource-based view, by applying it to port terminals; and Cruijssen, Cools and Dullaert's survey, which I repeat among 119 respondents and confirm almost item by item.
questions.why: Strong names the three extensions of 7.2 accurately. The others invent extensions the thesis never makes (all eight principles met inside, ports, a repeated survey, re-measured models) or reverse its findings on facilitators and on tolls aimed at carriers.
questions.follow_up: Why does the facilitator-binder line matter for a city deciding what to fund?

questions.question: How big is this contribution, honestly? Twenty-six interviews and a proposal that's never been tried anywhere.
options: Large: twenty-six interviews across eleven countries is more fieldwork than most of this field has ever done; so I'd claim the findings hold for European last-mile logistics generally, a population, not a mechanism, and that the rule is ready for cities to adopt as it stands. That breadth is what makes the contribution large.

Its size is best judged against the literature. Since 77 of 89 studies in the field are models, any fieldwork at all is a major contribution, whatever it happens to find, and that alone settles the question of doctoral weight.

Small, not modest, I accept: with four carrier voices and an untested proposal it's a scoping study, and the real contribution will come from the follow-up studies proposed in 7.5, so I'd present the thesis mainly as groundwork for them. That's the honest framing. Modesty serves a doctoral thesis well.

Modest, as it should be. Four findings rest on counts given before the argument, each traceable to a chapter and an appendix row. The fifth link is proposed, not found; no city has done what my last clause says. The claim is to a mechanism, not a population.
questions.why: Strong states the claim at its true size: counted findings, a proposed fifth link, generalisation to mechanism. The others overgeneralise to a population, talk the work down to a scoping study, or rest originality on the field's thinness rather than on what was found.
questions.follow_up: If I accept 'modest', what stops this being a master's dissertation?

questions.question: Your one sentence: which part is a finding and which part a proposition?
options: The first clause, about competition, is the proposition, because the survey couldn't separate size from overlap; the holder clause is the finding, because the locker test is significant and the interviews support the holder at the 0.9 bar. So the two halves should really be read the other way round.

It's a proposition throughout: because the design was theory-building, nothing in it counts as a finding; every clause is a claim offered for others to test; that's why Chapter 7 restates the whole sentence as five propositions. The design's purpose decides each clause's status, not the evidence. That's the safer reading.

A finding up to 'the street': competition for customers rather than a shortage of trust, and the line at the customer relationship. After that, that a no-stake holder must hold the shared point and a city keep it so, is a proposition; no city has done it yet.

It's a finding throughout: each clause carries a count from the twenty-six interviews, and the locker networks confirm the holder clause at p = .008, so the sentence as a whole is supported and its last clause is simply the policy that follows. No part of it is merely proposed.
questions.why: Strong gives 6.5's verdict. The others treat a result 'consistent with' the holder as confirmation, ignore that 6.5 calls the early clauses findings, or reverse the two parts and omit that the holder reaches 0.9 only under rule 1a.
questions.follow_up: What would a city have to do for the last clause to become a finding?

questions.question: What exactly is the 'new issue for investigation' you claim?
options: That carriers may not trust each other enough to share operating data, a problem the field had not identified before this thesis and which the binder now explains as the reason carriers refuse to share anything.
That the rules certifying shared last-mile points ask who may use them while carriers ask who holds them, that holders change hands, and that no rule found looks again when they do.
That the 2023 review's string missed the collaboration literature, an issue every reviewer in the field now needs to investigate when designing their own searches in the years ahead.

That lockers may cut emissions compared with doorstep delivery, which no study had measured until my scenario put a figure on the carbon a council area of 50,000 households would save each year from them.
questions.why: Strong is the fourth form of 7.2. The others name things the field already discusses (distrust), claims the thesis does not make (measured emissions; the scenario reports carbon but is not a measurement), or a finding about the review rather than the new issue.
questions.follow_up: What evidence do you have that holders actually change hands?

questions.question: Who begins a collaboration: why should anyone care? Surely what matters is whether it works.
options: Most of the 117 arrangements were begun by carriers, so the field was right to study carriers; what I add is that they need more support from those who convene them, and the initiator count in 4.5 shows where that support should go.

Because who begins bears on what it can be. Of 19 arrangements carriers began, 5 were between rivals and 2 operate, the container consortia and two bike couriers' joint bid. Shipper-led and city-led ones pool freight under a trustee, a permit or a client's instruction.

Fair point: I'd concede that who begins is mainly a descriptive category, and the real contribution is overlap; the initiator counts are context for Chapter 4 rather than part of the argument, so I wouldn't defend them hard. Overlap is where the weight lies. Initiation is secondary.

Shipper-begun collaborations always succeed and carrier-begun ones always fail, which the 117 rows show without exception, so knowing the initiator lets a city predict any arrangement's outcome before it starts. That predictive power is the real point.
questions.why: Strong uses 7.2's figures on carrier-begun arrangements. The others get the initiator count wrong (cities and public bodies began 42, carriers 19), drop an argument 7.2 relies on, or overclaim 'always' where the record shows exceptions.
questions.follow_up: Five between rivals and two operating: isn't that too small to carry a claim?

questions.question: You say the field's own models 'carry' your first finding. What do you mean?
options: I mean the Shapley value: the models show that a fair division of the gain is what makes rivals willing, so they carry the finding that fairness, a form of trust between the parties, is the real condition of collaboration. Fair division, in other words, is what binds rivals.

Yang, Dai and Ma prove rivals' coalition has a stable split only if the saving is no less than revenue lost to brand switching: my first finding as an inequality. I extend it to every exposure: rivals pool only when S plus P covers L plus W.

Berger and Bierwirth show network profit falls as carriers' service areas overlap more, which is the same as my finding that willingness falls with overlap; so the modellers had my result years ago and simply didn't name it. Read that way, their figures measure the cost of overlap, which is the refusal my interviews describe.

I mean that the models assume carriers are willing, so in effect they carry nothing; I cite them only to show the field's mathematics is irrelevant to what carriers actually do; that's why Chapter 6 sets them aside.
questions.why: Strong states the core condition and its extension (6.1, 6.3). The others reverse Berger and Bierwirth (profit rises with overlap, about 19, 67 and 155 per cent), turn the Shapley value into a trust claim, or dismiss the models the thesis uses.
questions.follow_up: Yang, Dai and Ma's result is about rural logistics. Why does it transfer to the city?

questions.question: If I'm a city transport officer, what's the single most useful thing your thesis tells me?
options: Stop asking carriers to collaborate with nothing to bind them, and judge shared points by who holds them: register each holder, look again on every change of control and at renewal, and write the vehicle-and-hour rule the same for every operator in a class.

Give your best hours to named, cleaner companies, so rivals who won't share a street can share the clock instead; Ghent shows that allocating hours to particular operators works, and it costs a council very little to run.

Ban carriers from owning lockers on your streets. That's the red-cell rule in its simplest form, and it's the quickest way to make every point in the city neutral without the expense of checking them. Ownership is the simplest test to apply, and residents gain from it at once.

Run trust-building workshops among your carriers and fund a consolidation centre; with goodwill built in stages and a fair split of the saving, the shared van can finally work in your city. Trust is what the field has always prescribed, and the thesis confirms it is still the missing ingredient.
questions.why: Strong is the first recommendation of 7.3. The others offer the hours-to-named-companies idea the thesis abandoned, the trust remedy it replaces, or an ownership ban the law forbids and the rule explicitly is not.
questions.follow_up: Why 'the same for every operator in a class' rather than a reward for the greenest?

questions.question: Your contribution leans on the holder, yet you admit the interviews support it only under a rule written after you saw the results. What's left?
options: Not much, if the holder falls, so I'd defend rule 1a as obviously correct, since any sensible coder treats a trustee as the holder; I don't think it should be described as a choice made after the results at all. The rule simply follows good coding practice.

The locker result on its own proves the holder, so the interview coding doesn't really matter. A permutation test at p = .008 is stronger evidence than any count of running rows, and that's what the contribution rests on.

Most of it. The holder is proposed, not found; the four findings stand without it. Three kinds of evidence bear on it: the 117, supporting it only under rule 1a, reported both ways; the lockers, consistent but not a test; and rules that never re-check.

The holder is proposed, not shown, so the honest course is to drop it and present the thesis as four findings. The fifth link was speculative from the start, and the question can be closed without it by saying that time allocated between operators didn't work.
questions.why: Strong separates found from proposed and lists the three kinds of evidence as 1.5 does. The others deny the rule was post hoc, overread a difference by owner class as proof, or abandon the answer to the question's second half.
questions.follow_up: If a reader rejects rule 1a outright, which of your five propositions survive intact?

questions.question: What papers do you plan from this thesis?
options: One monograph first, because splitting the chain into papers would lose the argument; journal papers can follow once the book is out and the framework is established.

Three: one on the survey's trust ratings, one on Ghent's camera system and permit categories, and one on the scenario's net value for councils, which is the most publishable result. Each would stand alone without the chain.

Three. The review's blind spot and the corrected search, from Chapter 2; the four findings of the interviews, from Chapter 4; and the red-cell rule with its evidence and objections, from Chapters 5 and 6.

Three: the four findings in one paper, the locker test in a second, and in a third the GREEN-LOG demand data I worked on, which would add a quantitative strand. That spreads the thesis's reach across several fields.
questions.why: Strong lists the three planned papers of 7.2. The others pick evidence the thesis treats as secondary, propose publishing GREEN-LOG data the thesis says no finding draws on, or invent a monograph plan.
questions.follow_up: Which journal would take the red-cell paper, and what would its reviewers attack first?

questions.question: 'A combination of concepts from four literatures.' Isn't new combination the weakest kind of originality?
options: It's actually the strongest kind, because combining ecology, management, economics and operations research has never been done in any field before; so the combination is original in itself, whatever object it's applied to. No one else has brought those four together. That alone is original.

It would be if the parts were the claim. It's new in its object: no study among the 241 reads rivals' refusal through all of them together, and none found reads it through who holds the meeting point. And it's one of four forms.

I agree it's weak, which is why I'd lean on the survey of 119 organisations as my main original evidence; the framework is a convenient way of organising the chapters rather than a contribution I'd defend on its own. Its numbers are new to the field.

Originality isn't really the test at this level; contribution to practice is. The rule for cities covers that, so whether the combination counts as original doesn't change the case for the doctorate. Examiners ask whether the work makes a contribution, and the practical rule plainly does.
questions.why: Strong places the novelty in the object and keeps it as one of four forms. The others overclaim a first-ever combination across all fields, lean on the survey that tests no link, or dismiss originality, which is the criterion.
questions.follow_up: Pick the one concept from another literature that does the most work. What would collapse without it?

questions.question: What does your thesis say to carriers themselves?
options: That their branded vans are a proven asset with shippers, so they're right to refuse arrangements that hide their livery, and should look for partners who let them keep it visible in every street. Visibility is worth protecting. Shippers notice the livery first.

Seek collaboration where markets don't overlap, at the depot, the vessel or the rail slot, or one border over; where they do overlap, ask who could bind it from outside and who holds the point; and measure the visibility you pay for.

That they should open their own lockers to rivals, because open is the same as neutral, and once a network is open other carriers will deliver into it as readily as into any other, whoever holds it. Openness is what carriers look for.

Merge, since a dramatic increase in market concentration is the remedy for the median firm's smallness, and larger carriers will find collaboration easier once there are fewer of them competing for each street. Scale, in their position, is the condition that makes partners easier to find.
questions.why: Strong is the carriers' paragraph of 7.3. The others revive the concentration remedy the thesis displaces, contradict 'open is not neutral', or treat the visibility premise as proven when no participant had measured it.
questions.follow_up: Why would a carrier pay attention to a thesis that says it has no power?

questions.question: You say the shipper side is 'under-examined as a category'. Isn't that a gap you created by defining collaboration widely?
options: The gap is established by my own 2023 review, which found no shipper-begun studies among its 49; that review is the evidence the gap rests on, and the 2026 update confirms what it found.

No, because the shipper side had never been documented at all before this thesis. Nobody had reported a shipper-led scheme, so the gap is an absolute absence, which is a stronger claim than 'under-examined'.

I did widen the definition deliberately, to open space for a contribution. A thesis frames its gap, and a wide definition is legitimate as long as I'm open about it, which I am from the first page of Chapter 1.

The wide definition is the field's: 'users, transport providers or shippers'. It defined widely and studied carriers. And the gap doesn't rest on my review. The two 2026 reviews have no category for who begins, and corrected strings found 13 of 241.
questions.why: Strong shows the definition is the field's and that the gap does not rest on his own review (1.6). The others admit manufacturing the gap, overclaim an absolute absence (a press distributor's scheme was reported in 2011), or rest the gap on the 2023 review, whose cards code one shipper.
questions.follow_up: If the shipper side is documented, why does counting it matter?

questions.question: What does the 2026 update contribute, beyond correcting your own earlier review?
options: It replicates the 2023 review exactly with a better database, confirming that the 49 were the right studies and that nothing important had been missed by the original string, which strengthens the review rather than correcting it. That's what a good update should do.

It shows the field has grown to 1,535 studies of horizontal collaboration since 2018, which proves the topic matters to researchers, justifies a doctorate on it and gives the thesis a much wider base than the 49. Growth on that scale speaks for itself.

It turns an impression into a count: strings written to find shippers found 13 shipper- or receiver-begun papers in 241, and none with a measured result from carriers' own collaboration. And the 2022 string returns only 39 of the 231 new papers.

It shows most papers name carriers as the initiator, so the field's focus on carriers was justified after all, and what it lacked was only fieldwork with carriers, which my interviews then supply. That fills the gap neatly. The field's instinct was sound.
questions.why: Strong reports what 2.2 and 7.1 draw from the update. The others mistake 1,535 records for studies, call a widened search a replication (it found 231 papers the 2022 string mostly could not see), or misread the initiators (128 name none; public bodies lead with 45).
questions.follow_up: If the 2022 string found only 39 of them, what does that say about your 49?

questions.question: Your four findings are essentially descriptive counts. Where's the conceptualisation?
options: The conceptualisation is the four pillars, trust, efficiency, innovation and sustainability, not the counts. They organise the findings in Chapter 4, and each count is read back to its pillar, which is what lifts the counts above description. Without the pillars the findings would be lists.

In the conceptual conclusions, each tested for whether observations support the concept as well as the fact. Willingness belongs to a pair of markets, not a firm; pooling is bounded by the customer relationship; durability belongs to the binder, not the parties.

The four are descriptive, I accept. The conceptual work in the thesis is all in the red-cell rule, which is where the theory comes together, so the findings chapter is meant to be read as the evidence base for that rule.

In the counts themselves, which are the concepts, not a step towards them. A figure like 95 of 117 is in effect a theory of binding, because a large enough count turns an observation into a general claim with no further step. Scale converts description into concept, which is how counting works.
questions.why: Strong gives 7.1's conceptual conclusions and their test. The others return to the pillars the data replaced, concede that the findings are only description, or confuse the count (the fact) with the concept it supports.
questions.follow_up: Take 'willingness is a property of a pair of markets'. What observation supports the concept and not just the count?

questions.question: What is your 'exposure term', and why is it part of the contribution?
options: It's the share of parcels exposed to theft or damage at an unattended locker, and it matters because security is the first thing a council must check before it awards a site to any holder.

It's a score I measured for each of the 43 networks, pair by pair, so it proves the gradient P5 proposes rather than merely being consistent with it, which is the core of the contribution. The scores are set out in the locker tables, network by network.

It's the measure of what a holder can expose. One term ranks every class of holder. A receiver costs a carrier only the display, a rival nearly everything the freight reveals. It's among what I claim the literature reviewed didn't have.

It's the cost of the wall, W, in my condition. It matters because walls are what make pooling possible, and the term lets a city price the wall it would need to build between two rival carriers at a shared hub.
questions.why: Strong defines the term as 7.2 and 6.3 do. The others confuse it with W, invent a theft measure, or claim pair-by-pair measurement where commonality was coded by the holder's class and the gradient is untested.
questions.follow_up: Where does a carrier's separated second version sit on that ranking, and why?

questions.question: What does your thesis tell funders?
options: That a grant is a binder and its end is the end of what it bound, so a grant should be written with the binder that will replace it.

That they should fund trust-building workshops between carriers; so arrangements can outlive the grant on goodwill once the money stops. Relationships are cheaper to sustain. Workshops cost far less than grants do.

That they should stop funding collaboration altogether, because every grant-bound arrangement in the record ended when its money did, so grants are wasted. Public money only postpones an ending that comes anyway.
That they should fund only carrier-led pilots, since carriers know their own networks best and pilots led by cities or academics rarely survive beyond the funding period. Others' pilots rarely last.
questions.why: Strong is 7.3's advice to funders. The others contradict the power finding, overclaim (of 21 grant-bound rows, 7 were operating and 8 were pilots still funded), or rely on goodwill the thesis says does not hold arrangements.
questions.follow_up: Give me an example of a binder that could replace a grant.

questions.question: Your title says 'competitive advantage', yet only 14 per cent of your survey respondents name it as a goal. Isn't the title misleading?
options: That's fair; I should have changed the title. The survey shows competitive advantage isn't relevant to collaboration, and keeping the registration's term was a matter of continuity rather than argument, which I'd now regret.

The survey is unreliable on that point. It was a self-selected sample with no response rate, so the 14 per cent can be set aside and doesn't bear on whether the title is apt for the thesis or for what the thesis argues.

Actually most respondents did name it, around 96 per cent, so the title reflects what organisations told me; the 14 per cent is the share who named sustainability as a goal, and sustainability is the term organisations care about most in their own reports.

The title keeps the registration's term, and the findings explain the figure. A saving both rivals receive equally buys neither an advantage; advantage lies in the customer relationship, where sharing stops. So 15 of 107 fits the thesis.
questions.why: Strong links the low figure to the efficiency finding and the boundary (2.7, 6.1). The others concede the title is wrong, dismiss the survey selectively, or misquote it: 96 per cent named cost reduction, and sustainability was named by 77.
questions.follow_up: So whose competitive advantage is the title about?

questions.question: Sternberg and colleagues found that outside facilitators didn't make collaboration work. How is your binder finding different?
options: We reach the same conclusion: outside parties can't help rivals collaborate, which is why the thesis ends by proposing that carriers should stop trying and leave the street to cities.

They studied carriers, not shippers, and I studied mainly shippers; so the two findings aren't comparable, and I don't think their result bears on mine one way or the other. Shippers and carriers face different pressures, so a facilitator's record with one says nothing about the other.

I agree: their data showed no evidence that outside facilitators enabled or sustained collaboration. A facilitator convenes and can't enforce. What survived in my record was bound, not only facilitated: the strong-control case, not the mild control they warn against.

It contradicts theirs: facilitation, not binding, is what my record shows succeeding, because 35 of my arrangements were held together by a neutral third party, which is exactly the kind of outside facilitator they said couldn't make collaboration work.
questions.why: Strong draws the facilitator-binder line of 6.1 and 7.2. The others treat a binding third party as a facilitator, misstate the thesis's conclusion, or get Sternberg's sample wrong: they studied shippers' collaborations.
questions.follow_up: Give me one arrangement in your record that was only facilitated, and what became of it.

questions.question: State your research question, exactly as the thesis puts it.
options: Why do competing carriers refuse to collaborate in European urban last-mile logistics, and how can trust between them be built so that collaboration succeeds?
Under what conditions does horizontal collaboration in European urban last-mile logistics succeed, and what achieves its aims where it does not?
Under what conditions does horizontal collaboration succeed, and can partitioning the last mile in time between operators replace pooling between carriers?
How does a neutral holder of shared parcel points change carriers' willingness to collaborate horizontally in European urban last-mile logistics?
questions.why: Strong is the question of 1.3 word for word. The others build in the trust premise the thesis rejects, revive the time-only answer that was replaced, or narrow the question to the holder, which is the proposed answer and not the question.
questions.follow_up: Which word in that question did you argue over longest?

questions.question: Your question has two halves. Does your final chapter actually close both of them?
options: The first half fully: the second half I'd say is left open for further research, because the holder hasn't been tried anywhere; so Chapter 7 closes the question as far as the conditions go and hands the rest to 7.5. That's the honest place to stop.

Both, fully and finally: the conditions are established by the counts, and the red-cell rule is shown by the locker networks and the scenario to achieve collaboration's aims, so nothing in the question remains open. The scenario's net value and the locker test together leave no part of the question open.

The four findings answer the question. The second half was about Ghent, and Ghent shows that allocating hours by permit achieves what pooling was asked to do, which closes it. Time allocated by permit is the answer the fifth objective asked for, and the holder adds detail to it.

Yes. First half: it succeeds where the parties aren't rivals at the doors, or a wall, penalty or no-stake owner outweighs it, and a binder not resting on goodwill holds it. Second half: a no-stake holder, a vehicle-and-hour rule and a re-checking city, stated as a proposition.
questions.why: Strong closes both halves as 7.1 does, labelling the second answer a proposition. The others leave the second half unanswered, overclaim that the rule is shown to work, or reverse what Ghent's own model expected.
questions.follow_up: If the second answer is untested, in what sense is the question 'closed'?

questions.question: Your aim has three movements. What are they, and where is each answered?
options: Trust, efficiency and innovation, with sustainability folded into efficiency; each movement is answered by a section of Chapter 4, and the survey gives each its scale in 5.3, so all three close in Chapter 5. That keeps the aim close to the registration.

Overlap, binding and the holder, each answered by its own objective, the first, third and fifth, as stated in 7.1, with objectives two and four supporting them rather than answering a part of the aim. Those three carry the aim between them. The others are support.

The conditions of success, answered by objectives one to four; why it so rarely succeeds between competing carriers, which those four answer together, argued in 6.1 and stated in 7.1; and whether its aims can be reached otherwise, objective five.

Literature, fieldwork and policy: Chapter 2 answers the first, Chapters 4 and 5 the second, and Chapter 7's recommendations the third, which is how the thesis is laid out from start to finish. The aim is really a plan for the thesis; so its movements are its parts.
questions.why: Strong maps the aim's three clauses as 1.3 and 3.1 do. The others substitute the pillars, confuse the aim with the chapter plan, or misassign objectives and drop two of them.
questions.follow_up: Which of the three movements is weakest in the evidence?

questions.question: Sub-objective 1A asks how willingness varies with operator size. What's the answer?
options: I couldn't answer 1A from the interviews, because only four speak for carriers; so size is answered by the survey instead, which shows collaboration rising from 20 to 47 per cent with company size. A survey across 109 firms is a better test of size than four carrier voices.

Size doesn't sort willingness. In ten mirror pairs the same firm or kind of firm says yes and no, and what differs is overlap. Willing and unwilling firms appear at every size. Where size sits beside overlap, as in the postal refusal, I record it.

Large firms refuse and small firms collaborate, as my 2022 idea predicted, and the survey's size gradient, large firms collaborating more, confirms that size is the variable that sorts willingness. The data bore out the big fierce animal: the large carrier stands alone because it is large.

Size matters only for small firms, which refuse larger rivals for fear of being taken over; large firms are indifferent to partners of any size, so 1A is answered with a threshold rather than a gradient. Large carriers simply have no reason to fear a smaller partner.
questions.why: Strong gives 4.2's answer with its caveat. The others revive the big fierce animal the data corrected (and the survey's gradient runs the other way and cannot separate size from overlap), invent a threshold, or hand 1A to a survey that tests no link.
questions.follow_up: Show me the pair where size and overlap are hardest to separate.

questions.question: Sub-objective 1C promised a comparison across eleven countries. With one to five interviews a country, isn't it unfulfilled?
options: It's fulfilled: willingness clearly differs by country, with the Nordic carriers the most willing and the southern ones the least, and Table 4.4 sets that ranking out country by country with the rows behind each, which is exactly the comparison and the answer 1C asked for.

The survey covers the country comparison, since its 119 respondents came from the same eleven countries as the interviews, and it shows the same pattern of willingness in each of them. That makes the survey the natural place for 1C.

I state that limit: with one to five interviews a country, the set can't show whether willingness varies by country. It shows refusals and agreements in the same countries, and that what varies is the instrument to hand, closed hours here, a number-plate day there.

It's unfulfilled, yes, and I'd drop 1C from the objectives. A comparison across countries needed a design I didn't have, and the thesis would be cleaner without promising something it couldn't deliver. Better to drop it than to answer it thinly.
questions.why: Strong gives 4.2's answer and its stated limit. The others invent a national ranking, abandon an objective rather than answer it as far as the evidence goes, or credit the survey with countries it never asked for.
questions.follow_up: If the instrument varies by country, why isn't that your finding for 1C?

questions.question: Objective 2: what's pooled, what's withheld, and where does the line fall?
options: Pooled: space, facilities, vehicles and infrastructure. Withheld: customers and operating data. The line runs where the customer relationship begins, and rivals' freight crosses it only where a third party, a reciprocal contract or a reputation system secures it.
Pooled: everything except the brand. The line falls at the livery: carriers will share almost anything, vans, depots, data and freight, so long as their vehicles stay visibly theirs in the street.

Pooled: freight and operating data, which are cheap to share electronically. Withheld: vehicles and depots, the expensive assets. The line falls at capital cost, because firms keep what they paid most for and share what costs them little. Cost decides what is shared.

Pooled: space and vehicles. Withheld: customers and data. And freight never crosses the line under any circumstances; that's why no row in Appendix H shows freight pooled between the parties. Freight is the one line rivals will never cross.
questions.why: Strong is 4.3's answer. The others reverse the line, put it at the brand clause that fell in the second coding, or overclaim: freight is pooled in 10 rows, 9 of them with a binder.
questions.follow_up: Why customers and data, and not vehicles, which cost far more?

questions.question: Sub-objective 3C asks how long each arrangement lasted. What did you find?
options: Durations weren't recorded consistently in the interviews; so 3C couldn't be answered from the record and is left to the deductive study in 7.5, which can measure them properly. Durations need records, and interviews can't supply them reliably.

Those that ran for years are held by something that needs no renewing by goodwill: a trustee and contract for six years, container consortia, a city's asset. Grant-bound ones lasted as long as the grant; those asked to hold themselves, as long as the signatures.

The longest-lasting were those resting on peer trust, which outlived their grants once the parties knew each other, so durability grows with the relationship rather than with any outside device, which is the point of 3C. Once the parties know each other, the binder becomes unnecessary and trust carries the arrangement on.

Every arrangement lasted roughly the same, three to five years, whatever bound it, so the binder affects whether an arrangement starts but not how long it then lasts, and 3C turns out to be independent of the binder.
questions.why: Strong summarises Table 4.7. The others reverse it (no arrangement outlived its binder on trust), claim the record is silent when Table 4.7 sorts durations by binder, or invent a uniform three to five years that appears nowhere in the sources.
questions.follow_up: Is 'lasted as long as the grant' a finding, or just what grants are?

questions.question: Objective five was about time. Your answer is about who holds lockers. Didn't you change the question to fit the answer?
options: It was rewritten in 2026, I accept, and the proposed answer with it; that's normal in emergent research: Trafford and Leshem allow objectives to follow the data, so rewriting it isn't a weakness of the design but a sign of honest research.
Really, time and the holder are the same idea: both share a scarce resource among rivals, one the clock and one the point, so nothing of substance changed between the first answer and the second.

No. The question stayed and the proposed answer changed, recorded as change 5 in Table 3.8. Time split between operators failed: Ghent expected no fall in suppliers' traffic in the open hours. It survives as the vehicle-and-hour rule, beside the holder.

The answer didn't change: Ghent shows that allocating hours works, and the holder was simply added later for lockers, as a second answer beside time rather than in place of it, one for the street and one for the point.
questions.why: Strong separates question from answer and gives the reasons of 3.8. The others concede a change of question that did not happen, blur two different instruments, or misreport Ghent, whose model expected suppliers' traffic to stay the same.
questions.follow_up: Then why does sub-objective 5C already name the holder?

questions.question: What are the four aims attributed to collaboration in 5A, and which does your rule promise?
options: The saving, fewer and fuller vans, lower emissions, a city easier to live in. The rule aims at the last through the vehicle-and-hour rule, bears on fuller vans only where carriers use the point, names emissions as a measure, and promises no saving.

Saving, trust, innovation and sustainability, the four pillars restated as aims; the rule delivers all four, because a neutral holder builds the trust on which the other three depend. Those four are what the field asked collaboration for, and the rule meets them all through neutrality.

The four aims as listed, and the rule's main promise is the saving: the 9 to 30 per cent that realistic pools achieve becomes available once a neutral holder removes the exposure. That saving is what makes the rule worth adopting.

The four aims as listed, and the scenario shows the rule cuts emissions by 28.1 tonnes a year in each council that adopts it, which is its strongest result. Carbon is the measure councils care about most, so that result is what the thesis leads with.
questions.why: Strong gives 5.1's aims and 6.3's precise claims. The others swap in the pillars, contradict 6.3 (the rule promises none of the 9 to 30 per cent), or turn a notional scenario's reported carbon into a result for every council.
questions.follow_up: If it promises no saving, why would any carrier support the rule?

questions.question: Where in the thesis is each objective answered?
options: The first four together in Chapter 4, and the fifth in Chapter 7, where the red-cell rule is set out in full; Chapter 6 is discussion only and answers none of them directly or in part.
The first in 4.1, the second in 4.2, the third in 4.3, the fourth in 4.4 and the fifth in 4.5; Chapter 5 adds the survey, and Chapter 6 discusses all five together before 7.1 closes them.
Each in its own chapter: the first in Chapter 2, the second in Chapter 3, and so on to the fifth in Chapter 6; so the chapters follow the objectives one to one. That symmetry is deliberate.
The first in 4.2, the second in 4.3, the third in 4.4, the fourth in 4.5, the fifth in Chapter 5 and 6.3; 4.7 and 5.4 set each against its evidence, and 7.1 answers the question.
questions.why: Strong repeats the mapping 1.3 gives. The others shift every objective by a section, move the fifth to Chapter 7 when 6.3 answers it, or invent a one-chapter-per-objective plan.
questions.follow_up: Why does the fifth need two places to be answered?

questions.question: You write that the objectives' 'wording is deliberately neutral; their order is not'. Isn't a loaded order a way of steering the answer?
options: The objectives were finalised after the findings, I admit, so they fit the findings by design; that's why the order looks loaded, and I think it's legitimate in emergent research.

The order traces an argument the chapters test, and parts failed: brand and size fell in the second coding, and time between operators didn't survive. Neutral wording lets each objective be answered against the argument, with evidence against counted as deliberately as for.

The order doesn't matter, because the survey tested each objective independently of the interviews, so any steering in the wording was corrected by the quantitative evidence. The quantitative strand was there precisely to check the qualitative one, and it confirmed every one of the five objectives.

It's standard practice: Trafford and Leshem require objectives to be loaded so the thesis has a clear argument, and an examiner should expect a thesis to steer its reader in that way. That's what objectives are for.
questions.why: Strong shows the argument was exposed to failure and partly failed (3.4, 3.8). The others misattribute a rule to Trafford and Leshem, confess to fitting objectives to findings, or credit the survey with tests it never made.
questions.follow_up: Give me one place where the evidence went against the order you chose.

questions.question: 5B speaks of 'the operating instance of time-based allocation in the record'. What is it, and what did it show?
options: Paris, where older vans may not run from eight in the morning to eight at night inside the A86; it showed that windows by hour cut freight traffic in the centre by about a third. Paris is the operating instance 5B refers to. Its rule is long-standing.
Ghent, and it showed that suppliers' traffic fell by 40 per cent in the open window once hours were allocated, which is why time is kept in the final rule as the penalty for staying out.

The Chinese express centre that tenders its operating hours between rival operators; it showed that tendering the clock between rivals works where the city itself holds the tender. Tendering the clock is the instance 5B names, and it shows rivals will share hours when a fair process allocates them.

Ghent, which writes hours into the permit, by category, in law. Its 2016 model expected delivery traffic to leave the closed hours but suppliers' traffic to stay 'the same size' in the open window, and in 2023 it announced the end of the privilege.
questions.why: Strong gives 5.2's reading. The others name a city that regulates by vehicle class and invent a result, misquote Ghent (the 40 and 31 per cent falls are traffic overall in 18:00 to 11:00; suppliers' traffic stays the same), or cite a model outside Europe.
questions.follow_up: Why does Ghent's own expectation count against your first idea rather than for it?

questions.question: Why one research question rather than a set of them?
options: One aim, five objectives with lettered sub-objectives, and a single question the last chapter must close. Objectives one to four answer its first half and five its second, so 7.1 can close it in its own words.
Because the survey could test one question, and keeping one question let the quantitative and qualitative parts address the same thing from two sides. One question kept the strands aligned.

The interviews were designed around that one question, which I put to every participant directly, so it had to stay fixed throughout the fieldwork and the writing; changing it midway would have broken the comparison across all twenty-six.

Examiners prefer brevity: the objectives are really separate questions anyway, so having one headline question is a matter of presentation rather than of design. A single question reads better on the first page.
questions.why: Strong gives the structure of 1.3 and how 7.1 closes it. The others reduce the structure to presentation, credit a survey that tests no link, or claim the question was put to participants when the guide asked about the four pillars.
questions.follow_up: Could the question be closed if objective five were dropped?

questions.question: Sub-objective 3A assesses 'the part played by trust'. Isn't your answer 'none'? That seems implausible.
options: Trust played a part only between shippers, never between carriers; that's why the shipper-led schemes worked and the carrier-led ones did not, and why 3A is answered by initiator. Carriers have too much at stake with each other, while shippers can afford to trust.

A large part, in fact. Respondents rated it highly, 89 of 119 at four or five, so trust is central to collaboration, and the binder is best seen as the way that trust is expressed in practice. The survey is clear on that.

Not none. Trust is what participants wished for at the start, reported after years of running, and placed in a trustee; six of 117 rows rested on their own trust. What the record doesn't show is trust starting or holding most arrangements.

Yes, none. Trust played no part in any of the 117 arrangements, which is the point of the substitution: every working collaboration in the record was held by something outside the parties. That's what the substitution means, taken at its word. Nothing else follows.
questions.why: Strong gives the three roles trust played in 4.4 and the six rows. The others overclaim 'none' (six rows rest on trust), treat survey ratings of importance as evidence of what binds, or invent a shipper-carrier split.
questions.follow_up: Which of the six trust rows worries you most?

questions.question: Objective 4: among whom did you assess power, and where does it sit?
options: Among carriers, shippers and receivers, and public authorities. It sits mainly with shippers, receivers and cities, who set terms, windows and hours; carriers are price-takers, choosing a moment inside what others set.

Among platforms, carriers and cities. It sits with the platforms and brokers, which began most of the 117 arrangements and control who meets whom in the market. Whoever starts an arrangement decides how it runs.

Among carriers, shippers and cities. It sits with the large carriers, who set market prices and decide routes, while shippers and cities react to the networks the carriers build. Scale gives them that power.
Among all parties equally: no one holds the power to reorganise flows alone, which is why every arrangement in the record needed a committee of equals to run it. Shared power needs shared governance.
questions.why: Strong gives 4.5's answer and its three groups. The others reverse it, misread the initiators (platforms began 20, cities and public bodies 42), or contradict the finding that committees of equals did not survive.
questions.follow_up: If carriers reorganise their subcontractors, aren't they powerful after all?

questions.question: Your aim asks why collaboration 'so rarely' succeeds between competing carriers. Where is that answered explicitly?
options: In 7.1, from 6.1: carriers serving the same doors fail the first condition, overlap; as peers with no principal, they seldom supply each other a binder; and they don't hold the power to reorganise flows, which sits with receivers, shippers and cities.

A lack of trust, which the catalogues of barriers list among their first impediments; Chapter 4 shows a lack of trust behind every refusal, and 7.1 states it as the reason, taking the participants at their word.

The aim's middle clause isn't answered directly. It's implied by the holder: once a neutral holder exists, the reasons for the rarity no longer matter to a city. The aim's middle clause was always a way into the holder; so answering the holder answers it as well.

Size: they are too small to gain from it, which is why market concentration is the remedy the literature proposes and the thesis accepts in 6.1, since small carriers can't absorb the cost of collaborating and fewer, larger firms would collaborate more readily.
questions.why: Strong gives the three-part answer of 7.1. The others return to the trust account the thesis rejects, accept the concentration remedy 6.1 displaces, or claim the clause is left unanswered.
questions.follow_up: Which of the three reasons would a carrier dispute first?

questions.question: You bound the research six ways. Why 'urban', and why 'the last mile' in particular?
options: Because emissions per kilometre are highest in city traffic; so the last mile is where the environmental case for collaboration is strongest and the policy interest greatest. That's where a study of collaboration should start. Cities fund what reduces their carbon figures.

Because that's where the GREEN-LOG demand data came from, and those data set the scale of the study from the start, so the boundary followed the data available to me. Practical access shapes every doctorate. That's how it began.
Rural logistics already collaborates successfully and needs no further study, so the urban last mile is the only place where the problem of refusal exists, and the only place worth studying.

Urban, because the refusal I explain is a refusal at the door, and the door is in the city. The last mile, because it's the leg the field's remedy was designed for and where the customer relationship is exposed.
questions.why: Strong gives the reasons of 1.4. The others rest the boundary on data no finding draws on, substitute an emissions rationale the thesis does not give, or overclaim about rural areas, which 6.3 leaves to further research.
questions.follow_up: Your one contradicting transcript is upstream and not urban. Should it count at all?

questions.question: Why include India in a thesis bounded to Europe?
options: It came in through referral sampling by accident; I'd remove it from the counts if I ran the study again, since it doesn't belong inside the boundary I set. Referrals don't respect boundaries, so it slipped in through one contact's network.

To show that the European findings hold globally: the Indian interview reports the same overlap pattern, which extends the claim beyond Europe and strengthens its generality. One comparator outside Europe is enough to show the pattern travels.

As a comparator. Its one interview stands in every count of twenty-six and is drawn on only where the text says so. The boundary is Europe because the regulatory layer the fifth link turns on is European in its density.

India is excluded from all the counts; that's why the thesis speaks of ten countries; it appears only in the participant table, for completeness. Counting it would have broken the European boundary, so it was kept out of every figure.
questions.why: Strong gives 1.4 and 3.3. The others overgeneralise from one comparator, disown a choice the thesis defends, or misstate the counts: the interview stands in every count of twenty-six.
questions.follow_up: Did anything the Indian participant said change a count?

questions.question: Sub-objective 5C asks whether the holder affects whether carriers share a point. Was it answered, given the holder is 'proposed, not found'?
options: As far as 5C asks, it was answered by Ghent's sustainable urban distribution class, which shows a neutral holder at work in a real city for six years, with the city checking it at each change. Six years of access is a long enough test for a holder.

Fully: the locker test establishes the holder's causal effect on carriers' use, and p = .008 leaves little room for doubt; so 5C is the best-answered sub-objective in the thesis. A difference that large, with a p-value that small, is about as close to causal proof as a doctoral study gets.

Not really. 5C was deferred to further research, because a sub-objective about the holder can't be answered until a city runs the rule and the networks are read again afterwards. Until a running scheme exists, nothing can be said about whether the holder affects carriers' use of a point.

Yes, as far as 5C asks. The lockers show a difference by owner class; the 117 support the holder only under rule 1a; nine objections are answered; the limits are stated. What's missing is a test in a running scheme, so it stays a proposition.
questions.why: Strong reports what 5C asked and what was and was not done. The others abandon the sub-objective, read a difference by owner class as cause, or treat Ghent's permit class as the holder test it is not.
questions.follow_up: What single result would make you say 5C had been answered 'no'?

questions.question: How do your objectives map onto your five links?
options: The links were derived from the objectives, which came from the four pillars: trust gave the binder, efficiency the boundary, innovation the holder and sustainability power. That derivation is what keeps the chain anchored in the registration. It's a tidy lineage.

One objective per link: overlap the first, the boundary the second, binding the third, power the fourth. The fifth link serves the fifth objective by a change of proposed answer, from time to the holder, while the question stayed.

Objectives one to four map onto the four pillars, and the five links sit across all of them, so no objective corresponds to a single link in the chain. The links cut across the objectives because each objective touches several of them at once.

Each link serves its objective, but the fifth link serves the first objective, since the proposed holder is what decides whether operators agree or decline to collaborate. Agreement depends on who holds the point. The holder is what decides willingness in the end.
questions.why: Strong gives the mapping 2.7 reports under Trafford and Leshem's tests. The others derive the links from the pillars the data replaced, deny the mapping, or attach the holder to the wrong objective.
questions.follow_up: Does a framework that changed its fifth link still pass Trafford and Leshem's coherence test?

questions.question: Your own 2023 review missed the horizontal-collaboration literature. Why should we trust anything built on it?
options: It missed very little: the one collaboration paper it lacked, Pomponi and colleagues, I added by hand, so the gap between the two searches is small and doesn't affect anything built on the review. So the gap between the two searches is mostly a matter of dates, not of the string.

The 2023 review followed PRISMA and Kmet's quality criteria, so its search was sound; the papers it didn't find were simply not about the last mile, and excluding them was a legitimate scoping decision rather than a blind spot. Scope is a choice. And that choice was a defensible one.

You're right to doubt it. I'd set the 2023 review aside altogether and rely only on the 2026 update, which is the stronger search; the 49 add nothing that the 241 don't already cover. Keeping the 49 only invites questions the update already answers better. A clean break is wiser.

Nothing rests on it alone. I kept the 49 and made what its string couldn't see my starting point. It returns none of the twelve citation-trail papers; with at most eight exceptions, the 2023 review didn't weigh the update's papers and reject them. It couldn't find them.
questions.why: Strong keeps the 49 and gives the test of the string and what the update found (2.2). The others defend a string that returns none of the twelve, discard the 49 the thesis keeps, or misread Appendix F: Pomponi was added by hand and the other eleven were never screened.
questions.follow_up: If the string couldn't see the literature, why keep its 49 at all?

questions.question: What, precisely, is the 'definitional blind spot'?
options: That the field defines horizontal collaboration too narrowly, as carriers only, which shut shippers out by definition; my contribution is to widen the definition so that they can be studied at last. Widening it is the necessary first step for the thesis and the field.

The definition always admitted shippers, 'users, transport providers or shippers', but the models made carriers the decision units and the shipper a demand point, and empirical work inherited that. The typologies never sort by competition or by who began.
Most papers confuse horizontal collaboration with vertical collaboration along the chain, so they count subcontracting between a carrier and its suppliers as if it were collaboration between rivals.

That the field never settled on a definition of horizontal collaboration at all; so each paper uses its own, and the literature can't be compared across studies until someone fixes the term once and for all. That's the blind spot.
questions.why: Strong states 2.3's blind spot: a wide definition read narrowly. The others deny the field has a definition, reverse the point (the definition was wide; the reading narrow), or substitute a different confusion the thesis does not claim.
questions.follow_up: Why would a field read its own definition so narrowly?

questions.question: The two 2026 reviews, of 194 and 133 papers, don't categorise who begins a collaboration. Couldn't that simply mean initiation doesn't matter?
options: No: those two reviews are of poor quality, so their categories carry little weight, and the absence of an initiator category says more about their authors than about the field.

Initiation clearly matters, not because the newer reviews say so, but because the Aloui review found 77 of its 89 studies were about who initiates collaboration, so the newer reviews simply dropped a category that already existed. Aloui's framework of drivers and barriers was built around it.

Absence from a map isn't evidence the ground doesn't matter. Where anyone looked, it did: Browne's surviving schemes were driven by a single commercial enterprise, not a co-operative with conflicting goals, and van Duin's three centres each went the way of whoever began them.

Possibly, and I can't rule that out. For that reason initiation is a secondary theme in the thesis, and I wouldn't want the argument to depend on it; overlap and binding carry the weight. Initiation was always the least developed strand of the argument.
questions.why: Strong answers with the evidence where initiation was looked at (1.2, 2.3). The others concede ground the thesis defends, attack the reviews without evidence, or misquote Aloui: 77 of 89 were models, and only 8 were fieldwork.
questions.follow_up: One study of three centres: is that enough to say initiation matters?

questions.question: How many of the 241 papers name a shipper or receiver as initiator, and why should a count of papers persuade me of anything?
options: Thirteen, from eleven author teams, though the strings named shippers to find them. A paper count measures the field's attention, not the world, and I use it that way. It makes 'under-examined' a count. Practice is tested in the 117 arrangements.

Twenty-nine; the rest name carriers, public bodies or no one. It persuades because it's a systematic count with stated rules, and a systematic count speaks for itself. A count with written rules and a second reading doesn't need further defence in a viva.

Forty-five, about a fifth of the set, which shows the shipper side is studied more than the field admits; the gap is in categorising those papers, not in their number. Public bodies often act for shippers, so their papers belong on the shipper side.

Thirteen, which proves shipper-led collaboration is rare in practice: if it happened often, researchers would have written about it; so the count measures the world as well as the field's attention. Researchers follow practice, so a small count of papers reflects a small count of schemes.
questions.why: Strong gives the figure and says what a paper count can show (2.2). The others infer practice from publication, or misquote the counts: 45 is public bodies and 29 is carriers.
questions.follow_up: Thirteen of 241 across nearly two decades: could the strings still have missed them?

questions.question: Your count of where the power sits in the update assumes your own claim. Isn't your literature chapter circular?
options: On that one count, yes, and I say so. Cards name who a paper treats as deciding, so naming shippers, receivers or cities counted as support; 38 of the 241 verdicts rest on that rule. It shows whom the field assumes decides. Power is tested in 4.5.

It is, and the whole update is circular in the same way, so I'd set all its counts aside and rely only on the 49, which were coded before the working claim existed. Better to lose the update's counts than to defend a rule that leans on the working claim.

No, the count is independent. Each paper's authors stated their own stance on where the power sits, and I recorded it, so no rule of mine entered the verdicts. The cards record the authors' own positions, so the count reflects the field rather than my rule, and it can stand as evidence.

It's partly circular, but supports outnumber contradictions by more than three to one on every link, so even a biased rule can't explain the direction of the result. A ratio of that size is robust to any reasonable change in how the verdicts were assigned. So the bias washes out.
questions.why: Strong concedes the one circular count and points to where the claim is tested. The others deny the decision rule, extend the circularity to counts it does not touch, or lean on a ratio that 2.2 says rests partly on that very rule.
questions.follow_up: Then why report the power count at all?

questions.question: State the trust position you depart from, at its strongest.
options: Trust is built in stages, governed by relationship as much as contract, and contracts can generate the conflict they were meant to settle: Pomponi's staged framework, Wallenburg and Raue, Schmoltzi and Wallenburg. I accept that and ask what my arrangements ran on.

The field assumes carriers already trust each other, so collaboration should come easily; I depart from that naive view by showing how deep carriers' distrust of one another runs. The field's optimism about collaboration rests on that assumption, and the interviews show it to be false.

The field believes trust doesn't really matter and that contracts alone can hold rivals together; I depart from that by showing that trust is what grows once an arrangement has run for some years. Trust, in their view, is an afterthought to the contract that binds them.

That contracts always outperform relational governance, which Wallenburg and Raue showed in their study of logistics cooperations; I depart from it by showing that contracts fail as often as trust does. That's the strongest form of the formal-governance view in the field.
questions.why: Strong states 2.4's position fairly before departing from it. The others set up straw men, or misread Wallenburg and Raue, who found formal governance increases the extent of conflict.
questions.follow_up: Which part of that position do your data actually contradict?

questions.question: Cruijssen, Cools and Dullaert found 50 of 67 providers didn't want an independent third party to coordinate. Doesn't that sink your binder and your holder?
options: It does weaken both, and I'd concede carriers will never accept a third party; that's why the red-cell rule has to be imposed on them by councils rather than agreed. Imposition is the only route left once carriers refuse.

That survey dates from 2007 and the market has changed since, so I don't think it needs answering; my interviews from 2024 are the more current evidence on carriers' attitudes. Attitudes to coordination have moved a long way since then, as the shared platforms show. Their survey describes a different market.

It's the field at its strongest, and I state it so. They wanted control and saw a third party as extra cost. But my binders are mostly outside the parties, and the rule hands no control to a coordinator: no operator is named, and neutrality is checkable market position.

Actually 50 of 67 did want an independent third party to coordinate, which supports my thesis; it was the minority who preferred to remain in complete control. Read properly, the Flemish providers were asking for a coordinator, which is exactly what the binder supplies. Their answer supports the thesis directly.
questions.why: Strong states the objection at its strongest and answers it from the record and the rule (2.4, 6.3). The others dismiss it by date, concede more than the record shows, or reverse the figure.
questions.follow_up: Isn't a council that awards sites just the third party they refused, in another hat?

questions.question: You say overlap runs through the evidence 'like a watermark'. If it's that obvious, how did the whole field miss it?
options: The field relies on surveys, and surveys can't capture overlap between pairs of firms; it took interviews to see it, which is the methodological contribution of the thesis. Surveys ask firms about themselves, never about pairs.

The field did test it, in Cruijssen's Flemish survey, but found the opposite, that overlap encourages collaboration; my contribution is to show that the survey was wrong. The field had its answer and drew the wrong conclusion; that's why overlap needed re-testing in the interviews.

I can't really explain it. I came across overlap almost by accident in the second coding, and I'd rather not speculate on why other researchers didn't see what the transcripts showed me. The data simply showed it. Sometimes a pattern is simply overlooked by everyone in a field.

It didn't miss overlap; it misplaced it. Modellers call customer overlap the source of the gain, once a barrier, but no study I reviewed sets market overlap beside willingness; their unit was the willing carrier. The clues were there in Browne, Gonzalez-Feliu and Allen.
questions.why: Strong places overlap where the field had it and names the unused clues (2.4). The others misdescribe the field (mostly models, not surveys), duck the question, or invent a test Cruijssen never ran.
questions.follow_up: Isn't 'the clue was there all along' just hindsight?

questions.question: What did the 49 studies of the 2023 review actually consist of?
options: Sixteen reviews, twelve models, ten empirical studies, eight frameworks and three reports; so the review was dominated by secondary work rather than by models of willing carriers. That balance is why the review felt so derivative. Models were a minority of the set.

Mostly shipper-led schemes, since the definition admitted shippers, and that is how the review first noticed that the shipper side had never been categorised as such. That's where the gap first showed. Shippers turned up almost everywhere in the forty-nine studies it kept.

Twelve reviews, eight frameworks, sixteen models, ten empirical studies, three reports. Almost every numerical result comes from a model, simulation or questionnaire; in at least 32 no one begins the collaboration. The only measured rounds are Allen's London vans.
Mostly empirical case studies of carriers collaborating, about 32 of them, which is why the review could synthesise strategies for parcel carriers with some confidence about what works.
questions.why: Strong gives Table 2.1 and 2.1's reading. The others turn the 'at least 32' with no initiator into empirical cases, swap the counts of reviews and models (12 reviews, 16 models), or invent a shipper-led set where one card codes a shipper.
questions.follow_up: If most are models, what did the review actually synthesise?

questions.question: The 49 and the 241 weren't selected the same way. Aren't your comparisons between them meaningless?
options: The 241 were also all read in full in September 2026; so they're as strict as the 49, and every comparison in Chapter 2 is like for like. So both sets passed the same full-text test. The comparison between them is therefore entirely fair.

Yes, meaningless, and I'd remove every comparison between them; the two searches answer different questions and should be reported entirely separately. Setting a looser set beside a stricter one invites exactly this question, and the cleaner course is to keep the two literatures apart.

They're directly comparable, not limited, because both runs followed PRISMA and Tranfield's guidance, and a shared protocol makes two sets equivalent whatever stage of screening each stopped at. A shared protocol is what comparability means.

Limited, not meaningless, and I say which kind each is wherever they stand together. The 49 were included after full reading; the 241 retained after title-and-abstract screening and the citation rule, 170 read in full. A stricter set beside a looser one.
questions.why: Strong states the difference and its consequence (2.2, 3.2). The others treat a shared protocol as equivalence, throw away comparisons the thesis qualifies, or misstate the reading basis: 170 full text, 63 abstracts, 8 records.
questions.follow_up: Give me one comparison that survives that limit, and one that doesn't.

questions.question: Why did the 2022 search string fail to reach the collaboration literature?
options: It didn't really fail; the papers it missed were outside urban logistics, and excluding them was correct for a review of the urban last mile. A last-mile review is right to leave the general collaboration literature aside. Focus is a virtue in any review.

It required the phrase 'last mile', so a paper saying 'horizontal collaboration' but not 'last mile' was invisible to it. It returns none of the twelve citation-trail papers and only 39 of the 231 new update papers; 192 fall outside its terms.
Because of the databases: OpenAlex simply holds far more papers than Scopus or Web of Science, so any search run on the older databases would have missed most of the field, whatever its terms.
The date rule did it: it set aside everything published before 2018, and once that rule is lifted, the original string finds most of the collaboration papers without any change to its terms.
questions.why: Strong names the cause 2.2 identifies. The others blame coverage (Culbert and colleagues find OpenAlex comparable to the other two), the date rule (192 papers fall outside the string's terms whatever their date), or deny the failure when nine of the twelve are freight papers.
questions.follow_up: Did the corrected strings introduce a bias of their own?

questions.question: Three of your twelve 'missed' papers are about video games, dairy farms and a growers' cooperative. Isn't that padding?
options: The 2022 string should have found them; so they show just how poor that string was at finding anything outside its narrow terms, which is the point of Appendix F. Any decent string would have picked up a paper with collaboration in its title.
They're padding, and I'd drop them; a test of a last-mile string should use freight papers only, or it isn't a fair test of what the string was written to find, and dropping them removes any doubt.

They show that horizontal collaboration works the same way across industries, which strengthens the generalisability of my findings well beyond freight and the last mile. Three industries agreeing with freight makes the pattern general. That widens the claim usefully.

They aren't part of the case; the claim that the string missed the collaboration literature rests on the other nine. The three name collaboration or coopetition in their titles and test, outside freight, conditions the freight papers raise.
questions.why: Strong states their role as 2.2 does. The others overgeneralise from three non-freight studies, discard papers the thesis uses as limits, or blame the string for missing papers a last-mile string could not be expected to find.
questions.follow_up: What limit does the video-games study set on your boundary of sharing?

questions.question: What does van Duin and colleagues' 2016 study tell you, and why does it carry so much weight?
options: It's the only study comparing who began each scheme. The city's centre lived on a 45 per cent subsidy, the landlord's made a profit, the retailers' broke even after a two-year grant, and carriers joined none. Who began went with how it turned out.
It shows consolidation saves about 45 per cent of delivery costs once a centre is running, which is the figure I use as the upper bound of the saving pooling can bring. That's the size of the prize.

It shows city-begun consolidation centres are the most profitable, because public backing brings them volume, so cities should lead every consolidation scheme rather than leave it to the market. Their subsidised centre outlasted the others because public money doesn't need to make a profit to survive.

According to it, carriers led all three centres successfully, which is the one piece of evidence in the literature that carrier-begun collaboration can work in the city. That makes it the field's best example of carriers taking the lead.
questions.why: Strong reports 2.3's reading. The others reverse the city result (it lived on a subsidy), invent carrier leadership (carriers took part in none), or turn a 45 per cent subsidy into a saving.
questions.follow_up: Three centres in one study: why is that 'the only' comparison?

questions.question: Holguín-Veras is central to your power link. What exactly did he show?
options: That carriers pass on 69 per cent of tolls to their receivers; so in practice the receiver pays and the toll reaches the right party after all, which supports pricing. So pricing the carrier works indirectly, through the receiver, which is enough. The toll still arrives.

That New York's tolls on carriers moved 36 per cent of container traffic into the night, which is the strongest evidence in the field that pricing the carrier changes flows. That result shows what a toll on carriers can achieve. No other instrument came close.
