That carriers set delivery times in 40 per cent of cases and receivers in 22; so tolls on carriers work, because the party who sets the time is the one who pays the toll. So the carrier is the party to price. Receivers follow what they're charged.

That the receiver decides. Receivers set delivery times in 40 per cent of cases, jointly 38, carriers 22; only 9 per cent of carriers could pass a toll on. A toll on the carrier vanishes from marginal cost and never reaches the decision.
questions.why: Strong reports 2.5's figures. The others reverse the shares, credit carrier tolls with PierPASS's result (charged to cargo owners, at the ports), or misread 69 per cent, which is the share of non-movers citing customer requirements.
questions.follow_up: He considered off-hour delivery only. Why stretch him to the whole day?

questions.question: The field's flagship review already warned that joint planning risks 'becoming a victim of competition' and proposed a neutral fourth party. Isn't your thesis just that, restated?
options: No, because they were wrong: a neutral party never works, as Sternberg and colleagues showed; so my rule deliberately avoids any neutral party at all and relies on the council alone. Neutral parties carry too much history with the carriers they once served and the firms they still serve.

Broadly yes: my contribution is to supply the empirical support their idea lacked, through the interviews and the locker networks, which is a legitimate contribution in its own right. That's a fair contribution for a doctorate to make, since fieldwork is what they lacked.

No, because they proposed trust-building between carriers, not a neutral party, so our remedies are entirely different and there's no overlap to answer. Their review is about building trust between carriers in stages, and a neutral party appears nowhere in it, so the comparison doesn't arise.

Cleophas and colleagues diagnosed it, then reached for an operator designed for the purpose, not the shape of the competition, and gave shippers only nudges. My rule names no operator and judges neutrality by how far the holder competes for each carrier's customers.
questions.why: Strong separates an operator designed for the purpose from a holder judged by market position (1.1, 6.3). The others concede the restatement, contradict the rule (which relies on a no-stake holder), or misquote Cleophas, who did reach for a neutral fourth party.
questions.follow_up: What would a 'neutral fourth party' fail on, under your four questions?

questions.question: What's the 'overlap paradox', and where does it come from in the literature?
options: The models put the prize where the interviews put the refusal: Berger and Bierwirth's profit rises about 19, 67 and 155 per cent from adjacent to identical areas. The pairs with most to save refuse, because where saving peaks, exposure peaks too.

That carriers with no overlap gain the most from collaborating, which is why they collaborate and overlapping carriers don't; the models and the interviews agree with each other. That's why the paradox is a paradox only in name: the models and the carriers point the same way.

It's Hardin's term from ecology for species that compete hardest where their niches are most alike, which I carry into logistics as an image rather than as a finding. It names the pattern in nature that the last mile repeats. The term travels well.

That overlap cuts the models' savings from 155 per cent to the 9 to 30 per cent realistic pools achieve; so overlap is what makes collaboration unprofitable in practice. The paradox is the gap between modelled and realistic savings. That gap is the whole story.
questions.why: Strong gives 2.2 and 6.3's paradox. The others misread the two figures, reverse the models (gain rises with overlap), or misattribute the term to Hardin.
questions.follow_up: If the paradox is real, why would any overlapping pair ever pool?

questions.question: What is the field's 'arithmetic' account of binding, and what does it quietly assume?
options: Fair division by the Shapley value and the core: Krajewska's template, Lozano's for shippers. It assumes, unstated, a party to run it. Vargas has a neutral trustee hold the data and execute the gain-share; Wang, Chen and Yu need an operating company.

Zero overlap between the parties is what it assumes, so it can't be applied to rivals at all and is irrelevant to a thesis about competing carriers. Rivals share customers by definition, which the models exclude from the start.

It assumes trust between the parties, which the Shapley value measures as each member's marginal contribution to the coalition's goodwill, so arithmetic and trust are one account, and fairness and trust are the same thing seen from two sides of the coalition.

It assumes carriers are unwilling, so it models refusal and computes the compensation needed to bring a reluctant carrier into the coalition on fair terms; that's the arithmetic's purpose, pricing reluctance so that a coalition can be bought into being by its members.
questions.why: Strong gives 2.4's account and its hidden assumption. The others misdefine the Shapley value, reverse the willingness assumption (the models assume willingness), or deny the overlap that Berger and Bierwirth's models depend on.
questions.follow_up: Who runs the division in your 117 arrangements?

questions.question: You cite the EU's URBANE framework, yet it concluded regulation is the only approach. Doesn't that contradict your demand-side finding?
options: In fact URBANE found that shippers had organised successfully in several European cities, so it supports the demand-side finding rather than contradicting it; it's the clearest support for the demand side in the literature I read.

URBANE's conclusion is right, and I'd concede that power sits only with regulators; the demand side has influence but can't be relied on to act, so the finding should be narrowed to cities, with shippers following them.

It names my mechanism and dismisses it by assumption: if carriers' customers organised, carriers would be forced 'by the market'; it assumes they won't, leaving regulation. My fourth finding includes cities, so regulation is part of it, not a rival.

URBANE is a project deliverable, not peer-reviewed research, so I don't think it carries enough weight to contradict findings drawn from twenty-six interviews in eleven countries. A project deliverable written to persuade funders can't weigh against evidence gathered in the field.
questions.why: Strong reads the footnote as 2.3 does and shows regulation sits inside link 4. The others concede too much, dismiss a source by its genre, or misreport it: the footnote assumes customers will not organise.
questions.follow_up: Where in your record did customers organise and force a change?

questions.question: What does the literature say about time windows as an instrument?
options: That narrowing a window for everyone raises cost and emissions, while aligning windows across cities lowers both. Those windows bind every operator alike; none tests narrowing one rival's window and widening another's. Only a Chinese model tenders hours between rivals.

That off-hour delivery always fails, because receivers won't open their doors at night, so the literature gives no support to any rule by hour at all, and that is why time was dropped from the rule in 2026 and replaced by the holder.

That windows allocated between rival carriers cut traffic in every city where they've been tried, which is the evidence base for the first form of my fifth link, hours given by a city to named companies, and the reason that form was kept.

That cities cooperating to set common windows is itself a form of horizontal collaboration between carriers, which is why Eren Akyol and De Koster sit at the centre of my set of papers on the subject and of the gap I describe.
questions.why: Strong reports 2.5's reading of the window literature. The others invent evidence for hours allocated between rivals, overclaim universal failure (several off-hour studies report positive effects), or confuse cooperation between cities with collaboration between carriers.
questions.follow_up: Then what did you expect Ghent to show that the literature hadn't?

questions.question: Altuntaş Vural and Aktepe already studied who holds networks of collection points. Isn't your holder link derivative?
options: Their study was in Istanbul, outside the boundary of the thesis; so it doesn't bear on a European holder rule and I don't need to distinguish it from mine. A European rule needs European evidence, and theirs isn't.

They found that neutral networks survive best, which supports my holder link directly, so their study is confirming evidence rather than a rival claim I need to distinguish. Priority belongs to them on this point.

Theirs asks who owns a facility network and whether it survives; mine asks who begins an arrangement and how far a holder's rivals deliver into its network. Points surviving where a large provider held them says nothing about rivals' use, which my test measures.

Partly, yes; the holder link applies their ownership finding to parcel lockers, and the locker networks extend their Istanbul case to Europe, which is the contribution, since extending a study to a new continent and a new kind of point is a contribution of its own.
questions.why: Strong distinguishes survival from use, as 2.3 does. The others concede derivation, misreport their finding (points survived where large logistics providers held them), or dodge by geography.
questions.follow_up: Doesn't their finding cut against you: big carriers' networks survive?

questions.question: Name the three gaps and the one issue that Chapter 2 leaves.
options: Overlap, binding and the holder are the three gaps, and the issue is time: no study has tested whether hours allocated between rivals may achieve collaboration's aims. Time is the gap the fifth link was built to fill.

The shipper side under-examined as a category; overlap called the source of the gain but never tested against willingness; and binding answered with trust or a division assuming someone runs it. The issue: rules ask who may use a point, carriers who holds it.

One gap only, the absence of measured results from carrier-begun collaborations; the three 'gaps' are really one, and the shared point is a recommendation rather than an issue. Everything else in the chapter follows from that one absence. The rest of the chapter is only elaboration.

A lack of trust between carriers, a lack of shared data and a lack of funding after pilots; the issue is emissions, which no study has measured directly in the urban last mile. Those are the barriers every review names, so they are the three gaps the thesis fills.
questions.why: Strong lists the end of 2.5 exactly. The others list barriers rather than gaps, collapse three gaps into one, or swap the holder (the issue) for time, which the thesis set aside as hours between rivals.
questions.follow_up: Which gap does the thesis answer least well?

questions.question: The 2023 review's screening was done by you alone. Isn't that a basic failure of systematic-review practice?
options: By me alone, as Table 3.3 says. So the 2026 re-run of its full-text stage was coded twice, every disagreement settled, 30 of 31 agreeing on subject, alpha .91, upholding 29 exclusions; and every update decision was logged with its reason.

No; single screening is standard practice in doctoral reviews, and the guidance I followed doesn't require a second screener, so there's nothing that needs correcting. A second screener would have added cost without changing the forty-nine in any meaningful way. No reviewer would expect more.

In effect there were two reviewers: my supervisors double-screened a sample of it, so the single-screener label in Table 3.3 understates the checks made in 2023, and their sample amounts to a second screening in all but name, and I report it that way.

It's a failure; that's why I discarded the 49 entirely in 2026 and rebuilt the literature base on the update alone. A review screened by one person can't be repaired afterwards, so starting again was the only defensible option left open to me.
questions.why: Strong admits the limit and names the corrective re-run (3.2, E.2.10). The others deny a limit the thesis states, claim a supervisor screening the record does not contain, or discard the 49 the thesis keeps.
questions.follow_up: Two of 31 met the criteria on the re-run. Doesn't that show the 2023 screen was too strict?

questions.question: Your 2023 screening log says Stage 5 eliminated 'those based on mathematical modelling', yet sixteen of the 49 are models. Explain.
options: Those sixteen are simulations rather than mathematical models, so the rule didn't catch them; the distinction is technical, but it holds, and the log is consistent. The log uses 'mathematical modelling' in its narrow sense, so simulations were never within the rule's reach.

It's an error I can't explain from the files, and it means the 49 would need re-screening from the start before anything in the thesis could rest on them. Until that's done, the review can't be said to have applied its own criteria consistently. Re-screening is the honest course when a log contradicts itself.

The cell says that, but the 49 show it wasn't applied as written, and the criteria table has no modelling exclusion. So the 2026 re-run applied the criteria as the table words them and as the 49 show them applied: nothing excluded on a ground one of the 49 also fails.

The sixteen were added by hand after screening because they were prominent, so the Stage 5 rule never applied to them and there's no inconsistency in the record. Hand-added papers are outside the stages by definition, so the rule couldn't have touched them at that stage or later.
questions.why: Strong gives the resolution recorded in Appendix E. The others misstate the hand additions (eight papers, seven of them in the 49), split hairs between models and simulations, or ignore the 2026 re-run that resolved the point.
questions.follow_up: Doesn't applying the criteria 'as the 49 show' make the re-run circular?

questions.question: What does the literature hold in the way of measured results from collaborations carriers began among themselves?
options: None, because measuring a running collaboration is impossible in logistics: firms won't release the data, so the absence tells us nothing about the world; the silence reflects access to data, not an absence of results from collaborations that ran.

About a third of the 241 report a measured result from a carrier-begun collaboration, mostly German surveys of logistics providers working together, which gives the field a substantial evidence base of its own on the question I ask here.

None, across the 49 and the 241. The collaborations that did report results, a Berlin micro-hub, a Taoyuan consolidation centre, shared electric deliveries in Athens, were convened by a ministry, a business district or a funded project.

Several: the Athens case, for instance, measured 35 per cent fewer kilometres from carriers' own collaboration, which is the best measured result in the field so far and the one the thesis leans on most.
questions.why: Strong reports 1.1 and 7.1. The others misread Athens (a simulated shared operation under a funded project), invent a third of the set (the German surveys report no operating result), or overclaim impossibility when eleven of the 241 measured a running collaboration.
questions.follow_up: Eleven papers measured a running collaboration. Who began those?

questions.question: Hariadi and colleagues say competitive pressure is the 'primary catalyst' of collaboration. That flatly contradicts your overlap finding.
options: It's one paper against twenty-six interviews, so it can be set aside; a single contrary finding doesn't need answering in a thesis built on counts across eleven countries, and the weight of evidence on my side settles the matter without any further argument from me.

I accept it, and it weakens P1: overlap may sometimes encourage collaboration; so the proposition should say that willingness 'usually' falls as overlap rises. A softer wording keeps the proposition honest about what overlap does.

They studied video games, not freight, so their finding about competitive pressure doesn't transfer to the last mile, where the shared thing is a street, and a product is shared differently from a street, so their result can't be carried across to carriers.

It's the one flat denial in the update, met in Chapter 6. Competitive pressure is indeed what sends a firm to a collaboration; overlap is what stops it at the door. Pressure is why a firm needs collaboration, not why it agrees.
questions.why: Strong separates the push to collaborate from the refusal at the door, as 6.1 does. The others dismiss evidence by number, concede a weakening the thesis does not accept, or misattribute Le Roy's video-games study to Hariadi.
questions.follow_up: How would you tell pressure and overlap apart in a single firm's decision?

questions.question: Biomimicry? Isn't the biology just decoration?
options: Decoration, mostly: the biology is illustrative, and I'd be content to cut it; the argument stands on the interviews and the locker networks without any images from nature, which help the reader but carry no weight.

No, the biology is evidence. Firms obey the same laws as species; so Gause's experiments show that overlap causes refusal, and the interviews simply confirm in logistics what ecology already proved. Nature has tested the principle far longer than any study could. The interviews only illustrate it.

Two different kinds of thing. The ecology, Gause, Hardin, Paine, is a declared theoretical perspective, held to the same standard as the others, with claims carried by the interviews. The red cell is a labelled design guide, not evidence, as Cornelissen advises.

Biomimicry is a recognised management theory in its own right, not a borrowed image, with its own journals; so using it needs no further justification in a business and management thesis. Its standing settles the question of fit.
questions.why: Strong distinguishes the ecology as perspective from the red cell as labelled design guide (1.6, 2.6). The others treat biology as evidence about firms, give up a declared perspective, or justify it by status rather than fit.
questions.follow_up: Name one claim in the thesis that would fall if the ecology were removed.

questions.question: Why Gause and Hardin for overlap, rather than a management theory?
options: Because management theory has nothing to say about competition between firms that serve the same customers; ecology is the only field that has studied that kind of overlap in depth. Management studies of rivalry stop at the single firm. Ecology goes further.

Hardin proved the principle holds exactly for firms, with known limits, which makes it a safer basis than an exploratory management study of three industries; Bengtsson and Kock offer only an exploration.

Both are used. Gause and Hardin give the principle: complete competitors can't coexist, so carriers chasing the same customers would be expected to refuse. Bengtsson and Kock place the line: competition and cooperation separate by proximity to the customer.

Gause measured firms as well as species in his experiments, so his principle applies to carriers directly, without the translation a management theory would need; his bottles of protozoa were a model of markets as much as of nature.
questions.why: Strong shows ecology and coopetition doing the job together (2.6). The others ignore Bengtsson and Kock, misdescribe Gause's microcosm, or contradict Hardin, who wrote that the exact limits of the principle were not yet understood.
questions.follow_up: Firms choose; protozoa don't. Where does that break the analogy?

questions.question: Hardin himself wrote 'we still do not comprehend the exact limits of the principle'. How can you lean on it?
options: That's why link 1 is a regularity in twenty-six interviews, not a law. I carry the limit: Gause's microcosm had one niche and no agency; firms choose, and the container wall's work is done here by the customer, who can't be in two vans.

Later ecology resolved those limits; so the principle is now well defined, and leaning on it is no riskier than leaning on any established theory in management. Modern niche theory has mapped exactly where competitive exclusion holds and where it fails. The doubt is historical now.

The twenty-six interviews confirm the principle as a law for logistics, which settles the question of its limits in this field at least, whatever ecologists still debate. Twenty-six accounts in eleven countries are enough to make the principle a rule of this industry. Ecologists' doubts don't apply here.

I don't lean on it; the ecology is there as an image, not evidence, and the overlap finding stands on the interviews without help from competitive exclusion. The interviews carry the finding, and the image decorates it for the reader. Hardin's caveat doesn't touch it.
questions.why: Strong states the limit and how it shapes the claim (2.6). The others invent a resolution, deny a declared perspective, or turn a regularity in twenty-six accounts into a law.
questions.follow_up: What plays the part of the 'container wall' when two carriers share a city?

questions.question: What job does coopetition do in your chain, and what's its limit?
options: It explains trust between rivals, how they can compete and cooperate at once on goodwill; its limit is that it ignores contracts, which is why I add Williamson's hostages beside it. Coopetition is, at bottom, a theory of how rivals learn to trust each other enough to cooperate. That is the job it does in the chain.

It does every job in the chain, from overlap to the holder, and has no real limit in logistics, since carriers are the textbook case of firms that compete and cooperate at once. It's the most complete theory in the chain.

It explains the holder, by showing rivals share a point when they cooperate; its limit is that it applies to lockers only, not to vans, hubs or consolidation centres. Lockers are where rivals meet, so that's where coopetition applies, and nowhere else in the last mile. That narrows coopetition to a single, precise job in the chain.

It locates links 1 and 2. The proximity rule predicts refusal at the door, and Scherrer's cities granting space only to collaborating rivals show a city binding them. Limits: three industries in two countries, and Le Roy's finding that where the shared thing is a product, not a street, overlap can be survived.
questions.why: Strong gives coopetition's one job and stated limits (2.6). The others misread it as a theory of trust, break the one-job rule, or attach it to the wrong link.
questions.follow_up: Why is the last mile 'closest to the customer' and not the depot?

questions.question: Le Roy and colleagues found that collaborating with a direct competitor raised market performance. Doesn't that refute your first two links?
options: Le Roy actually found the opposite, that collaborating with a direct rival harms performance; so the study supports my links rather than threatening them. That reading is what makes it useful to the thesis rather than a threat. It's an ally, not a rival, to the first link.

No; it's the boundary in another industry. Their rivals launched a product together, sharing resources and market outcomes, so no customer was exposed and nothing crossed the pooled-withheld line. It measures performance, not willingness: a limit on link 2.

Le Roy's sample was too small to bear the weight, a handful of products, so the result doesn't stand against twenty-six interviews and 117 arrangements. A small study can't outweigh a record built across eleven countries. Scale settles that question quickly.

It weakens them, I accept, but video games aren't logistics, so I set the result aside rather than answer it; a different industry can't refute a finding about carriers. Each industry has its own rules of rivalry, and logistics isn't games, however similar the pattern looks.
questions.why: Strong reads the result through the boundary as 2.6 and 6.1 do. The others half-concede and dodge, misstate the sample (763 video games), or reverse the result.
questions.follow_up: When would a last-mile collaboration be like a joint product launch?

questions.question: How does the resource-based view explain the boundary of sharing?
options: It explains why rivals' freight crosses the line under a binder: a resource becomes shareable once a contract protects it, which is Barney's central point about sustained advantage. Contracts make rare resources shareable, which is the heart of the theory. Barney says as much himself.

It predicts that vehicles are the decisive resource, because they're the most expensive, so carriers should withhold vans and share customer lists, which is what the record shows. Expensive assets are the ones a firm protects. Cost is the best guide to value in a shared depot.

The resource-based view says firms share their rarest resources to build alliances, which is why carriers share depots, their scarcest asset, and keep the commoner operating data to themselves. Depots are scarce in cities, so they're what carriers prize. Scarcity drives the sharing.

What operators pool, space, facilities, vehicles, infrastructure, is valuable but not rare, imitable and substitutable, so sharing gives nothing away. What they withhold, customers and data, is rare and hard to imitate. The line is where Barney would draw it.
questions.why: Strong gives 2.6's reading of Barney. The others reverse it, give Barney a job the thesis assigns to binding, or rank resources by cost rather than by rarity and imitability.
questions.follow_up: Is a customer list really inimitable, when a rival can poach customers anyway?

questions.question: Barney's sustained advantage needs imperfectly mobile resources. Vans and drivers are rented by the day. Doesn't that break your use of the resource-based view?
options: Barney's conditions don't require immobility; valuable and rare is enough, so the rented vans pose no difficulty for the argument about the boundary. Rarity alone sustains an advantage, and rented vans are rare enough at peak. Immobility adds nothing to it.

Vans are imperfectly mobile because they carry the firm's livery, as stated in the visibility finding; so the resource-based view applies to them after all. Livery fixes the van to the firm. So vans count as rare and hard to copy, as the view requires.

It does break it, and I'd replace the resource-based view with transaction-cost economics, which doesn't need immobile resources to explain what firms keep from rivals. Transaction costs explain what firms keep without Barney's conditions. That's the cleaner theory here.

It's the stated limit, and it sharpens the argument. Because vans, drivers and space can be rented, nothing rentable sustains an advantage; the customer relationship can't be rented, so it's what competition is left to be about.
questions.why: Strong turns the limit into the argument, as 6.1 does. The others lean on an unmeasured brand premise, abandon the theory, or misstate Barney's conditions.
questions.follow_up: Can't a carrier 'rent' customers by buying a smaller rival?

questions.question: Why transaction-cost economics, and where do you part from Williamson?
options: Williamson showed trust is unnecessary in exchange, and I agree with him entirely; the binder is simply his hostage under another name, held between the parties, and hostages make trust redundant, as he argued.

For one concept, the hostage: commitment is credible when withdrawal costs more than performance, and every binder is costly to walk away from. I part from Williamson on who holds it: his pass between the parties; mine mostly sit with an outsider.

It predicts rivals exchange hostages directly with each other, and my record confirms it: most arrangements are bound by what the carriers swap between them, with swapped parcels and volumes serving as the hostages in almost every case I coded in Appendix H.

It explains overlap, since rivals with common customers face higher transaction costs, and overlap raises the cost of every transaction between them; I part from Williamson on hierarchy, which he favours as the solution to those costs and which I don't favour at all.
questions.why: Strong gives the one job and the departure (2.6, 6.1). The others give the theory the wrong link, claim full agreement where the thesis parts company, or reverse the record (95 of 117 bound from outside, mostly by a third party).
questions.follow_up: Is a grant really a hostage? Who holds what of whose?

questions.question: What does agency theory add that Ostrom doesn't?
options: Agency theory and Ostrom do the same job, so I use them interchangeably: both are about collective action among firms that share a resource, both describe how a group polices itself, and splitting them would be artificial.

It says what a binder is: a principal, a party that can monitor and sanction. Rivals of equal standing have none unless someone outside takes the role. So the eight arrangements asked to hold themselves failed, and Sternberg's facilitators too.

It explains why agents come to trust their principals over time, which is how a binder turns into trust once an arrangement has run for some years, as the participants described. That's how trust is built under a principal. Agency theory is, at heart, about loyalty.
It shows carriers are agents of the city, so a city can simply order them to share a point; that's the legal basis on which the red-cell rule is built.
questions.why: Strong gives agency theory's job (2.6, 6.1). The others turn it into a theory of trust, deny it a distinct role, or overreach to a power to order sharing that the rule explicitly does not claim.
questions.follow_up: Could a trustee be an agent of the parties rather than their principal?

questions.question: Ostrom's commons are governed by their own users. Your binders come from outside. Isn't using Ostrom a misreading?
options: Her principles fit as stated, without a limit: the eight are met inside the parties in my working arrangements, so they are commons in the sense she meant, and Ostrom's fisheries and city logistics share the same structure of users governing a shared resource themselves.

You're right, it's a misreading, and I'd remove Ostrom; agency theory does the same work in the chain without the mismatch between users and outsiders, and a cleaner chain is worth losing one perspective for.

It's the stated limit; her institutions were made by users, often in 'the shadow of a court order'. I use her principles as a checklist: five of the eight are met in my record, but supplied from outside the parties. That's the extension.

No, because Ostrom argued that outside authorities always undermine a commons, and my finding simply confirms her warning in the setting of urban logistics, where outside authorities crowd out the parties' own self-government and their rules.
questions.why: Strong states the limit and the five principles met from outside (6.1). The others overclaim all eight inside, misstate Ostrom, or give up a perspective the thesis defends.
questions.follow_up: Which of the five is weakest in your evidence?

questions.question: Which of Ostrom's eight principles do you not read against your arrangements, and why does that matter?
options: Congruence with local conditions, collective choice and low-cost conflict resolution. It matters because Appendix H codes one binder per row, not the principles, so they're read by class of binder, and I don't claim the full set.

Monitoring and graduated sanctions, not the others, because no arrangement in the record had either; that's the gap the red-cell rule's test parcels and remedies are designed to fill, so those are the two principles the rule supplies from outside the parties.

Defined boundaries and nested enterprise, because neither applies to a city, only to natural resources such as fisheries and irrigation systems, so city arrangements aren't commons in her sense at all.
None; I read all eight against every arrangement in Appendix H and found each one supplied from outside the parties, which is the strongest form of the claim and the one Chapter 6 makes.
questions.why: Strong names the three 6.1 sets aside and why. The others name principles the thesis reads as met (monitoring, sanctions, boundaries, nesting) or claim all eight were coded, which Appendix H does not do.
questions.follow_up: Collective choice is surely central to collaboration. Why leave it out?

questions.question: The coalition models assume willingness. Why use them at all in a thesis about refusal?
options: To show that they're wrong. Every coalition model fails once it meets real carriers, and Chapter 2 uses them only as the example of what the field got wrong. Chapter 2 sets them up so that Chapter 4 can knock them down. Nothing in them survives the fieldwork.

Because one contains the refusal: Yang, Dai and Ma's core exists only if the saving covers revenue lost to brand switching. I extend it to S plus P at least L plus W. Its limit: it assumes the willingness the interviews deny.

Because they prove that trust stabilises coalitions: a fair Shapley split builds the goodwill that holds rivals together, which is what I call the binder. That's why the arithmetic of a fair split appears in Chapter 2 beside trust. Fairness is trust in numbers.

They don't assume willingness; Berger and Bierwirth model carriers refusing to sell requests, which is where the refusal enters the field's mathematics. Their models include carriers who decline to sell.
questions.why: Strong gives the coalition literature's job and limit (2.6). The others dismiss the models the thesis builds on, turn arithmetic into trust, or misquote Berger and Bierwirth, who assume carriers willing to sell at an acceptable price.
questions.follow_up: What is 'transferable utility', and why can't exposure of customers be paid across?

questions.question: Explain S + P ≥ L + W in plain words, and say where binders fit.
options: Rivals pool when the saving plus the penalty covers the loss plus W, the weight of trust between them; the more they trust, the smaller W and the easier pooling becomes. Trust is the cheapest wall of all; that's why it appears in the condition.
S is supply, P is price, L is labour and W is wages: carriers pool when supply and price together cover their labour and wage bill, which is the cost case for collaboration.
Rivals pool when the saving plus the penalty covers the exposure plus the wall. Walls raise S, grants cut L and permits add W, and trust lowers the whole right-hand side of the condition.

Rivals pool only when the saving plus any penalty for staying out covers the exposure of customers, brand or data plus the cost of the wall that stops it. Walls cut L, grants raise S, permits add P, and the holder lowers L.
questions.why: Strong states the condition and the mapping of 2.6 and 6.3. The others misassign the binders, invent the terms, or define W as trust when it is the cost of the wall.
questions.follow_up: Is the condition testable, or is it true by definition?

questions.question: Why signalling theory, and why for only one finding?
options: It's used across all five links, since every carrier signals quality to shippers, and the signal is what each link ultimately turns on. Quality signals run through every relationship in the chain, from the shipper to the door.

It serves the visibility veto alone. Spence, and Milgrom and Roberts, let me state it testably. A branded fleet is an honest signal to shippers only if it costs a weak carrier more, or gains it less. No one who described the veto had measured that.

Because it proves branded vans win shippers' contracts; that's why the visibility finding is one of the four main findings of Chapter 4. The theory explains why shippers reward branded fleets, and that reward is why carriers refuse to share their vans. Signalling carries that whole argument.

Signalling explains overlap: carriers signal their territory with branded vans, so where two signal in the same street, they refuse to collaborate, which is link 1. A brand is a territorial marker, much as an animal marks its ground.
questions.why: Strong gives signalling's single job (2.6, 4.6). The others attach it to overlap, treat an unmeasured premise as proven and promote a minority finding, or break the one-job rule.
questions.follow_up: If the veto is real but empty as an explanation, why keep it?

questions.question: You invoke Zahavi's handicap, which biologists have largely given up on. Why?
options: The handicap has been shown to hold in logistics by McLeod and colleagues, who found brand identity to be the first barrier to consolidation among the carriers they studied, which gives the image empirical support in freight.

It's cited with its discipline's correction: Penn and Számadó find no support for the handicap, since honesty can evolve through differential benefits as well as costs. So the van is honest only if a weak carrier pays more, or gains less; unmeasured.

I don't cite Zahavi; the thesis uses Spence alone, precisely because the handicap principle has been discredited in its own discipline, and citing Zahavi at all would have suggested I accepted a principle the field has abandoned and that freight has never tested.
It's still the standard model of honest signalling in biology, and the peacock's tail is the clearest image of a costly display that a reader will recognise at once, which is why the thesis uses it.
questions.why: Strong reports how 2.6 cites the handicap with its correction. The others misstate the state of biology, deny a citation the thesis makes, or overread McLeod, who drew the barrier from one company and measured nothing.
questions.follow_up: What would a 'differential benefit' look like for a large carrier's vans?

questions.question: What does the economics of control contribute to the holder link?
options: It proves that neutral holders cause higher use of a point, which is why the locker test can be read as confirming the holder causally rather than by association; ownership theory makes that causal interpretation entirely safe.

It's about who owns the delivery vans, and it explains why carriers refuse to rent vans from a rival that could withdraw them at short notice, since whoever controls the van controls the delivery and the customer at the door.

Grossman and Hart put ownership in residual control; competition policy made that a test of a facility's holder, since conduct rules don't remove the incentive; Chen separates market commonality from resource similarity. Hence link 5's variable: who holds, and what it sells.

It shows that open access is enough to make a point neutral, since the holder's residual control lapses once rivals may use it, which is the basis of the German postal rule and of every access rule the thesis reviewed.
questions.why: Strong gives the eighth body's job (2.6). The others reverse it (ownership controls whatever the access rule says), turn a theory into proof, or misplace it on vans rather than shared points.
questions.follow_up: Chen's two kinds of overlap: which one does the rule check, and why not the other?

questions.question: Eight bodies of theory. Isn't that a patchwork?
options: A patchwork is a strength. The more theories a thesis draws on, the more robust its findings, because each theory confirms what the others say from a different angle, so breadth of theory is itself a form of rigour.

It is, and on reflection I'd reduce them to the four pillars, which gave the fieldwork a single coherent framework before the links emerged from the data; simplicity would have served the examiners better.

Each has one job, none another's: Gause and Hardin overlap, Barney the boundary, Ostrom, Williamson and agency theory the binder, the trophic cascade power, the economics of control the holder. Table 2.2 sets each beside its finding, limits stated.

They're unified because the eight come from ecology in the end, as stated in Table 2.2: coopetition, the resource-based view and agency theory are ecological ideas applied to firms. That common origin is what holds them together.
questions.why: Strong shows the one-job discipline and Table 2.2. The others confuse quantity with robustness, retreat to the framework the data replaced, or claim a false common origin.
questions.follow_up: Which theory could you drop with least loss, and what would go with it?

questions.question: The trophic cascade: what is it, and is it more than an image?
options: It's Paine's term for a change at one level of a food web reorganising those beneath it. Here the receiver, who places the order, not the carrier, is that level. It's read beside Holguín-Veras: the evidence carries the claim; the concept names the structure.

It's the movement of goods down the chain from shipper to carrier to receiver, and the thesis uses it to describe the direction in which parcels travel through the city. Goods cascade down the chain, which is all the term means here. Paine meant nothing more.
It's an image with no role in the argument; the power finding rests on the interviews and wouldn't change without it. Paine's term adds colour, not content, to the chapter.

It's proof that carriers sit at the top of the chain, since they reorganise the flows of every party below them, as predators reorganise the levels beneath them. The carrier is the predator in this web, and everything below the carrier adapts to its routes.
questions.why: Strong defines it and states its role with the evidence (2.6, 6.1). The others misdefine it, reverse the finding, or deny a declared perspective its role.
questions.follow_up: In a food web the cascade runs from the top. Who is the top predator in yours?

questions.question: Ecologists say temporal partitioning is rare. Why did you ever think time would separate carriers?
options: Rare in nature or not, time works for carriers, and Ghent proves it: its permit hours separate operators successfully, which is why time stays at the centre of the rule, with the number-plate cameras enforcing it at every gate.

I carried that limit. Schoener ranks time the rarest axis; Kronfeld-Schor and Dayan tie it to endogenous rhythm, which I read as receivers' opening hours. And time between operators did fail in 2026; it survives only as the vehicle-and-hour rule.

Ecology shows time partitioning is the commonest way species coexist, so it was the natural first form of the fifth link and the strongest of the ecological ideas, and Ghent's permit hours then confirmed it for carriers.
I didn't; time was never part of the thesis, and the holder was the fifth link from the start of the fieldwork, its first form; time came in later, if at all, as an afterthought.
questions.why: Strong states the limit and what became of time (2.6, 6.3). The others reverse the ecology, misreport Ghent, or deny a change the thesis records in 3.8.
questions.follow_up: So what is the 'endogenous rhythm' of a parcel locker?

questions.question: How does your 'big fierce animal' survive into the final thesis?
options: Intact: large carriers refuse because they're large, and small ones share because they have nothing to defend, which the size gradient in the survey confirms, so the image fitted the data from beginning to end.

It survives as the red-cell rule, not as a finding: the big fierce animal is the holder with a stake, and the red cell is the holder without one, which is how 6.4 uses it and how Chapter 6 introduces the rule.

It's discarded entirely, because the data showed size doesn't sort willingness, so the image has no place left in the final argument of the thesis, and keeping it would only have muddied the explanation.

Sharpened. What makes the animal fierce is territory, not size. The large carrier refuses at home, where every door is a rival's, and swaps parcels abroad. Kept where structures match, the refusal; dropped where not: what thins with size is margin.
questions.why: Strong gives 6.4's sharpening. The others keep the size reading the data corrected, discard an image 6.4 keeps, or confuse it with the red-cell design guide.
questions.follow_up: Is a small cargo-bike firm a 'small fierce animal'?

questions.question: Your red-cell analogy: what exactly does it give the rule, and where does it break?
options: It gives the rule its costs: a check per point is priced by analogy with how often the spleen filters each cell, which is where the £400 to £1,500 comes from. That's how the analogy gives the costing a physical basis.

It proves neutral holders work, because evolution has tested the design in the body for millions of years, so the rule rests on the most tried mechanism there is; biology has run the experiment for us, and the rule inherits its results.

Two checkpoints and a remedy: the nucleus pushed out as the cell forms, the check at award; the spleen testing cells in circulation, the re-check on change of control; an inclusion removed, separation. Limits: birds' red cells keep their nucleus, and the spleen holds no hearing.

It's a memorable slogan for the rule and no more; the thesis would lose nothing if the image were removed from Chapter 6, since analogies of that kind belong in a talk, not in a thesis that claims to propose a workable rule.
questions.why: Strong gives what the guide supplies and its stated limits (2.6, 6.3). The others treat biology as proof, invent an origin for a cost built from a council's licence cost and test parcels, or dismiss the guide's role.
questions.follow_up: If a holder can regain a 'nucleus' overnight by a sale, what does the analogy predict?

questions.question: Why these theories and not others? Why not institutional theory or stakeholder theory?
options: Stakeholder theory is in the framework already, under power, and institutional theory under the binder, not left out. Both are present under other names, so the chain already covers them.

Because these are the most-cited theories in the logistics literature, and choosing the field's own theories made the thesis easier to place in its journals and to defend. Familiar theories are easier for examiners and reviewers to assess fairly. Theories outside the field would have looked eccentric to them.

Because each was taken where the data first needed it, not chosen in advance. The first four links were named by the data before by a theory, each needing one job done. Trafford and Leshem's unity test then forbids one theory duplicating another's job.

Institutional and stakeholder theory were both tested in the interviews and rejected by the participants; so they had no place in the framework. Participants found them abstract and unhelpful when I described them.
questions.why: Strong gives the reason 2.6 and 2.7 give: each perspective used where the data needed it, one job each. The others give a reason of convenience, invent a test the interviews never made, or claim theories the framework does not use.
questions.follow_up: Pick a theory you considered and rejected. What job couldn't it do?

questions.question: What does mutualism, the legume host, add to your argument?
options: It's the source of the red-cell rule's name, since the legume host gives up part of itself to feed its partners, as the red cell gives up its nucleus to make room for what it carries.

Partners policed by a host rather than trusting each other: legume hosts sanction nodules whose bacteria fix too little nitrogen. It's an analogy for partner control by sanction, sitting with the economics of control behind the holder principle.

It's evidence that carriers sanction one another in shared hubs, as nodules are sanctioned, which is how the binder works without any outside party. Hubs where carriers sanction each other are the mutualism the analogy describes. No outsider is needed.

It shows that symbiosis rests on mutual trust between partners, which is why I use it to argue that trust grows once an arrangement has run for some years and needs no outside party, host or binder to sustain it.
questions.why: Strong gives 2.6's use of Kiers and colleagues. The others reverse it (policing, not trust), confuse it with the red cell, or turn an analogy into evidence about carriers.
questions.follow_up: In your rule, who plays the host?

questions.question: Your framework emerged from the data. How can theory chosen after the data be anything but post hoc rationalisation?
options: Trafford and Leshem allow an emergent framework if the emergence is shown, and I show the order. The first coding broke the pillars, the second tested the working claim and dropped brand and size. Each concept names what would count against it.

The theories came first, in 2021, and the data confirmed them, so the framework isn't really emergent; I describe it that way out of modesty rather than accuracy, since calling a framework emergent is a convention of qualitative writing that examiners expect to see.

It is rationalisation, I accept, but that's true of all theory-building, so it isn't a particular weakness of this thesis or a reason to doubt the findings; all frameworks are rationalised after the event, mine included.

Post hoc reasoning is normal in qualitative research, so I don't think it needs a defence; interpretation always follows the data, and every framework is built after the fact, so defending mine would concede a problem that simply isn't there at all.
questions.why: Strong gives the shown sequence and the disconfirmers (1.6, 2.7, 3.4). The others dodge, contradict the record (the 2021 framework was the four pillars), or concede a charge the thesis answers.
questions.follow_up: Show me the disconfirming observation for the binder, and whether you found one.

questions.question: How do the four pillars relate to your final framework?
options: Trust became the main binder, efficiency the boundary of sharing, innovation the holder and sustainability power, so each pillar maps onto exactly one link. That one-to-one mapping is why the framework is described as emergent.

The pillars remain the framework, and the five links sit beneath them as sub-themes: overlap under trust, the boundary under efficiency, and so on through the chain. The links refine the pillars rather than replace them. Nothing in them was actually overturned by the data.

Efficiency was rejected entirely as irrelevant, while trust, innovation and sustainability survived as the main drivers of collaboration in the record. The saving moved no one; so efficiency had no role left in the chain. Only three of the pillars survived the fieldwork.

The fieldwork was designed under them, and each became a finding. Trust survived as supplied from outside; efficiency the driver that moved almost no one, since an equal saving buys neither rival an advantage; innovation a facilitator; sustainability a by-product.
questions.why: Strong gives what 2.7 and 6.2 say each pillar became. The others keep the replaced framework, invent a one-to-one mapping, or misstate efficiency, which was the real driver and at the same time no driver.
questions.follow_up: If the pillars were wrong, why keep an interview guide built on them?

questions.question: Why critical realism, rather than interpretivism or positivism?
options: Positivism needs a full list of operators to sample from and a tested measure of willingness; the field has neither. Interpretivism won't hold that markets and binders exist however well they're described. I wanted a mechanism tested against cases that should break it: retroduction.

Because interpretivism isn't scientific and positivism is outdated, so critical realism is the paradigm that produces facts about the world in management research today, not opinions. Facts need a realist paradigm, and this is the realist one.

Critical realism allows statistical generalisation from small samples, which neither of the others does, so it let me claim the findings for European carriers as a whole with twenty-six interviews behind them, and read the locker networks as a sample of that population rather than as cases.

It's the most flexible paradigm: it lets a researcher combine methods without having to justify each one, which suited a staged design with interviews, documents, a survey and statistics drawing on very different kinds of evidence, each read for what it can show.
questions.why: Strong gives the reasons of 3.1 and Table 3.2. The others misstate what critical realism allows (generalisation to the mechanism, not statistically), treat it as licence to skip justification, or dismiss the rival paradigms by caricature.
questions.follow_up: What would a critical realist accept as evidence that a mechanism did not fire?

questions.question: What is retroduction, and how did you actually do it?
options: Coding inductively until themes emerge on their own, without prior theory, and letting the themes stand as the explanation once they stop changing between transcripts. That's the most faithful way to let mechanisms emerge from what participants actually said, without imposing a frame on them. Prior frameworks bias the reading.

Stating a hypothesis in advance and testing it against measurement, which is what the locker permutation test and the survey did for each of the five links in turn. Hypotheses tested against data are what make a mechanism credible to a reader. That's the core of retroduction as I used it.

Reasoning from a pattern recurring across cases to the mechanism that would produce it, then testing it against cases that should break it. So the interviews were searched for evidence against the mechanism as carefully as for it, and the holder set against the 117 and the networks.

Inferring a general law from many observed cases and then predicting new cases from it; that's why the propositions in Chapter 7 are stated as laws for others to apply in their own cities. That's what retroduction means. Laws are what mechanisms become once tested.
questions.why: Strong defines retroduction and shows it in the design (3.1). The others describe induction-to-law, pure induction, or deduction, the modes Table 3.2 sets against it.
questions.follow_up: Give me a case that 'should have broken' the mechanism and didn't.

questions.question: Wynn and Williams give five principles for critical realist case research. Show me each in your design.
options: Events: the arrangements of Appendix H and Chapter 4's refusals. Structure and context: the markets and the cities. Mechanism: overlap and binding. Corroboration: every transcript's second reading and the counts. Triangulation: review, interviews, documents and survey against one another.

Events: the survey's 119 responses. Structure: the four pillars. Mechanism: trust between carriers. Corroboration: Ghent's documents. Triangulation: the two runs of the review, which check each other's results. Each check is independent.

Events: the three locker sales. Structure: EU law. Mechanism: the holder. Corroboration: the 2023 review. Triangulation: the interviews alone, read in two halves by the same coder. That covers all five principles without strain on any of them. It fits neatly.

Events: the twenty-six interviews. Structure: the codebook. Mechanism: the red-cell rule. Corroboration: the scenario. Triangulation: the locker networks read against the survey responses. Each principle maps onto one stage of the design, from the fieldwork through to the final proposal and its scenario.
questions.why: Strong gives the mapping of 3.1. The others assign the principles to the wrong evidence: the pillars and trust as structure and mechanism, a design proposal as mechanism, or one source as triangulation.
questions.follow_up: Which principle does the design meet least well?

questions.question: Describe your four stages and how each fed the next.
options: First, the 2022 to 2023 review, whose blind spot became the gap. Second, the 2024 interviews, coded three times, with the survey beside them. Third, Ghent's documents and the corrected review. Fourth, in October 2026, the 117 recoded, the rules and lockers reviewed, the scenario built.

First the survey, which identified the themes; then the interviews, built on its results; then Ghent as a case study of those themes; then the review, to place the findings in the literature. The survey framed what followed.

First the interviews; then a survey built from their findings; then validation of the framework by expert panels drawn from the participants; then a case study of Ghent's operators and register. That is the design the ethics committee approved in February 2024, and the thesis follows it stage by stage.

First the review; then Ghent; then the interviews, designed to test what Ghent showed; then the locker networks, which were the final test of the time allocation Ghent uses. Ghent came first because time was the first form of the fifth link, and everything else built on it.
questions.why: Strong gives the four stages of 3.1 and Figure 3.1. The others reorder them, describe the ethics application's plan (survey after interviews, expert panels, case studies) rather than what was done, or misplace Ghent and the lockers.
questions.follow_up: Which stage changed the design most, and how?

questions.question: Only four of your twenty-six interviews speak for carriers. Isn't that thin for a thesis about carriers?
options: It's thin, and I'd withdraw the overlap finding until more carriers are interviewed; the other three links can stand on the wider set, but overlap is about carriers and needs their voices. A finding about carriers should rest on carriers' own words, not on reports from people across the table.

Four is enough, because saturation is usually reached within twelve interviews, so four carrier voices inside a set of twenty-six is well within what the methods literature expects for a qualitative study. The methods literature is clear on that point for qualitative work of this size.

Most participants are carriers in effect, if you count the consultants and academics who once worked as operators, so the carrier perspective is better covered than four suggests. Their operating experience counts, so the carrier perspective runs through far more of the twenty-six than the party labels show.

It's the one kind of party I call thin. But the mix was chosen for the question. Who begins a collaboration and what binds it needs those who convene, fund, regulate, study and broker them, who've watched carriers for years, and the coding required evidence against.
questions.why: Strong states the limit and why the mix fits the question (3.3, 3.7). The others lean on Guest's twelve, which the thesis explicitly does not rely on, withdraw a finding counted across all twenty-six, or relabel non-carriers as carriers.
questions.follow_up: Did any of the four carrier voices contradict the overlap reading?

questions.question: How did you sample, and how did you guard against the bias that referrals bring?
options: By snowball from one well-connected contact whose network reached every kind of party; the bias is low because that contact knew the whole field and introduced me to each kind. A well-connected starting point is the efficient way into a small field where everyone knows everyone.

Purposively, for information-rich cases of each kind of party, found through the projects and publications where they'd done the work; then by chain referral. Referrals run along one network, so I started chains from each of three kinds of party, in eleven countries.

Through the survey: respondents who left an email address were invited to interview, which kept the two parts of the design linked and the sample consistent. Linking the survey to the interviews in this way gave both parts a common base of organisations to draw on throughout.

Randomly, from a register of last-mile operators, which removed referral bias altogether and made the twenty-six a representative sample of the industry in the eleven countries. That's the strongest form of sampling available.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.3's sampling and its control. The others invent a register (none exists), start every chain from one person (the bias Biernacki and Waldorf name), or claim email addresses the thesis says were never read.
questions.follow_up: Starting from three kinds of party still leaves three networks. Is that enough?

questions.question: How do you know you reached saturation with twenty-six interviews?
options: Guest, Bunce and Johnson show that most themes appear within the first twelve interviews, a count, not a judgement, so twenty-six is more than double what's needed, and saturation was reached comfortably by the midpoint. That's the standard benchmark cited across qualitative research, and twenty-six clears it twice over.

Data saturation in Saunders and colleagues' sense, 'identifying redundancy in the data': a new participant of a kind described what the set already held. Reached by kind of party, not count, which is why carriers are thin. Guest's twelve came from a homogeneous sample.

Theoretical saturation, not data saturation: no new concept appeared after the twentieth interview; so the five links were complete well before the last interviews were held in September 2024. The last six interviews added no new code, which is what theoretical saturation means. Twenty would have been enough.

Saturation can't really be known in advance or afterwards, so I don't claim it; twenty-six was simply the number of people who agreed to take part in the time available. Claiming saturation would overstate what any study can know. Honesty requires me to say so plainly, here and in the methods chapter.
questions.why: Strong names the kind of saturation and how it was judged (3.3). The others rest on Guest, whom 3.3 sets aside, claim theoretical saturation the thesis does not claim, or abandon the question.
questions.follow_up: If carriers didn't saturate, why is overlap a finding rather than a hypothesis?

questions.question: Malterud and colleagues' 'information power': how does your study score on it?
options: The need was low on all five; so in principle ten interviews would have sufficed, and twenty-six gives a large margin of safety for every finding in Chapter 4. Those dimensions together mean the set is comfortably large for every claim in the thesis, including the holder and its tests.

Low need on four dimensions: a narrow aim; participants chosen for having convened, funded, regulated, brokered or refused the very thing; coding against a stated framework; strong dialogue, 16 of 26 running forty minutes or more. Higher on one: the analysis runs across cases.

The need was high on each of the five dimensions, as I stated in the design, because the topic is broad and the participants varied; that's why I interviewed thirty people rather than the usual dozen or so. A varied set needs more voices.

Information power may not apply under critical realism, which judges a sample by the mechanism it reveals rather than by a count or the quality of its participants. Counts of participants belong to other paradigms, not to a realist one concerned with mechanisms. The paradigm decides the sample.
questions.why: Strong reports 3.3's assessment, including the one dimension where need was higher. The others reverse it, dodge it, or overclaim low need on every dimension when the analysis runs across cases.
questions.follow_up: Sixteen of twenty-six ran forty minutes. What about the other ten?

questions.question: The guide planned 45 to 60 minutes. Your median was 43, and one interview lasted 8. Does that weaken the data?
options: It would have, so I excluded A5 and the other short interviews from the counts; that's why some of the counts in Chapter 4 are out of fewer than twenty-six. Short interviews carry too little to count, so leaving them out protects the counts from thin evidence. The counts are firmer for it.

Length doesn't matter in qualitative research; a short interview can be as rich as a long one, so I don't treat the lengths as relevant to the strength of the evidence at all. Depth comes from the participant's experience, not from the minutes on a recording. Experts get to the point quickly.

They ran 8 to 74 minutes, 20 hours 5 minutes in all, median 43; 16 of 26 ran forty minutes or more. Most that closed early did so because the person had said what they came to say. The shortest, A5, is flagged as thin, and no finding rests on it.

No, because the median was 60 minutes, at the top of the planned range; the eight-minute call was a technical failure, and that participant later completed the interview in writing. The written answers filled the gap, so no interview was lost to the analysis.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.3's figures and how the short interview is handled. The others misquote the median and invent a written completion, contradict the rule that every transcript stays in every count of twenty-six, or wave length away.
questions.follow_up: Why keep A5 in the denominator if no finding rests on it?

questions.question: You interviewed, you coded first, and you wrote the claim. Isn't the analysis just you agreeing with yourself?
options: That exposure no procedure removes, and I name it. My answer: two later codings without the first's notes; halves coded separately; evidence against required; every transcript re-read blind, 112 of 130 stances the same. And the second coding threw out my own brand and size clauses.

Written criteria remove the exposure: every coding followed them, and once the rules are written down, who applies them makes no difference to the result, so my expectations couldn't enter. That's the whole point of writing them down.

No, because an independent second coder agreed with me on all 130 stances, which rules out my expectations shaping the counts in any of the five concepts. That level of agreement leaves no room for the interviewer's expectations to enter. The agreement figures speak for themselves here.

It's unavoidable in a doctorate with one researcher, and the reader has to take the analysis on trust; that's true of every single-author qualitative thesis, and examiners accept it as a condition of the degree. Mine is no exception.
questions.why: Strong names the exposure and the controls (3.4, 3.7). The others deny an exposure the thesis names, give up on controls, or misquote the agreement (112 of 130) and invent an independent coder.
questions.follow_up: If brand fell, why did you raise it in five interviews in the first place?

questions.question: Why code the transcripts three times? What did each coding do?
options: The first coding was of the survey, the second of the interviews and the third of the Ghent documents; so 'three codings' means three sources read against one codebook. Each source got its own coding pass.

The first coding was against the five-concept codebook, the second against the working claim, and the third under the four pillars, as a final check that the pillars still held. Ending with the pillars confirmed that the original framework still held at the end of the analysis.

Three different coders each coded the full set once, and the three sets of codes were compared, which is where the agreement of 112 of 130 stances comes from. Three coders gave three independent views of every transcript, which is the standard for reliability. Each worked alone.

The first, under the guide's four headings, broke the pillars and gave the working claim. The second, in 2026, tested that claim against the transcripts alone, evidence for and against: brand and size fell. The third coded against the rewritten codebook, each half twice.
questions.why: Strong gives the sequence of 3.4. The others invent three coders, confuse codings with sources, or reverse the order, which matters because each coding tested the one before.
questions.follow_up: Why test the working claim rather than code straight against the five concepts?

questions.question: Why raw agreement for the transcripts but Krippendorff's alpha for the arrangements?
options: Cohen's kappa was used for both, and the thesis reports it as alpha for the arrangements only because that's the convention in operations research journals. The two measures are near enough the same that the label makes no difference to the result.

Because alpha came out too low on the transcripts, so I reported raw agreement instead, which is the usual fallback when a coefficient is disappointing in a small set; raw agreement looks better there, and that's a perfectly legitimate reason to choose it over alpha for transcripts.

With four stances, thirteen transcripts a half and a fifth concept mostly silent, a coefficient says less than listing the eighteen differences, as Table 3.6 does. For the 117 the unit is the arrangement, the codes nominal, the cases 117: alpha fits, against .800 and .667.

Raw agreement is always the better measure, being easier to read; I'd have used it for the 117 arrangements too if the analysis software had allowed, since a percentage is what every reader understands, so it should be the default measure in any thesis.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.4's reasons for each measure. The others imply a coefficient was hidden, misstate the measures (kappa is used only for the survey's open answers), or claim raw agreement is always better.
questions.follow_up: What would a chance-corrected coefficient have shown on time, where nineteen are silent?

questions.question: Eighty-six per cent raw agreement over four categories, many of them 'silent'. Isn't that inflated by silence?
options: 86 per cent is above Krippendorff's bar of .800 for firm conclusions, so even allowing for silence the agreement on the transcripts is firm. Krippendorff's bar is the standard any coder is judged against.

Silence could flatter it, and time shows where: 25 of 26 agree on time, with nineteen silent in each reading. That's why I give the eighteen differences by concept and transcript rather than one coefficient. They fall on twelve transcripts, five of them on B8 and B10.

No, because silent stances were excluded before agreement was computed, so the 86 per cent is agreement on substantive stances only, with silence playing no part in it; most codebook studies report agreement in that way, and it's the conventional treatment of a stance that says nothing.

Yes, considerably; once silence is removed the true agreement is nearer 50 per cent, which I report in Appendix I as the more honest figure alongside the headline. The lower figure is the one a careful reader should use.
questions.why: Strong concedes the risk, shows where silence flatters the figure and lists where the differences fall (3.4, Table 3.6, Table 5.10). The others misdescribe the computation, invent a 50 per cent figure found nowhere in the sources, or compare raw agreement with a bar set for alpha.
questions.follow_up: Which concept would you trust least on the agreement figures, and why?

questions.question: What does 'directed content analysis' mean for your coding of the 117 arrangements?
options: Hsieh and Shannon's form: a written codebook fixed each variable's values and decision rule, and each code came from the row of Appendix H and its passage in the transcript, quotation recorded. Piloted on ten rows; version 3 separated the holder; each version coded twice.

Automatic counts of keywords in each row, so that the frequency of words like 'neutral' or 'contract' set each code without any interpretation by the coder, which removes the coder's judgement from the codes altogether and makes them perfectly repeatable.

Open coding without a codebook, letting categories emerge from each row and then grouping them into variables once all 117 had been read and compared. A codebook would only have imposed my expectations.

A single pass by hand through the 117 rows against a short list of themes, with the resulting codes then checked against the interview counts for consistency; one careful pass is enough when the themes are clear from the start.
questions.why: Strong describes 3.4 and Appendix L. The others describe open coding, keyword counting, or a single pass, none of which matches a written codebook coded twice in two versions.
questions.follow_up: Why pilot on ten rows rather than code all 117 at once?

questions.question: Some of your version 2 alphas are poor: the penalty at .54, the flows at .55. Why should I trust results built on those?
options: I report them as below the bar, pass by pass, unmerged. The results I lean on use the firm codes: holder class .88, rivalry among co-users .85, neutral holder .84, market commonality .84. And the penalty never splits the passes among rivals not far from the customer.

Both are above Krippendorff's tentative bar of .667, so tentative conclusions are justified, and I draw nothing firmer than that from either of the two codes. Tentative conclusions are what those two codes support, and that's how I use them in Chapter 4. Chapter 4 never leans on them.

Alphas below .800 are normal in qualitative coding and need no special handling; I treat all the version 2 codes alike, whatever their agreement. Low agreement is normal for codes like these, and no reader expects otherwise in qualitative work. I see no reason to treat them differently.

I re-coded the penalty and the flows until both reached .800, so the final codes are firm even though the first passes were not. Re-coding until the bar was met is how the codes were made firm enough to use.
questions.why: Strong reports the weak codes honestly and says where the results rest (3.4, Appendix L). The others misplace .54 and .55 above the .667 bar, ignore the bar, or describe recoding until agreement, which the record does not contain and which would be fishing.
questions.follow_up: If flows is at .55, how can 'thin flows' be a condition in your analysis?

questions.question: Why crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis, and with what thresholds?
options: Because the question is which conditions are present wherever an outcome is. Crisp-set, at conventional thresholds: sufficiency 0.8, re-run at 0.75 and 0.9; necessity 0.9, nine in ten running rows. Checked by dropping each case and recoding helpers and public bodies as never neutral.

Because it gives significance levels for small samples. I took necessity at 0.8 and sufficiency at 0.9, the stricter bar for sufficiency because sufficiency is the stronger claim of the two, and that ordering protects the stronger claim.

It handles fuzzy membership, so each arrangement was scored from 0 to 1 on every condition, with 0.5 as the crossover point for presence, capturing the degrees of presence that a yes-or-no code would simply lose in rows like these.

It lets the researcher choose thresholds after seeing the data; I set necessity at 0.86 so that the holder result could be reported as met, and choosing thresholds that way is accepted practice in the method when cases are few.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.4's reasons, thresholds and checks. The others claim significance testing and swap the thresholds, describe fuzzy sets, or misstate the record: without rule 1a the holder is 0.86 and is reported as below the bar.
questions.follow_up: Why should necessity need a higher bar than sufficiency?

questions.question: Your holder result depends on a coding rule added after you saw the results. Isn't that circular?
options: It would be if hidden. Rule 1a codes a scheme-running trustee as holder and its hired operator as helper; without it, the tie-break left the trustee coded nowhere in the three trustee-network rows. With it, 9 of 10 running rows; without, 6 of 7, below the bar. Both reported.

Yes, it's circular, so I'd drop the holder from the thesis entirely and close the question with the four findings alone, since a result that depends on a rule written after the results shouldn't be in a thesis at all.

It isn't circular, because rule 1a was in the codebook from the start; it appears late in the record because the trustee rows happened to be coded last. The record makes it look late, but the rule itself was there from the first row.

The rule doesn't change any result: the holder meets the bar with or without it, so the timing of the rule is irrelevant to what the thesis claims; the trustee rows are only three of the 117, too few to move any result in either replication.
questions.why: Strong states the rule, why it was added and both results (4.4, 3.7, Appendix L). The others deny the timing, deny the effect (three rows change and the count falls to 6 of 7), or abandon the second half of the answer.
questions.follow_up: Why is a trustee that hires an operator really the holder, and not the operator?

questions.question: What do you mean by 'replication' in the comparative analysis?
options: Each version 2 pass was paired with a version 3 pass, and the two pairs were run separately, not merged, so a result had to hold in both: rival or joint holders running in 5 of 8 rows and 5 of 7, for instance.

Repeating the analysis on a fresh sample of 117 arrangements drawn from the literature, not the interviews, to confirm the interview results in an independent set. A fresh sample from the literature tests whether the result travels beyond the interviews. And it did travel, which strengthens the holder.

Running the same data through the software twice to check that it gives identical output, which it did in every case; so the results are replicated. Identical output on a second run confirms the analysis and its coding.

Coding by two different people in two countries, each with their own codebook, not one shared, whose results were then compared and reconciled. Independent coders with their own codebooks are the strongest form of replication, because no rule is shared between them. That's what replication means in this method.
questions.why: Strong describes 3.4's two pairs of passes. The others describe a software rerun, invent two coders and two codebooks, or invent a second sample.
questions.follow_up: If the two replications disagreed on a result, what would you report?

questions.question: Ghent is one city. One city is thin evidence for a rule.
options: I studied Ghent as a full case study, not a document analysis, with its operators and its permit register as well as its plans; so the evidence is deeper than one city might suggest. Reading the operators confirmed what the plans said about the regime.

Ghent is representative of mid-sized European cities, so what its regime shows can be generalised to the others, which is why one city is enough for the purpose here. What holds in Ghent will hold in cities like it across the continent. Mid-sized cities face the same freight problems wherever they are.

One city is enough when the effect is as large as Ghent's: delivery traffic fell sharply in every window after the plan took effect in 2017. An effect of that size speaks for itself, whatever the number of cities.

It isn't offered as proof. Ghent is the one European city brought to my notice that writes hours into the permit, by category, in law. Its plans, read as a document analysis, give the vehicle-and-hour rule its instrument, conditions and costs, not its proof; neither counts deliveries by window.
questions.why: Strong states what Ghent is used for and not used for (3.5, 5.2). The others overgeneralise, claim operators and a register the thesis did not read, or invent a measured fall the plans never counted.
