questions.follow_up: Then what would it take to test the rule by vehicle and hour properly?

questions.question: Scott sets four tests for documents. How did the Ghent plans pass them?
options: Authentic, credible, representative of what happened on the street, not just of the plans, and meaningful, because the permit counts in the 2023 plan confirm the 2016 expectations. The two plans together show the regime working as the city intended.

Authentic because a Dutch speaker verified them; credible because the city is a public body; representative of all Belgian cities; and meaningful because they were read in an official English translation. That covers all four tests at once. Nothing in Scott's list is left unaddressed.

Authentic: the city's own plans, held as the PDFs Appendix J reproduces. Credible as the regime's statement of what it allocates and expected, not of the street. Representative of the written record, not the regime. Meaning held by setting each extract beside its rendering.

They passed all four by being peer-reviewed: Amaral and colleagues and later authors had already published on the plan, which settles authenticity and credibility together. Published scholarship is the best test of a document's standing, better than any check of my own. Scott's tests add little to that.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.5's reading of Scott. The others invent a Dutch speaker and an official translation, confuse later scholarship with document tests, or claim the plans show the street and report counts they do not.
questions.follow_up: Which of the four tests is weakest for the 2023 plan?

questions.question: You don't speak Dutch. How can we trust your renderings of the Ghent plans?
options: A Dutch-speaking colleague checked every rendering against the original, so the translations can be taken as reliable even without the Dutch printed beside them. That check is why the renderings can stand on their own without the originals. Appendix J is there for the record.

Translation accuracy matters little for a document analysis, since the argument rests on the city's figures, which are the same in any language, not on its wording. Figures don't need translating, and they're what the argument actually uses from the plans. Wording is secondary for this purpose.

I worked only from the English summaries the city publishes alongside its plans, so no translation of my own was needed for any of the extracts. The city's own summaries are the safest source of what it meant by its plans. Translation of my own only adds risk to the reading.

Each rendering was checked against the Dutch, a second translation made independently of the first, and a dictionary. No Dutch speaker checked them, which I carry as a limit, so every extract sits in Dutch beside the English. The reader has the last word.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.5's checks and the stated limit (7.4). The others invent a Dutch speaker, wave translation away when key quotations are words (the 'same size' passage), or invent English summaries.
questions.follow_up: One word, venstertijd, flips meaning between the plans. How did you catch it?

questions.question: Your survey asks about the four pillars, not your links. Why include it?
options: It tests links 3 and 4 statistically, since its trust items and its question on partners measure binding and power directly across 119 organisations. That's what a survey run alongside interviews is for: testing what the interviews find.

For scale only. It opened on the day of approval, before the interviews produced the links, so it asks what the guide asked: no significance test, no population inference, no link tested. It sets what organisations say about trust beside what they use.

It's the main evidence for the binder: 119 organisations are a larger base than twenty-six interviews, so the survey carries the weight on what holds arrangements together, and the interviews supply the illustrations that bring its figures to life.

It validates the framework, as the ethics application planned: respondents' answers confirm each of the five links in turn, which the interviews alone couldn't do. Validation by respondents is the quantitative half of the design, as the application set out.
questions.why: Strong states the survey's limited role (3.6, 3.8). The others credit it with tests, validation or evidential weight that 3.6 explicitly denies.
questions.follow_up: Then what would you lose if the survey were removed?

questions.question: A self-selected sample with no response rate. Isn't the survey worthless?
options: Self-selection was corrected by weighting the responses by company size, so the survey's percentages reflect the industry, not my networks; weighting is standard practice for industry surveys of this kind and removes the bias a self-selected sample may bring.

No, because the response rate was high: 119 of 132 responses were usable, about 90 per cent, which is strong for an industry survey and supports the percentages I report, since few industry surveys do better.

Worth scale, not inference. A non-probability sample along my networks: no response rate can be computed, none claimed; no significance test; respondents may include interviewees. It sets what 119 organisations say about trust beside what the 117 arrangements show.

Worthless, yes; I include it only because the ethics application required a quantitative part, and I'd cut it from a revised thesis altogether, since it adds little to the argument the interviews make.
questions.why: Strong states what the survey is worth (3.6). The others mistake the usable share for a response rate, disown a part the thesis uses, or invent a weighting never applied.
questions.follow_up: Who, plausibly, chose to answer, and how might that tilt the trust ratings?

questions.question: Your ethics application promised correlation and regression on the survey. Why didn't you run them?
options: Regression isn't permitted under critical realism, which rejects statistical inference; so the paradigm ruled it out once I had adopted it. Statistics belong to positivism, which the thesis rejected at the outset.

The analysis software available to me couldn't handle the items that allowed several answers, so regression wasn't feasible on this form. A different tool would have made regression possible on the same data.

Because the sample selected itself through my networks, and a self-selected sample supports no estimate beyond itself, as Fowler says. So it's read in counts and cross-tabulations. The plan is reproduced in Appendix C, and the change recorded as change 2.

I ran them, but nothing came out significant, so I left the results out and reported the descriptive tables instead, which are easier for a reader to follow; non-significant results add nothing for a reader, so omitting them is normal practice.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.6's reason and where the change is recorded. The others describe unreported analyses (which the record does not contain and would be selective reporting), blame software, or misstate the paradigm, which uses statistical tests elsewhere in the design.
questions.follow_up: Is a cross-tabulation by company size not already an inference?

questions.question: Why OpenAlex for the update, rather than the four databases of 2022?
options: Reproducibility: anyone can rerun a search on a public index; four databases behind logins allow it only for subscribers. Culbert and colleagues find OpenAlex's coverage comparable to Web of Science and Scopus, with fewer abstracts, so doubtful records got a second pass.

Coverage: OpenAlex holds far more papers than Scopus or Web of Science, so a single index could replace four databases with better coverage than all of them together, and a bigger index means a fuller search.

OpenAlex carries a full abstract for every record, unlike the subscription databases, which made title-and-abstract screening more reliable than in 2023 and a second pass on doubtful records unnecessary for any of the six strings.

Because my institutional access to the subscription databases had lapsed by 2026, so an open index was the only practical option for the update, and OpenAlex was the obvious replacement once the subscriptions had gone and the four databases with them.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.2's criterion and evidence. The others overclaim coverage (comparable, not greater), invent a practical reason, or reverse the abstracts point (OpenAlex carries fewer).
questions.follow_up: If OpenAlex has fewer abstracts, didn't your screen miss papers?

questions.question: What is the thirty-citation rule, and why did you adopt it?
options: In the update, a paper published before 2018 was kept only if cited thirty times or more. The 2023 review kept earlier papers by judgement; a threshold anyone can apply better meets Tranfield and colleagues' demand that a review be transparent and reproducible.
It kept the set below 250 papers, which was the most I could card in the time available before submission; so it's a practical limit rather than a principle. Time limits shape every review.

Every paper with fewer than thirty citations was excluded whatever its date, to keep the set to work the field had already taken up and tested in its own citations. Citations show which papers the field has already tested and found worth using. Older papers needed the same test.

It's OpenAlex's default filter for older records, so I applied it as the index presents it rather than setting a rule of my own for the update. Using the index's own filter keeps the search reproducible for anyone who runs it. Defaults are the easiest thing for anyone to repeat.
questions.why: Strong states the rule and its reason (3.2). The others apply it to every date, attribute it to the index, or give a motive the thesis does not state.
questions.follow_up: Doesn't a citation threshold favour old, popular work and the field's own blind spot?

questions.question: You re-ran the 2023 full-text stage. What prompted it, and what was the result?
options: The 2023 stage had lost its files, so I re-ran it from the 860 records, which produced a new set of 49 that happened to match the old one exactly. Starting again from the records was the cleanest course. Nothing else would have been defensible to an examiner.

A reviewer asked for it. The re-run found 27 exclusions standing and 4 papers that might meet the criteria, which were then added to the review, making 53 studies. Reviewers often ask for this, and it strengthened the record. The review is now complete at 53.

The 2023 record gave exclusion reasons by topic, and PRISMA 2020 asks for reasons per study that might seem eligible. So 31 candidates were coded twice against the 2023 criteria: 29 exclusions stand, 2 meet them, neither a kind the 49 lack; alpha .91.

PRISMA requires every stage to be re-run in any update. The re-run confirmed all 31 exclusions; so the 2023 stage was shown to be faultless after all. A clean re-run is the best outcome a review can hope for. It closes the question for good, as far as I can see.
questions.why: Strong gives the reason and the result of 3.2 and E.2.10. The others invent a reviewer and misquote the result (29 stand, 2 meet, none added), overstate both PRISMA and the outcome, or describe a re-run from 860 records that never happened.
questions.follow_up: Two papers met the criteria. Why not add them to the 49?

questions.question: What's your unit of analysis, and why not the firm?
options: The firm, because firms make the decisions; the arrangements are how I describe what each firm did, but the conclusions are about carriers as organisations. Firms are what the findings ultimately describe, carrier by carrier.

The interview, because each transcript is one testimony, and the counts in Chapter 4 are counts of transcripts rather than of anything else. Each testimony is one case, so the interview is the natural unit for every count.

The collaborative arrangement: each observed or attempted collaboration, by overlap, what was shared and what bound it. Willingness concerns a pair of markets and binding an arrangement; neither is a property of a firm.
The city, because the power to reorganise flows sits with cities; so each city's arrangements form one case for the analysis. Cities make natural cases.
questions.why: Strong gives 1.4. The others make the firm the unit, confuse a unit of counting (the transcript) with the unit of analysis, or make the city the unit.
questions.follow_up: If the unit is the arrangement, why count stances by transcript at all?

questions.question: You count transcripts and you count rows. Why two units, and how do you avoid counting things twice?
options: Rows are unique schemes, because duplicates were merged when Appendix H was built; so there's no double counting anywhere in the 117. Merging duplicates is standard practice when building a table of cases from interviews.

A transcript is one testimony, so stances are counted by transcript: saying a thing three times is saying it once. Arrangements are counted by row, one per description, so a scheme two people described is two rows. The A half's 56 rows hold 51 to 52 schemes.
Each scheme is counted once, under the first participant who described it, so 117 is the number of distinct arrangements in the record. Counting each scheme once avoids inflating the binder counts.

I count mentions across all transcripts rather than transcripts themselves, which gives more statistical power and avoids losing what a participant chose to repeat. Counting mentions also captures emphasis, which matters when a participant keeps returning to the same point. A transcript count would throw away much of what was said.
questions.why: Strong gives the two units of 3.1 and 3.4 and the row rule. The others count mentions, or claim the 117 are distinct schemes when a scheme described twice is two rows.
questions.follow_up: Does counting accounts rather than schemes inflate the 95?

questions.question: How did you code the owners of the 43 locker networks, and how reliable was it?
options: Each owner was coded twice, with alpha .91 on the class and .80 on neutral against rival-held, over 43 periods, one for each network in the review. Both are firm on any bar, so no further coding of the owners was needed after that.

Each owner was coded twice, independently, as neutral or by the kind of rival holding it: alpha .87 on class and .81 on neutral against rival-held, over 47 ownership periods, a network sold in the window counting once per owner.

The carriers coded the owners themselves, through a short questionnaire asking which networks they regarded as neutral and which as a rival's. Carriers know best which holders they trust with their parcels.

Each owner was coded once, from the network's own website, since ownership is a matter of public record and needs no second reading to be reliable. Public ownership records are unambiguous and need no second coder. A second coder would only repeat the first.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.5's coding. The others misquote the alphas and the periods (47 periods, .87 and .81), skip the second coding, or invent a questionnaire.
questions.follow_up: Why count by ownership period rather than by network?

questions.question: Why a permutation test for the locker networks, rather than a regression?
options: The Fisher test on carrier pairs is the main result, at p below .001, and the permutation test is a secondary check on it, run for completeness. Pairs give many more data points; so they carry the result. Indicative results are still results.

With only 26 ownership periods in the test, no regression was run. The permutation test counts each period once, and I rest on it: 46.0 against 21.3 per cent, p = .008. The pair-level Fisher tests agree, but pairs aren't independent, so they're indicative.

A permutation test establishes cause where a regression only shows association, so it lets me say that the holder causes carriers' use, which is what makes the result a finding rather than a proposition.

A regression was run as well and confirmed the result, controlling for network size and country; the permutation test is reported because it's easier to explain to a reader. The regression adds controls the permutation test lacks, so it's the stronger check. Both point the same way.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.5 and 5.2's reasoning. The others invent a regression, rest on the pair tests the thesis calls indicative, or credit a permutation test with causal proof.
questions.follow_up: What is being permuted, exactly?

questions.question: How was your savings scenario built, and why call it a scenario rather than a forecast?
options: By calibrating Ghent's camera data to a British council, which makes it a forecast for any council that adopts a similar access regime, since Ghent's cameras give the only measured base available anywhere in Europe for a rule of this kind.

For one council area of 50,000 people, not households, with five inputs taken from national statistics, so it's a forecast in everything but name, and councils can read their own figures off it directly without adjusting anything for their own streets or residents.

A notional area of 50,000 households; thirteen inputs, each sourced or marked as assumed; low, central, high and worst cases; only the increment over today's redirection counted. Eight inputs are assumptions, so it shows scale and drivers, not a prediction.

From the regulator's published failed-delivery rates for each UK council, which give the scenario a measured base rather than assumptions about redirection, so every council in the country could use its own figures without modelling anything.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.5 and Appendix N's construction. The others misstate households and inputs, invent official failure rates the UK does not publish, or invent a Ghent calibration.
questions.follow_up: Which two inputs move the result most?

questions.question: You call the design 'qualitative at its core', yet it has alphas, comparative analysis, Fisher and permutation tests. Is it mixed methods, and does your paradigm allow it?
options: A staged design under critical realism, qualitative at its core, with counts and tests in later stages. The paradigm allows it because each method is read for what it can show. Counts show how widely a pattern holds, never a test; the locker test shows a difference, not a cause.

Critical realism forbids statistical inference; so the tests are best read as illustrations, not tests, and they carry no weight in the argument of the thesis. Treating them as illustration keeps the paradigm consistent from start to finish.

It's really a quantitative design that calls itself qualitative; the statistics carry the findings, and the interviews illustrate them for the reader. The counts and tests decide each finding, and the quotations show what they mean in practice. Calling it qualitative is a convention of the field rather than a description of how the findings were reached.

It's mixed methods, so the paradigm allows it: each part of the design automatically validates the others, which is what makes the findings robust across all five links. Mixing methods is itself the source of robustness.
questions.why: Strong gives Table 3.1's description and 3.4's limit on counts. The others invert the design, misstate the paradigm, or treat mixing as self-validating.
questions.follow_up: Where in the thesis is a count most at risk of being read as a test?

questions.question: Your field is small and specialised. How did you protect participants' identities?
options: Participants' names were kept in the transcripts and the appendices, but their employers were removed, which is enough protection in a field of this size. In a small field, removing the employer is what matters most for anonymity. Names alone tell a reader little without the organisation behind them.

Each participant chose a pseudonym, used throughout the thesis, and approved every quotation attributed to it before the thesis was submitted. Approval of each quotation gave participants control over how they appear in the thesis.

Anonymity wasn't needed, because every participant was speaking in a public or professional capacity and agreed to be identified by name. Professional speakers expect to be named and usually prefer it.

Everyone is a code; no participant or employer is named; organisations by type; roles that would narrow to one person widened; the eleven countries given as a set, never against a code; a scheme named only if public record and describable by more than one person.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.3's choices. The others keep names, invent pseudonyms and quotation approval, or contradict the confidentiality promised in the information sheet.
questions.follow_up: Country by country in 4.2, couldn't a reader still identify someone?

questions.question: Every interview was online and in English. What did that cost you?
options: Online because participants sat in eleven countries, and video calls serve interviewing where distance would exclude people. All in English, all by me. The costs show: B8 has phone audio and limited English, A9's answers were typed in afterwards, and a call is easier to end.

It cost nothing of substance; online interviews are equivalent in every respect to face-to-face ones, and English is the working language of the whole sector in every country, so the medium made no difference to what people would say.

Being online meant I couldn't record, so the transcripts were reconstructed from my notes straight after each call and checked against my memory, and notes written immediately after a call are almost as accurate as a recording would be.

I used interpreters for the participants whose English was limited, so language cost nothing, though it lengthened some of the calls, and interpreters made every interview as clear as the ones held in English.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.3's reasons and the costs the record shows. The others deny any cost, invent interpreters, or contradict the record: all were recorded, 24 with video and 2 as audio.
questions.follow_up: Did shorter online calls change what people were willing to say about rivals?

questions.question: Isn't overlap just size in disguise? Large carriers overlap with everyone.
options: The mirror pairs hold the firm constant. The same small cargo-bike operator refuses a rival at home and pilots elsewhere; the same postal operator refuses consolidation at home and swaps parcels across the border. Willing and unwilling firms appear at every size.

No, because large carriers don't really overlap with everyone; they specialise in segments such as express or bulky goods, so their overlap is no greater than a small firm's. A parcel giant and a cargo-bike firm rarely want the same customer in the same city street.

Size was ruled out statistically by the survey, which shows no relationship between a company's size and whether it collaborates now, so overlap is the only variable left standing. Once size is set aside by the survey, the interviews only need to show where the refusals fall.
In effect, yes: overlap and size go together so closely in this industry that the two can't be separated; that's why I renamed the size effect 'overlap' once the interviews had shown it to me.
questions.why: Strong answers with the mirror pairs, which hold the firm constant (4.2). The others concede the conflation, misreport the survey (collaboration rises with size there, 20 to 47 per cent, and it cannot separate size from overlap), or invent specialisation.
questions.follow_up: In which pair does size differ as well as overlap?

questions.question: Tell me about the one transcript that contradicts overlap.
options: There isn't one; every transcript that speaks to overlap supports it, which is why the count is unanimous in both readings and overlap is the firmest of the links.

A4, the trustee, whose two rival manufacturers pooled their distribution for six years, which is the clearest case in the set of overlapping firms collaborating, and one its own participants described as 'really based on trust'.

B8, the owner-operator courier, whose load-sharing platform passes jobs to rival couriers every day with nothing binding them, which contradicts overlap directly in the urban last mile and is coded as the one case against.

A2, the retired modeller: two rival manufacturers back-hauled because their distribution directors played golf and trusted each other. I record it as a contradiction, but it's shippers' freight, 'not specifically urban', upstream, inside a trade body.
questions.why: Strong identifies A2 and its context (4.2). The others name B8, whose platform is bound by reviews and insurance and is the boundary's contradiction, claim a unanimity the count lacks (15/1/5/5), or cite A4, which is the condition working under a trustee.
questions.follow_up: Golf is trust. Why doesn't that case damage the binder link too?

questions.question: Two direct rivals pooled their distribution for six years. Doesn't that refute your first link?
options: It does qualify the link: it shows that long-standing trust between rivals can overcome overlap; that's why I treat trust as a second route to collaboration. By the end, the trustee was a formality and the relationship carried the arrangement.

No. It's the condition working. It ran on a trustee, one multilateral contract, a gain-share and a planning cell removed from both boards. The parties 'never knew this gap', how much more efficient the other was. An owner with no stake outweighed the exposure.

It's an outlier, one arrangement among 117, and I set it aside when stating the finding, since a single case can't refute a regularity counted across twenty-six transcripts in eleven countries, and a regularity that broad can carry one exception without losing any of its force.

They weren't really rivals: their products differed enough that they didn't compete for the same customers, which is why the pooling worked for as long as it did; the trustee's role was administrative, because the two firms sold to different buyers through different channels in different regions.
questions.why: Strong reads the case as the first link's own exception clause (4.2, 4.4). The others dismiss it, contradict the record (direct rivals for the same customers), or reverse the thesis on trust.
questions.follow_up: Isn't 'unless a no-stake owner' an escape clause that makes P1 unfalsifiable?

questions.question: What are your mirror pairs, and what work do they do?
options: Ten pairs of carriers of the same size, one willing and one unwilling, which show that within a size band something other than size decides who collaborates. Holding size constant is what lets overlap emerge as the variable that decides between them in the end.

Ten pairs, each a yes and a no from the same firm or kind of firm; what differs is whether they compete for the same customers in the same place. They hold the firm constant, so size can't explain. 'It's not their city. There's no market competition.'

Pairs of countries matched on size and density, one where carriers collaborate and one where they don't, which is how sub-objective 1C was answered in Table 4.4. That comparison is what sub-objective 1C needed, and it shows a clear north-south pattern.

Five pairs of interviews in which two people from the same organisation were asked the same questions, so their answers could be compared as a check on the reliability of each account. Where the two accounts agree, I treat the arrangement as reliably described. That's what each pair is for.
questions.why: Strong describes Table 4.2. The others invent paired interviews and the wrong number, confuse the pairs with country comparison, or describe pairs of different firms when the pairs hold the firm or kind of firm constant.
questions.follow_up: If the pairs were chosen to show overlap, aren't they selected on the outcome?

questions.question: Where in the firm is the refusal decided?
options: At the vehicle: drivers resist sharing vans with a rival's staff, and the refusal travels up from the depot to the managers, who then cite it to the city as the reason. The people who would share the van are the ones who decide whether it happens.

Higher than the vehicle. Three participants in three countries placed the veto in a head office that wasn't in the room. Local managers who see the saving agree; the head office holding the market vetoes, once ordering its logos be seen, not shared on one vehicle.

With the local managers, not head office, who fear losing their own territory; head offices generally favour collaboration for the saving, but can't overrule their branches on local matters. Head offices defer to the people who know the street, so local knowledge carries the final decision.

With the shippers, who forbid their carriers from collaborating with rivals; the carrier's own head office plays no part in the decision at any stage. Shippers decide who carries their goods, and they don't want them mixed with a rival's. Carriers simply follow those instructions to the letter.
questions.why: Strong reports the head-office veto of 4.2. The others locate the refusal with drivers, reverse the branch and head-office roles, or move it to shippers.
questions.follow_up: How does the head-office veto fit overlap, rather than size?

questions.question: Overlap scores 15, 1, 5, 5 in the third coding but 12, 0, 7, 7 on the second reading. Which do I believe?
options: The higher one, 15 for; the second reading was a check on reliability rather than a coding in its own right, so its counts don't replace the first and needn't be reported beside it. The second reading exists to test the first, not to compete with it.

Both. Two readings of the same twenty-six, both reported wherever I count. The direction holds, and on the second reading nothing contradicts it. The readings agree on overlap in 20 of 26 transcripts, and P1 rests on both, side by side.

The second reading, which shows overlap is weaker than I first thought, so I'd now describe it as a minority finding rather than the first link of the chain. A finding that weakens on a second look should be reported as weaker, and I'd rather be cautious.

Average the two: about 13.5 for, which is the most balanced figure and the one an examiner should hold me to when weighing the first link, since averaging is the fair way to combine two readings of the same transcripts.
questions.why: Strong reports both readings as the thesis does (Table 4.9, Table 3.6). The others pick the friendlier figure, invent an average, or misread 12 for, none against, as a minority.
questions.follow_up: Which way did most of those six differences run?

questions.question: In the far north, carriers collaborate. Doesn't that show density, not overlap, is what matters?
options: It's the strongest evidence I have for overlap, because it shows the same carriers collaborating where they don't compete, observed directly by the participant over many years. A consultant who has worked in the region for years is a reliable witness to what carriers do there.

It's only a consultant's inference, flagged wherever used, and it differs in density as well as place, which is why thin flows entered as a condition, after the first results and reported so. The pairs differing chiefly in place carry the overlap reading.

Density and overlap are the same thing in practice: where density is low there's no overlap; so the far-north case simply confirms the first link rather than competing with it. Low density is simply what an absence of overlap looks like on the ground, street by street.

I excluded the far-north case from the 117 because it lies outside the urban last mile; so it plays no part in any of the counts in Chapter 4. Rural cases fall outside the boundary I set in 1.4, so leaving it out was consistent.
questions.why: Strong treats the case as the inference it is and notes the post hoc thin-flows condition (4.2, 3.7). The others conflate density with overlap, overstate an inference as observation, or misstate the record: it stands as row 42 of H.1.
questions.follow_up: Could thin flows, not a no-stake holder, explain all your exceptions?

questions.question: Your first finding says 'unless a wall, a penalty or an owner with no stake'. What are a wall and a penalty? Give an example of each.
options: A wall is the trust that keeps rivals from cheating each other, and a penalty is the fine a carrier pays for a late delivery under its contract with the shipper. Both describe how the parties behave towards each other once an arrangement is running.

A wall is the carrier's brand, which marks its vans off from a rival's, and a penalty is the visibility it loses if it shares a vehicle with a competitor. Both are about how visible each carrier remains in the street. Visibility is the common thread.

A wall is a consolidation centre, which physically separates rivals' vans, and a penalty is the subsidy a city withdraws if the centre fails to cover its costs. Both appear in the record; that's why the first finding names them together. That's how I coded them.

A wall keeps the parties apart: in the narrowed coding, data separation, contracts, white labels, physical separation. A penalty is a cost a party bears if it stays out: a permit or access rule, which is why the vehicle-and-hour rule survives as P.
questions.why: Strong gives the definitions of 4.2 and the codes of 4.4 and 6.3. The others make trust, a hub or the brand into the wall, and misdefine the penalty.
questions.follow_up: Is a trustee a wall or a holder, and why did that change matter?

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'Shared Space, Separate Freight' come from?
options: From A7, a scholar describing platforms that work: 'They share only the space … they don't mix their [freight]'. That sentence is the regularity the thesis is named for.

From Ghent's 2023 urban logistics plan, which uses the phrase to describe the city's distribution platform and the partners that work through it. The participants then used it independently, which confirmed it as a regularity.
From the director of the shipper-side pooling platform, B1, describing how members' loads are combined under a trustee. His platform is the clearest working example of it in the whole record.
From my notes of 2022, where I first wrote it as a slogan for the project before the interviews took place. The interviews then bore it out, which is why it became the title.
questions.why: Strong attributes it to A7 (4.3). The others place it in a city plan, in the 2022 notes, or with B1, whose platform does pool shippers' loads under a trustee.
questions.follow_up: Is a title taken from one participant's sentence a finding or a slogan?

questions.question: Freight is pooled in ten of your rows. How is that 'separate freight'?
options: In nine of the ten a binder stands between the parties; in the tenth the participant named none. Data crosses only through a third party. And in the urban last mile, none of the 117 shows rivals pooling freight without something outside binding it.

Ten of 117 is under ten per cent, which is too few to matter; so the title describes the overwhelming pattern and the exceptions can safely be left aside. The title describes the pattern, and a pattern doesn't need to be exceptionless to hold across a record.

Those ten aren't really pooling; they're occasional favours between operators that don't amount to an arrangement, so the title stands without any qualification. A favour between operators doesn't have the structure, the terms or the duration of an arrangement.

Freight is pooled in most of the 117 rows, in fact; the title refers to what carriers say they want, not to what the arrangements in Appendix H actually do, and their wish is the regularity, because it's what they return to in every account they give.
questions.why: Strong gives 4.3's account of where freight crosses and what stands under it. The others redefine the ten away, dismiss them by proportion, or contradict the boundary finding.
questions.follow_up: The tenth row, with no binder named: what was it?

questions.question: A national postal operator and a global express carrier deliver each other's parcels across a border. Doesn't that break your boundary?
options: No. The freight crosses where the customers don't overlap. It's a reciprocal trade at matched price, 'a kind of trades agreement', each invisible in the other's market, recorded as 'an assignment from higher level'. A reciprocal trade is itself a binder.

They aren't rivals: one is a postal operator and the other an express carrier, so they serve different customers everywhere, not just across the border. Their markets don't meet, at home or abroad, so the swap tells us nothing about rivals. No rivalry is involved.

It's held by trust between the two firms' managers, built over years of working together; that's why it doesn't need a binder of any kind. Personal ties between the managers are what keep the swap running year after year.
It does break it, and I treat it as the exception showing the boundary is a tendency rather than a rule; two branded rivals pooling freight is the opposite of separate freight.
questions.why: Strong reads the swap as freight crossing where customers do not overlap, under a reciprocal trade (4.2, 4.3, 4.4). The others concede a break, deny the rivalry at home (the same operator refuses consolidation at home), or invent a trust basis.
questions.follow_up: Who ordered the swap, and what does that tell you about power?

questions.question: The boundary counts move from 16, 1, 6, 3 to 21, 0, 2, 3 on the second reading. Why such a jump?
options: The second reading was the more careful of the two, so it corrected errors in the first; the 21 is the figure to rely on, and the first reading, made more hurriedly, can be set aside as superseded.

A coding error in the first reading was found and corrected, and the second reading's count replaced it everywhere in the thesis, so the corrected figure is the one a reader should rely on throughout Chapter 4.

Five new transcripts were added between the two readings, which raised the number supporting the boundary from sixteen to twenty-one; the added transcripts all supported the boundary, which is why the count rose so sharply.

Every boundary difference on the A half runs one way. The first reading records freight or data pooled under a binder as mixed, the second as satisfying; five of the A half's twelve differences fall there, and both readings are reported.
questions.why: Strong explains the one rule on which the readings split (3.4). The others call one reading more careful, invent added transcripts (both readings cover the same twenty-six), or claim a correction when both readings are reported.
questions.follow_up: Which rule do you think is right: mixed, or satisfying?

questions.question: Which transcript contradicts the boundary of sharing, and how do you handle it?
options: A2, the retired modeller's back-haul between rival manufacturers, which pools freight on friendship and so contradicts the boundary outright, in the urban setting as well. Friendship, not a binder, held that one together. It's the case that tests the line.

A4, the trustee's pooled distribution, where two rivals shared freight and planning, which is the clearest crossing of the line anywhere in the set. Shared freight and shared planning cross the line twice over in that one case. It's the plainest example.

None does; the boundary is supported or silent in every transcript, which makes it the strongest of the four findings in both readings. With no contradiction at all, the boundary is the firmest link in the chain. The count shows it plainly, in both readings of the record.

B8, the owner-operator courier's load-sharing platform, on which a job and its customer pass to a rival daily. Its coding was qualified because the platform's reviews and insurance bind each exchange: a reputation system securing what would be exposed.
questions.why: Strong names B8 and why its coding was qualified (4.3). The others name A2, the overlap contradiction, deny the one contradiction (16/1/6/3), or cite A4, where a trustee binds the crossing.
questions.follow_up: Is a platform's reputation system really 'outside' the parties?

questions.question: Why should operating data be withheld? Data sharing is everywhere in policy now.
options: Technology is the limit: carriers lack the systems to share data, and once those improve the boundary will move, so the same logic that pooled space will pool data too, just as readily and for the same savings.

Because of data-protection law, which forbids carriers from sharing customer data with competitors, so the withholding is legal compliance rather than strategy, and carriers would share far more of their data if the law allowed it.

In my record data is shared freely between rivals; it's freight that's withheld, which is why the policy push for data sharing is working where pooling hasn't. Data spaces are now part of most city logistics plans.

In the record, data crosses only through a third party; trust alone gave a covenant of 40 companies no data in four years. The EU recommends a neutral trustee so parties needn't share directly. And volumes a rival could back-engineer are rare.
questions.why: Strong rests on the record, the EU trustee and the resource-based reading (4.3, 4.4, 2.4, 6.1). The others reverse the boundary, substitute a legal reason the thesis does not give, or make technology the driver when the thesis finds innovation a facilitator only.
questions.follow_up: Ghent made data sharing a condition of its permit class. Did that work?

questions.question: Where freight is pooled in shipper-led schemes, who does the pooling?
options: The owners of the freight. Two rival manufacturers pooled distribution under a trustee; a shipper-side platform pools members' loads 'not showing the individual members'; rival publishers set up an independent operator. Carriers carry what owners pooled.

The cities, which direct shippers' goods into a consolidation centre and pool them there before the last leg into the centre of town. Cities have both the power to direct goods into a centre and the land to put it on.

The platforms, acting on their own account, which buy capacity and resell it; so the pooling belongs to no shipper in particular. Platforms aggregate demand from many shippers, which is what pooling means in practice. They own the pool.
The carriers, who combine different shippers' loads on one van as a matter of routine; the shippers rarely know that their freight has been pooled with anyone else's.
questions.why: Strong gives the second link's last clause and its cases (1.5, 4.3, 2.2). The others give the pooling to carriers, cities or platforms acting for themselves, against the record.
questions.follow_up: Why do shippers pool where carriers won't?

questions.question: What bound the 117 arrangements? Give me the classes and the counts.
options: Ninety-five from outside the parties and twenty-two on the parties' own trust, which makes trust the second-largest class in the record after the neutral third party and the main rival to the binder account.

Ninety-five from outside: a grant 35, a neutral third party 21, a regulation or permit 17, a contract 12, and the rest smaller. Six rested on the parties' own trust, ten on nothing, and six weren't stated. The grant leads the list.

Ninety-five from outside: neutral third party 35, grant 21, regulation, permit or mandate 17, contract 12, client's instruction 5, prior vertical relationship 3, reciprocal trade 1, platform reputation 1. Six on their own trust; ten on nothing; six not stated.

One hundred and five from outside the parties, led by the neutral third party at 35; six on the parties' own trust; and six where no binder was stated, with nothing in the record running on no binder at all, failed or not.
questions.why: Strong gives Table H.3's counts. The others swap the neutral third party and the grant, inflate the total to 105, or misread 22, which is the 117 less the 95, as trust.
questions.follow_up: Which class surprised you most?

questions.question: Your participants say they trusted the trustee. Isn't trust in a trustee still trust, and so still the explanation you reject?
options: It's still trust, but that doesn't matter, because 89 of 119 survey respondents rate trust highly anyway, so the thesis sits comfortably inside the trust literature after all, and the binder is a refinement of the trust account rather than a rival to it at all.

No, because the trustee was a legal entity under contract, and contracts by definition exclude trust; once a contract exists, trust has no part left to play in the arrangement at all, so the question doesn't arise.

In the end the binder reduces to trust, not to a hostage: whoever holds the arrangement, the parties have to trust someone, so trust remains the underlying condition of the collaborations in the record, the trustee included.

Trust in a different object: a third party, not each other. In the six-year pooling the trustee held each side's figures, so they 'never knew this gap'; platform members send data 'in the trust that won't be shown to anybody'. A binder holding the hostages.
questions.why: Strong distinguishes the object of trust and reads the trustee as a binder holding each party's hostages (4.4, 4.2, 6.1). The others reduce the binder to trust, rest the distinction on a definition (relational and formal governance coexist, 2.4), or lean on survey ratings that test no link.
questions.follow_up: Would the pooling have survived if the trustee had sold delivery to the same customers?

questions.question: What became of the arrangements that had no binder at all?
options: Ten ran on nothing, and five of those had ended by the interview. Of the twenty-three that failed or never ran, eight had been asked to hold themselves.

Every one of the ten failed without exception, which is the strongest single piece of evidence for the binder link in the whole record, since no outside party can end an arrangement that it doesn't hold.
They were rescued by grants, which turned them into bound arrangements, so none of the ten ended in failure. Turning to a grant is the usual way such arrangements are saved.
They were the most durable in the set, because with no outside party they couldn't be ended by a grant or a contract running out.
questions.why: Strong gives Table H.3 and 7.1. The others reverse the outcome, overclaim that all ten failed (five ended), or invent rescue by grants.
questions.follow_up: Five of ten survived with no binder. Why doesn't that trouble P3?

questions.question: What does a grant bind, and for how long?
options: A grant builds lasting trust between the parties, so grant-bound arrangements usually continue on goodwill once the money stops; that's why funders should keep paying for pilots. The grant seeds the relationships, and the relationships then carry the arrangement on. That is why grants matter so much.

The 21 grant-bound rows had all ended by the interview, which shows that grants bind nothing at all beyond a short pilot period; a grant buys a pilot and nothing more, so funders should stop paying for them.

Grant-bound arrangements outlast every other class, because public money brings a stability that contracts and trustees can't match over the long run. Contracts and trustees can be walked away from far more easily than public money.

What a grant binds, it binds for its own length. Of 21 grant-bound rows, eight were pilots inside their funding, seven operating, six ended; four of the twenty-three failures ended with their grant. 'After the end of the project, they are not profitable.'
questions.why: Strong gives 4.4's figures and its rule. The others turn grants into trust-builders, overclaim their durability, or overclaim their failure (seven were operating).
questions.follow_up: If grants bind only for their length, why do cities keep funding pilots?

questions.question: Isn't your binder the same thing as your holder? A neutral third party both binds and holds.
options: Separate roles, coded separately. Of 36 rows whose first binder is a neutral third party, the point is held by a no-stake third party in only six; a helper in six, a public body in nine, a rival in two; nine have no shared point, four unclear.

They're the same thing under two names: whoever binds an arrangement also holds the point where the parties meet, so the holder adds nothing new to the binder. Treating them as one role makes the chain simpler without losing anything the evidence shows. Splitting them is a distinction without a difference.

They differ only in timing: a party binds an arrangement at the start and holds its point once it runs, so every binder becomes a holder in the end. Binding comes first and holding follows, so the two are stages of one role. The record shows that sequence.

The holder is always the binder, but the binder isn't always the holder; so the holder is a subset of the neutral-third-party rows, all 35 of them. Every neutral third party that binds an arrangement also ends up holding its point. That is exactly how the rows are counted.
questions.why: Strong gives 4.4's cross-count showing the roles diverge. The others merge them, claim every neutral-third-party row has a no-stake holder (only six do), or invent a sequence.
questions.follow_up: Then why do neutral third parties so rarely hold the point?

questions.question: Four rows run on peer trust alone. Don't they contradict you?
options: Each of the four joins firms that don't compete, so all four fall outside a claim that's about competing carriers only, and none of them needs an answer from me beyond saying so.

Not at all: all four failed, so they show what happens without a binder rather than contradicting the finding, because peer trust alone never lasted anywhere in the record, which is exactly what the binder link predicts for arrangements with nothing outside them.
There are no such rows. Every row in Appendix H names an outside binder of one kind or another, which is what makes the binder finding unanimous across all 117 accounts of arrangements in the record.

The cases the claim must answer: a rural case offered only as an inference; a dairy and a vegetable supplier who don't compete; four friends' cargo-bike cooperative, dissolved; and two bike couriers' joint bid, rivals at the door, for one tender.
questions.why: Strong lists the four as Appendix H and 7.1 do. The others say all failed (two did not), say none involves rivals (the bike couriers are rivals), or deny the rows exist.
questions.follow_up: Which of the four would a sceptic pick, and what would you say?

questions.question: Two bike couriers bid jointly with nothing binding them. Isn't that your binder finding falsified?
options: Yes, it falsifies P3, so I'd restate the proposition as 'most horizontal collaborations last as long as their binder', which survives the exception. A softer proposition fits the record better and loses nothing important.

No, because the city that asked for their quotes bound them through the tender; so the procurement rule is the binder and the case confirms the finding. The city holds the tender, so the city is the binder, as in so many other rows.

No, because the two couriers weren't rivals: they served different parts of the city, so the case falls outside the claim about competing carriers. Couriers in different districts don't share customers, so they aren't rivals for this purpose. Their customers never met at all.

It's the one exception between rivals, recorded as such: one tender, running at interview, nothing on record holding them once it's won. P3's falsifier is an arrangement that outlived its binder on trust or dissolved while its binder stood; this is neither.
questions.why: Strong records the exception and tests it against P3's falsifier (7.1, Appendix L). The others deny the rivalry, invent a binder the coding rule excludes (a rule that only supplied the occasion is not a binder), or weaken P3 needlessly.
questions.follow_up: What would you need to see to call it a real counter-case?

questions.question: Your twenty-three failed and unrealised arrangements: what had they been asked to run on?
options: All twenty-three failed because the parties overlapped. Overlap alone explains every failure in Table 4.6, whatever each arrangement was asked to run on, so the binder adds nothing to the account that overlap doesn't already give us, row by row.

Eight were asked to hold themselves: a neutral hub, a mobility platform, a conference appeal, a chief executive's signature, a head-office refusal, a retailer consortium, a heat network, the covenant. Four ended with their grant; three failed on cost recovery.

Most failed on technology: the platforms and data systems didn't work well enough, and better systems would have saved most of them, which is why innovation, not binding, is the constraint that decides what survives.

Most failed because their grants were too small. With adequate funding all twenty-three could have run, so money rather than binding decides what survives, and the remedy is simply larger grants, paid for longer.
questions.why: Strong summarises Table 4.6. The others make technology the cause (the thesis finds innovation a facilitator only), make grant size the cause (four ended with their grant), or overclaim one cause for all twenty-three.
questions.follow_up: Why count a hub a city proposed as 'asked to hold itself'?

questions.question: Who began the 117 arrangements?
options: A city or public body 45, a carrier 29, a platform 20, a shipper or receiver 13, and the rest mixed or not named in the participant's account. Those are the counts I give for the 117 in Table 4.8.
A city or public body 42, a platform or broker 20, a carrier 19, a shipper or receiver 15, an academic project 14, a city with a project 1, and 6 couldn't be placed.
A shipper or receiver 42, a city 20, a carrier 19, a platform 15, and academic projects 14, with the remaining seven not placed.
A carrier 42, a city or public body 20, a platform or broker 19, a shipper or receiver 15, an academic project 14, and the rest couldn't be placed. Carriers lead the table quite clearly.
questions.why: Strong gives Table 4.8. The others swap carriers and cities, give the update's counts of papers (45, 29, 20, 13) instead of arrangements, or put shippers first.
questions.follow_up: Carriers come third. Why isn't that a finding about carriers' power?

questions.question: Who begins an arrangement isn't who has power. Cities begin plenty of things that carriers then run as they please.
options: Initiation is power by definition: whoever begins an arrangement sets its terms and controls it from then on, so the count of 42 begun by cities settles where power sits without further evidence, and the transcripts only illustrate what that count already shows.

Agreed, initiation isn't the whole of it. The claim rests first on the transcripts, 18 for, none against: receivers set windows, shippers dictate terms, cities write permits, carriers choose a moment inside what others set. Initiators add to that; they don't carry it.

In fact carriers began most of the arrangements, so the count supports their power; cities usually come in later to formalise what carriers have already set up between themselves, which is why the initiator column favours the carriers.
Power is unclear in the record, I concede. The initiator count is the only evidence I have, and it can't bear the weight I put on it in Chapter 4, so I'd rather concede the point than overstate it.
questions.why: Strong separates initiation from power and rests the claim on the transcript counts (4.5, 2.7). The others equate the two, misread the count (carriers began 19), or abandon the transcript evidence.
questions.follow_up: Give me one case where a carrier reorganised flows on its own initiative.

questions.question: What is 'the receiver's clock'?
options: The delivery deadline a carrier promises its shipper, which the carrier sets for itself and then plans its routes around, street by street, so the receiver simply accepts whichever window the carrier chooses to offer.

Ghent's closed hours, from 11:00 to 18:00, during which the loading-and-unloading category may not enter the car-free areas; the thesis uses those hours as its main example of the receiver's clock at work in a city, written into the permit.
The carriers' shift pattern, which fixes when vans can leave the depot and so sets the earliest and latest delivery times on every round, for every receiver on it and every party up the chain.

The hours when receivers will take goods in, the limit on any rule by hour. An order for eleven on Wednesday, ten minutes' tolerance, removes the scope for collaboration before any carrier is asked. It extends Holguín-Veras beyond the off-hours.
questions.why: Strong defines it as 5.1 and 7.2 do. The others confuse it with Ghent's closed hours, or place the clock with carriers, reversing the power finding.
questions.follow_up: At a parcel locker, does the receiver's clock still bind?

questions.question: You call carriers 'price-takers'. On what evidence?
options: The trustee put city carriers' margins at between 9 and 30 per cent, which sounds healthy but leaves no room to absorb collaboration's costs, so carriers take whatever price shippers offer and can't pay for a partner's delay or a shared hub.

Carriers set prices in the market, as large firms do, but take the delivery times their receivers set, so 'price-taker' is really shorthand for 'time-taker' in the thesis, and the margin evidence plays no part in that argument.

The trustee put city carriers' margins 'between minus two and plus 2%'. Carriers choose a moment inside what others set and reorganise only within their own networks or subcontractors'. Holguín-Veras found only 9 per cent of carriers could pass a toll on.

The trustee put margins at between 6 and 25 per cent, and carriers can't raise prices above that band without losing their shippers to rivals, which is what makes them price-takers rather than price-setters in the market.
questions.why: Strong gives 4.5's evidence. The others misquote the margin with the realistic pool saving (9 to 30) or Fernández's modelled saving (6 to 25), or contradict 'price-taker'.
questions.follow_up: A large carrier subcontracting its last mile: price-taker or principal?

questions.question: One participant says shippers are 'every bit as suspicious' of mixing goods with competitors as carriers are. Doesn't that undercut shippers as binders?
options: Shippers never pool with competitors anywhere in the record, so their suspicion is beside the point: what they think of their own rivals has no bearing on whether they can bind other parties such as carriers.

That participant is wrong; shippers are far more open than carriers, which is why shipper-led schemes succeed, and one sceptical voice doesn't make a pattern across twenty-six transcripts, so I'd set the remark aside as an outlier in the set.

It fits. Overlap applies to anyone sharing customers, shippers included; power is about who can reorganise flows and supply binding, not who trusts. Rival shippers pooled under a trustee, and Sternberg's facilitated shippers failed partly for lack of self-determination.

It does undercut it, and I'd concede that shippers have no real power to bind; the binding in the record comes from cities, not shippers, and shippers follow the city's lead rather than setting terms of their own for the carriers they hire.
questions.why: Strong reads the quotation through overlap and power as 6.1 does. The others dismiss the participant, concede more than the record shows, or contradict it (two rival manufacturers pooled under a trustee).
questions.follow_up: So is a shipper a binder, or a party that needs one?

questions.question: The visibility veto: what exactly did you find?
options: It's a majority finding: most participants said carriers refuse to share because branded vans would disappear from the street, which is why it sits beside overlap in the first link as one of its two parts, and why the thesis leans on it so heavily.

When I put the idea it was accepted in three of five interviews, and eight more participants raised it unprompted, so it's well supported, as stated in Chapter 4, and stands among the thesis's main findings, beside overlap and the binder, as a reason in its own right.

When I put the idea, in five interviews, it was declined in all five, and I count that as declined. Eight raised the veto unprompted, three first-hand; none had seen it measured. A minority finding, stated as a testable claim.

It's established by McLeod and colleagues, who measured the effect of losing brand identity on carriers' business, and my interviews confirm their measurement across eleven countries, so the veto rests on a measured base rather than on accounts.
questions.why: Strong gives 4.6's counts and status. The others promote a minority finding, credit McLeod with a measurement never made, or misreport the five prompted interviews (all five declined).
questions.follow_up: Why count your own prompts as 'declined' rather than leaving them out?

questions.question: What do the three sales of locker networks show about 'drift by sale'?
options: None of them is relevant, because all three networks were already held by rivals before they were sold, so nothing about their holder changed when ownership passed, and there's no drift for the rule to catch in any of them.

It reads both ways. GLS ended its cooperation after Austrian Post took over a telecoms operator's stations; De Buren passed to DHL Group with no exit on a sale-day statement; myflexbox, sold to Deutsche Post, is the baseline, its listed carriers unchanged. No rule re-checked.

In the three cases carriers left the network within weeks of the sale, and the pattern was the same each time, which shows that a sale to a rival drives carriers out wherever the record can see it, whoever the buyer is.

They prove that a sale to a rival always reduces carriers' use, since three sales pointing the same way is enough to establish it; that's why the re-check is the rule's strongest part, and no counter-example exists in the record.
questions.why: Strong reports the three sales as 5.2 and 7.4 do, both ways. The others claim every carrier left (De Buren showed no exit; myflexbox is a baseline), turn two cases into a proof, or misstate the holders (myflexbox was neutral-held before its sale).
questions.follow_up: If myflexbox's partners stay, what does that do to P5?

questions.question: What did Ghent's 2016 plan actually change?
options: It took effect on 3 April 2017: a permit was needed at every hour, enforced by 27 cameras and a €55 fine. Twenty-six categories became fourteen, thirteen with round-the-clock access; only loading and unloading is windowed, 18:00 to 11:00 in the four central areas.

It took effect in 2017 and introduced a low-emission zone with time windows for every category, enforced by police officers on the street rather than by cameras, with a permit needed only in the closed hours and no fine for a first entry.
It took effect on 24 October 2016, with 14 cameras and a 27-euro fine, and cut the permit categories from 26 to 13, every one of them windowed by hour, loading and the platform's class included.

It took effect on 3 April 2017 and gave every category the same window, 18:00 to 11:00, so all operators, whatever their permit, were separated in time alike, and the platform's class lost its privilege from the first day the cameras ran.
questions.why: Strong gives 5.2's figures. The others confuse the draft's date with the start and garble the cameras, fine and categories, invent a zone and patrols (the low-emission zone dates from 2020), or window every category when only one is windowed.
questions.follow_up: Why does it matter that only one category is windowed?

questions.question: Ghent's own model expected traffic to fall by 40 per cent. Isn't that a success for allocating time?
options: The 40 and 31 per cent falls are traffic overall in the 18:00 to 11:00 window. For that window the city expected 'the traffic attributable to suppliers remains the same size'. Deliveries leave the closed hours without suppliers sharing. Neither plan counts deliveries by window.

Yes: a 40 per cent fall in traffic is a substantial effect, and it's the main reason I retained time in the final rule as the access rule by vehicle and hour, since that fall is precisely what allocating time is meant to purchase.

Suppliers' traffic is where the 40 per cent fall came, which shows that allocating hours made suppliers consolidate their deliveries to fit the window, exactly as the regime intended when it wrote the hours into the permit.

The model is a projection and Ghent's figures are unreliable, so I set the 40 per cent aside and draw no conclusion from the plan either way, since a projection proves nothing about what actually happened on the city's streets.
questions.why: Strong reads the model correctly (5.2, Table 5.4). The others treat an overall projected fall as success for allocation, misattribute the fall to suppliers, or discard the document whose 'same size' sentence carries the argument.
questions.follow_up: Then why does the access rule survive at all?

questions.question: What happened to Ghent's 'sustainable urban distribution' permit class?
options: It gave one class access only between 18:00 and 11:00, the same hours as loading and unloading, but let its vehicles pass the cameras without being fined, and that exemption from fines is all the class ever amounted to in practice.

It was the only delivery class with every hour, every car-free area and the three camera cuts, from April 2017; by autumn 2023 conditional on membership, pilots and data sharing. The 2023 plan announces its end: cargo bikes always, other motorised vehicles outside closed hours.

It was abolished in 2017, only a few months after the plan began, because carriers refused to join the city's platform, and it was replaced by a general window for everyone, which is the regime the 2023 plan describes and keeps unchanged for every category.

It was extended in 2023 to every operator using electric vans, so the privilege became the general rule: any clean vehicle may now enter the car-free areas at every hour, a rule by vehicle that names no operator and needs no platform behind it.
questions.why: Strong gives 5.2's account. The others invent an early abolition, reverse the 2023 change (cargo bikes always; other motorised vehicles outside the closed hours), or misdescribe the class's hours.
questions.follow_up: Why does the end of that privilege support a rule that names no operator?

questions.question: The locker networks: what's the headline result, and what doesn't it show?
options: Neutral-held networks reach 46.0 per cent of main carriers against 21.3 per cent, p = .008, which shows that a neutral holder causes carriers to use a network; with a p-value that small, chance is ruled out and the holder is the cause.

Neutral-held networks reach 64 per cent of main carriers against 21 per cent, and the result holds pair by pair for every carrier tested, so it isn't an average effect but a difference every carrier shows on its own.

The headline is the national-name check, 10 against 2 at p = .039, a test within the same carriers, not across networks, consistent with the holder effect and stronger than a comparison across networks, so the permutation test is a backstop.

Across 26 ownership periods, neutral-held networks reach on average 46.0 per cent of a country's main carriers, rival-held 21.3, p = .008 by permutation. A difference by owner class, consistent with the gradient, not a test of it, and with quality, price and terms unmatched.
questions.why: Strong gives 5.2's result with its limits. The others read cause into it, misquote the figure (46.0) and claim a pair-by-pair test never made, or promote a secondary check the thesis calls a direction, not a proof.
questions.follow_up: Which confounder worries you most, and how would you rule it out?

questions.question: By owner class the share falls from neutral 46, through retailers 42 and carriers' subsidiaries 29, down to postal operators 15. That's your gradient proved, isn't it?
options: The order is wrong: retailers with their own delivery should rank below carriers' subsidiaries, so once they're placed correctly the classes cut against the gradient rather than for it, and P5 is weakened, not proved.

It is: the classes fall in the order market commonality predicts, from neutral holders down to postal operators, so the gradient P5 proposes is now established for European networks, and six classes in order is strong evidence.

It's irrelevant, because the classes are coded by ownership, and ownership has nothing to do with market commonality between a holder and the carriers it serves, so the ordering tells us nothing about P5 either way.

Consistent with one, but the classes are too small to test it and commonality is coded by class, not measured. Same carriers, by group 7 against 2 (10 equal), sign test p = .18; by national name 10 against 2 (9 equal), p = .039. Direction, not proof.
questions.why: Strong gives 5.2's reading and the same-carrier check. The others treat an ordering of small classes as proof, invent a contrary prediction, or deny the link between holder class and commonality that the thesis draws.
questions.follow_up: Where does the one joint network, at zero, sit on that gradient?

questions.question: Isn't the red-cell rule just the neutral fourth party the field has always reached for?
options: That's objection two. The council designs no bundler and names no operator. Neutrality rests on the holder's market position, what it sells and to whom, which a contract can record but not create. Carriers need trust only a fact the council can check, and re-checks.

No, because a fourth party is a private operator, and my rule makes the council itself the operator of every shared point on its land. With the council running the points, there's no third party left for carriers to distrust, and every carrier is treated exactly alike.

Broadly, yes: the contribution is to give that old idea its legal form, its costs and its remedies, which the field never worked out, so the novelty lies in the detail of the instrument rather than in the principle behind it. That is still a real contribution to the field and to councils.

No, because fourth parties have always failed, as Sternberg and colleagues showed. My rule instead relies on a holder that signs a binding neutrality contract with the council, and that signed promise is what carriers can trust when they hand over parcels. Nothing more is needed.
questions.why: Strong gives objection two's answer (6.3, Table 6.1). The others concede the restatement, make the council an operator (the rule is not a city delivery service), or rest neutrality on a contract's promise, which the rule says can record but not create it.
questions.follow_up: How does a council 'check a fact' about a holder's market position?

questions.question: Is your rule lawful?
options: In England at least it is. English law sits outside the Services Directive, so an English council can ban carriers from owning lockers on its streets; the European route is harder, but England can show the rule working first.

It's shaped by law. Barring carrier ownership restricts shareholding under Article 15 of the Services Directive; barring holders from selling delivery restricts combined activities under Article 25. So ownership stays out of permits; on its own land the council buys neutrality as a service.

Article 101 of the Treaty requires councils to keep shared infrastructure neutral, so the rule applies an obligation competition law already places on cities, and a council that ignored it would be the one acting unlawfully under the Treaty.

Strictly, no. Any holder condition breaches the Services Directive, so the rule can only ever be voluntary: a neutral label that holders may choose to seek, with no consequence on council land or anywhere else for the holders who don't.
questions.why: Strong gives 6.3's legal shaping. The others misread Article 101 (it bars agreements between firms), give up the two tiers the law allows, or ignore that the English route is a lease under the general power, not a ban.
questions.follow_up: What's the open legal question you can't answer?

questions.question: What are the four questions every shared point is asked?
options: Its price per parcel; its size in compartments; whether it's sited within 500 metres of homes; and whether it opens at every hour, since those are what decide whether residents use it. Use is what counts in the end, for residents and for the council.

Who stands behind it; whether it, or anyone behind it, sells delivery to the served carriers' customers; whether it can see, keep or steer what passes; and whether it takes every carrier's parcel for every resident.

Whether any carrier holds more than a quarter of its shares; whether it carries a neutral label; whether it's insured against loss; and whether it shares its delivery data with the council each month. Each is easy to check.

Who owns it; whether it's open to at least three logistics firms, as Munich requires; whether it stands on public land; and whether it charges every carrier the same price per parcel delivered. Each is a matter of record.
questions.why: Strong gives the four questions of 6.3. The others fold in Munich's 'at least three logistics firms', an access test the rule moves beyond, list siting and service features, or invent an ownership threshold the rule keeps out of every condition.
questions.follow_up: Which of the four is hardest to answer from the outside?

questions.question: What is 'the dot', and what follows it?
options: A mark on the council's map for each neutral point. When a point fails a check it's closed at once and its parcels are redirected to the nearest neutral point, which is the remedy a holder takes seriously enough to change.

A sign of a stake, which brings a fine of 55 euros for each breach, rising with every repeat, as Ghent fines vehicles at its cameras; the rising cost gives the holder every reason to sell its stake as quickly as it can, and most holders would sell within the year.

A sign of a stake, which brings ninety days' notice and then withdrawal of the permit at each point the holder runs, on council land and off it alike; a long notice is fair, and losing the permits together is what makes the sanction bite on a holder.

A sign of a stake, after the inclusion the spleen removes. It brings written notice with evidence and thirty days to explain; on council land, an order to separate within six months, or the site passes to the next-ranked holder, with appeal. The point stays in service.
questions.why: Strong gives 6.3's remedies in order. The others close the point (the point stays in service throughout), borrow Ghent's camera fine, or invent a notice period and a remedy that falls on permitted points as on council land.
questions.follow_up: Why should the point stay open while the holder is under notice?

questions.question: How does a council actually find a stake?
options: By surveying the carriers who use each point every year. They're best placed to say whether a holder treats their parcels worse than a rival's, and they have every reason to report it, so theirs is the most reliable test. Carriers see it first.

By checking on paper, in registers and published terms, and in the post. Each term the council buys ordinary deliveries through every point under tracer names, so a reused name or a rival's parcel treated worse shows on the doorstep. Records can hide; parcels can't.

By asking each holder to certify every year that it sells no delivery to the carriers it serves. A false declaration would expose it to penalties, so the certificate keeps the holder honest at almost no cost to the council. Most holders would comply without complaint.
By monitoring each point with cameras, as Ghent monitors its car-free cuts; so the council has a continuous record of who handles which parcels and when, which no occasional check could match.
questions.why: Strong gives 6.3's physical check. The others rely on self-certification (behavioural promises do not remove the incentive), cameras the rule does not propose, or the carriers' own reports.
questions.follow_up: Couldn't a holder spot test parcels and treat them well?

questions.question: Why is the rule limited to shared parcel points, and not hubs or consolidation centres?
options: Because a locker on the round adds no handling stage, while a neutral hub a city proposed was refused for adding a second handling. So the scope is lockers and shop points within about a five-minute walk; house-door boxes are out, and rural areas are left to further research.

Because the locker networks were the only data available to me. With comparable data on hubs, the rule would cover consolidation centres in exactly the same way, since the holder question is identical whatever the kind of shared site. Data drove the scope, as it should in any proposal built on evidence.

Hubs are already well regulated by planning law, while lockers may fall between the cracks. The evidence is much the same for both; it's the regulatory gap that differs, so the rule goes where no rule exists yet.

Because lockers are far cheaper to build than hubs or consolidation centres, so a council can afford many more of them for the same budget and reach more residents for each pound it spends on the scheme.
questions.why: Strong gives 6.3's reason and scope. The others give reasons the thesis does not (planning law, cost, data availability), and the last ignores the refused neutral hub.
questions.follow_up: If a hub adds handling, why did the trustee-run network work?

questions.question: 'Open is not neutral' looks too strong. PostNL opened its lockers and a carrier did join.
options: PostNL isn't relevant, because it's a Dutch case and the rule is written for English and EU councils, so the example sits outside its scope and doesn't need answering.

It isn't too strong, and I say so: GLS announced it would join but never did, so PostNL's opened lockers remain closed to a rival carrier in practice; an announcement isn't use, and the flat claim survives the PostNL case intact.

As a flat claim it is too strong, and I say so. No carrier had used PostNL's opened lockers by November 2023, but in January 2024 GLS announced it would start that March. So the rule claims a gradient, not all or nothing.

It is too strong, and it undermines the rule. If one rival carrier joins an opened network, access, not the holder, turns out to be enough, and the holder doesn't matter to carriers after all; so the rule should certify by access like the existing ones. That's the honest conclusion.
questions.why: Strong concedes the flat claim and restates the gradient (6.3). The others contradict the record (GLS announced it would begin that March), overcorrect into abandoning the holder, or dodge on geography inside the EU.
questions.follow_up: How steep would the gradient have to be to matter to a council?

questions.question: Isn't your rule just the telecoms access rule applied to lockers?
