options: No, because the telecoms code was repealed some years ago, so there's nothing left for the rule to borrow from it now, and any resemblance between the two is purely coincidental.

In part, and it's credited as such. What the thesis adds is the finding that parcel-point rules reviewed have no holder test, the evidence one is needed, and a physical check, the council's own parcels, in place of a regulator's returns.
No: telecoms regulation deals with tariffs and wholesale prices, not with who holds a facility; so there's no real overlap between that code and a rule on who holds a shared parcel point.

Yes, entirely, and that's its strength: a rule already proven in telecoms needs no new evidence to work for lockers, so the thesis can rely on that record and spend its effort on the costs and the checking instead.
questions.why: Strong credits the borrowing and names what is new (6.3). The others deny holder tests in telecoms that 2.5 cites, claim the borrowing needs no evidence, or invent a repeal.
questions.follow_up: Why isn't a regulator's return good enough for parcel points?

questions.question: A carrier's wish for control and quality might explain refusal just as well as the holder does.
options: Control and quality are what the holder determines, so they aren't a rival explanation at all; they're simply the channel through which the holder works, and the objection collapses into the proposition.

Objection five. Holding the carrier fixed points the same way: seven groups to two, p = .18, and ten national names to two, p = .039, a direction, not proof. Quality, price and terms weren't matched, so that part stays open.

It can't, because control and quality were measured for every network in the review and found equal across holders, which rules them out as an explanation of why carriers favour neutral-held networks.

It could, and I'd accept it as the better explanation, a direction, not proof. The holder is one possibility among several, and the locker data can't choose between them; so the rule rests as much on hope as on evidence. I'd say that openly in the viva.
questions.why: Strong gives objection five's answer and leaves the open part open (6.3, 7.4). The others claim quality was measured (it was not), concede too far, or fold the objection into the holder by definition.
questions.follow_up: What data would let you hold the network constant as well?

questions.question: Won't your rule shrink the supply of parcel points, if carriers refused a site simply build on private land?
options: It will, and the rule handles it by requiring each carrier that builds its own lockers on private land to co-fund a neutral network in the same area, which may keep the supply of points up.
It won't, because carriers will always prefer council sites to private land, so ranking can only move investment towards neutral points, never away from them, and the supply of points will only grow.

It's objection six. The rule bans no one's lockers and ranks only the council's own sites, so the risk is the slower investment ranking may bring, and I name it. No carrier co-funds the neutral networks Thiele describes.
Supply doesn't really matter: a handful of neutral points used by every carrier serves residents better than many points each used by a single carrier, so fewer points is the better outcome.
questions.why: Strong gives objection six and its named risk. The others deny the risk, invent a co-funding requirement the rule does not contain, or dismiss supply when the rule sites points within a five-minute walk.
questions.follow_up: Is slower investment a price worth paying, and who pays it?

questions.question: Separation as a remedy was first written about the size of firms. Isn't borrowing it inconsistent with your finding that size doesn't matter?
options: It is inconsistent, and I'd drop separation from the rule: the site passing to the next-ranked holder is enough of a remedy on its own, without borrowing a remedy from a theory of size that the thesis itself rejects in Chapter 4.

Separation still applies only to the largest holders, so nothing is inconsistent: small holders are exempt from the remedy, as the 2022 notes intended for firms that had grown past a certain size in their market, whatever their position.

It's objection seven. The remedy is applied openly to position, not size: the 2022 notes' 'second version run by completely different people' applied to a holder's market position, fitting the finding that territory, not size, makes the animal fierce.

Separation comes from EU competition law, not from my notes, so its origin in a theory of size isn't relevant here, and the rule simply borrows an established remedy that regulators already apply to other sectors.
questions.why: Strong gives objection seven's answer (6.3). The others drop a remedy the rule keeps, reintroduce a size threshold, or misstate where the remedy came from (the author's notes of 2022).
questions.follow_up: What does 'run by different people' mean in practice for a carrier's locker arm?

questions.question: What does a check cost, and who pays for it?
options: About £400 to £1,500 a point a year, paid by central government through a new grant, so councils bear none of the cost and every council can adopt the rule without touching its own budget or charging holders.

About £7,000 a point a year, built from the Department for Transport's value of time, since the check exists to save residents' time, and paid from the council's general budget rather than by holders.

About £400 to £1,500 a point a year: one borough's pavement-licence cost, £306.51 to £423.55, plus some two dozen test parcels at about £4. Paid by an audit charge on leases; on highway permits, capped at the cost of granting them.
About £42,000 a point a year, paid by the carriers that use each point in proportion to the parcels they deliver into it, so those who benefit from the check are the ones who pay for it.
questions.why: Strong gives 6.3 and Appendix N's costing. The others invent a figure and a basis, misread £42,000 (the central case's total for 60 points), or invent a central grant when the charge falls on leases.
questions.follow_up: On highway permits the charge is capped. Does the check still pay for itself there?

questions.question: What does your rule actually deliver? Give me the number.
options: About £262,000 a year for every council that adopts it, plus the 9 to 30 per cent saving carriers get once they pool through neutral points. Those two figures together are what a council can expect. Councils need a single headline figure, and that is the honest one.

The rule delivers the 9 to 30 per cent saving that realistic pools achieve, because a neutral holder removes the one barrier that stopped carriers pooling, and that saving, passed on to residents, is the reason to adopt it.

It compels nothing and promises none of the 9 to 30 per cent pools save; it removes one barrier. The scenario's central case nets about £262,000 a year for 50,000 households, the low case loses £12,000, the worst £150,000; eight of thirteen inputs are assumptions.

I can't give a number; the scenario is too uncertain to quote, and any figure would be a guess, so I'd rather not put one on what the rule delivers until a council has tried it, counted the result and published what the count showed.
questions.why: Strong gives 6.3's precise claim with all three cases. The others turn a notional area into every council and add a saving the rule does not promise, claim that saving outright, or refuse a figure the thesis does give.
questions.follow_up: If the low case loses money, why should a council try it?

questions.question: Break the scenario's central case down for me.
options: 84,000 depot trips avoided and 280,000 hours saved; time worth about £1.7 million; carriers save £106,000; checking costs £42,000; net about £1.72 million a year once every failed delivery in the area is counted as avoided by the rule from its first year.

33,600 depot trips and 28,000 hours saved a year, about 9,100 by households without a car; time worth about £198,000 at £7.08 an hour; carriers save about £106,000; checking 60 points at £700 costs £42,000. Net about £262,000.

33,600 trips and 28,000 hours saved; time worth about £198,000; carriers save about £106,000; checking 100 points at £1,500 costs £150,000; net about £154,000 a year in the central case, before any carbon saving is counted or priced.

33,600 trips and 28,000 hours saved; time worth about £106,000; carriers save about £198,000 on redeliveries; checking 60 points costs £42,000; net about £262,000 a year, with carriers rather than households without a car the main beneficiaries of the rule.
questions.why: Strong gives Appendix N's central case. The others confuse 84,000 depot trips and 280,000 failed first attempts with savings and borrow the high case's net, swap the time and carrier figures, or put the worst case's checking cost into the central case.
questions.follow_up: Which of those figures rests most heavily on an assumption?

questions.question: Aren't you counting redirection to nearby points that already happens?
options: No; only the increment counts. Trips avoided are depot trips times r minus r0: the share redirected under the rule minus the share redirected today. The result turns on that share and the time each trip saves.

Partly: I subtract a fixed 10 per cent for existing redirection, the industry average for parcels sent to a point after a failed attempt, which keeps the calculation simple to reproduce. Any council could repeat it without specialist help.
It counts all redirection to points, but that's conservative rather than inflated, because it understates how many residents would use a neutral point once one exists nearby.
No, because no redirection happens today; in the UK every failed first delivery goes back to the depot, so the whole effect of the rule is new.
questions.why: Strong gives the increment rule of Appendix N. The others admit counting existing redirection, contradict the r0 input (some redirection already happens), or invent a fixed percentage.
questions.follow_up: Where did your value of r0 come from?

questions.question: Why don't you price the carbon in your scenario?
options: I do price it, at the government's carbon value, and it's the largest single term in the £262,000 net value of the central case, ahead of residents' time.
I report it, 28.1 tonnes a year in the central case and 243.2 in the high, but I don't price it, so the net figure is only residents' time and carriers' savings minus the cost of checking.

The scenario saves no carbon at all: residents walking to a point replace a van at the door, so the two effects cancel out and there is nothing to price, and putting a price on nothing would only mislead councils.

Because the carbon savings are already counted inside the carriers' redelivery saving, since fewer van trips means less fuel; so pricing carbon separately would count the same saving twice in the net figure.
questions.why: Strong gives Appendix N's choice. The others deny any saving, invent a priced term (the net is time plus carriers' saving minus checking), or invent a double-counting rationale.
questions.follow_up: Would pricing carbon have changed the low case's sign?

questions.question: Lockers can be worse than the doorstep if people drive to them. Haven't you just moved the van trip into a car?
options: Driving to a locker still saves emissions overall, because one car trip replaces several failed van deliveries and a return trip to the depot, so it isn't a concern for the rule and needn't shape where the points go.

No, because the scenario assumes that no resident drives; car trips aren't part of the calculation at all, so the problem simply doesn't arise in any of the figures I report, and the rule needs no siting condition.

It may raise emissions where residents drive, I concede, but its case rests on residents' time rather than carbon, so a little more carbon is an acceptable price for the hours saved, and most councils would accept that trade if they were asked to make it openly.

They can, as Niemeijer and Buijs found, so the rule covers points within a five-minute walk and sites them within about 500 metres: locker share rises from 11 to 53 per cent as distance falls from 2.5 to 0.5 kilometres. Plus a checkout default, with opt-out.
questions.why: Strong gives Appendix N's answer and 6.3's pull. The others misdescribe the scenario (it values car emissions at 0.167 kg a kilometre), assert an unexamined saving, or concede more than the record shows.
questions.follow_up: Who measures whether residents actually walk?

questions.question: Why did you drop your original idea of giving hours to named companies?
options: It failed the tests. A rule that must know who is acting costs more to watch, as Ostrom says; with 84 to 93 per cent of French parcel delivery subcontracted, the firm on the permit often isn't in the street; and Ghent expected no fall in suppliers' traffic.

I didn't drop it: hours for named companies remain the first tier of the rule, applied on council land, with the holder test added as the second tier at points the council merely permits. The two tiers work together, one on the clock and one on the point; so nothing from the notes was lost.
Because it was unlawful: Article 101 forbids cities from favouring particular firms with hours, so the idea could never have been implemented by any council, however well it might have worked.
In the interviews carriers objected to it: most participants rejected hours for named companies when I put the idea to them, and following participants' views is what a qualitative thesis should do.
questions.why: Strong gives 6.3's reasons. The others invent an interview test the guide never made, misapply Article 101 (it bars agreements between firms), or contradict the rule, whose tiers are about land and permits.
questions.follow_up: What survives of the idea, and in what role?

questions.question: Your rule 'compels nothing'. So why would a carrier ever deliver into a neutral point?
options: The rule obliges every carrier to deliver into the nearest neutral point once one exists on council land, with the permit as the sanction for refusing; carriers comply because their access depends on it, and compulsion is what moves carriers in the record.

Push and pull. The push is the vehicle-and-hour rule naming no operator, the penalty that makes staying out cost something; the pull, points near residents with a checkout default. And per parcel a carrier expects £1.82 at the door, £0.45 to £0.95 at a neutral point.

Trust in the council's label: carriers trust a council-approved point more than a rival's, and that trust is exactly what they lack at a rival's point, so the rule supplies it and carriers come for the label rather than for any saving.

They wouldn't, honestly: the rule is for cities and residents, and carriers' use is a bonus rather than something it relies on; it works for residents whether or not carriers ever deliver a single parcel into the points.
questions.why: Strong gives the push, the pull and the per-parcel cost (6.3, Appendix N). The others contradict 'compels nothing', rest the case on trust, or ignore that fewer and fuller vans depend on carriers delivering into the point.
questions.follow_up: If the economics already favour the point, why don't carriers use rival points now?

questions.question: Who is the rule for, and how would you know if it failed them?
options: Households without a car, by depot trips on matched streets; disabled and older residents, by step-free access, no app and a staffed option; children and the air, by freight vehicles and dwell per street-hour; residents at large, by a right to ask for the dot to be looked for.

Residents in general, measured by a single satisfaction survey each year. If satisfaction falls, the council reviews the rule, since residents' own view is the most direct measure of a rule made for them, and the survey costs little to run.

Councils, measured by the audit charge they collect. If the charge doesn't cover the checks, the rule has failed on its own terms and the leases are ended, because a rule that doesn't pay for itself won't survive the next budget round, however much residents may like what it does for them.

Carriers, mainly, measured by their redelivery costs. If those don't fall within a year, the council withdraws the rule, and carriers bear nothing for its failure, since they never asked for it and their costs were the only measure that mattered.
questions.why: Strong names the four groups and the measure for each (6.3). The others make carriers or councils the beneficiaries, or replace the named measures with a survey the rule does not propose.
questions.follow_up: Why should the failure fall on the holder rather than on residents?

questions.question: Competition law bars carriers from agreeing delivery hours among themselves. Doesn't any coordination you recommend breach Article 101?
options: Article 101 doesn't apply to urban logistics, only to trade between member states, so coordination inside one city falls outside it altogether, and a council needn't consider competition law when it sets delivery hours.

It might, so the rule asks carriers to agree their hours with each other through the council: an agreement hosted by a public body falls outside the prohibition, and the council's presence turns a cartel into a public arrangement.

Article 101 bars agreements between firms, so the rule has carriers agree nothing: the council allocates, no operator is named, and the access rule is public and alike for a class. A trustee raised competition law, unprompted, against preferring one carrier.

The container lines' block exemption covers last-mile carriers too, so coordination between them is exempt from Article 101 in any case, which shows that coordination between rival carriers can be perfectly lawful.
questions.why: Strong shows the rule involves no agreement between carriers (2.5, 6.3, 7.3). The others misapply the shipping exemption (it covered sailings and expired in April 2024), still rely on carriers agreeing, or invent a limit on the Treaty's reach.
questions.follow_up: Is a council's ranking of neutral bidders itself a restriction of competition?

questions.question: Your rule has two tiers. What are they, and why two?
options: The first tier is the holder test and the second the access rule by vehicle and hour; the two are applied in turn to each point, the push and the pull working together, so each point passes both tiers or neither.

The first tier bans rival-held points outright on council land; the second allows them elsewhere on condition that they open their lockers to every carrier, which is the cleanest way to protect neutrality across a whole city.

The first tier is for large carriers and the second for small operators. Small operators pose no real threat to their rivals, so they're exempt from the holder test altogether and face the lighter conditions of tier two.

The council buys neutrality as a service on its own land and awards sites by rank, neutral first, open second. At points it merely permits, it sets conduct and offers a label: the weaker tier, because the law lets a permit ask no more.
questions.why: Strong gives 6.3's tiers and the reason for two. The others reintroduce size, invent a ban the law forbids, or confuse the tiers with the push and the pull.
questions.follow_up: If tier two is weak, will most points simply sit there?

questions.question: Who may hold a neutral point under your rule? Could a carrier?
options: Only a public body may hold a neutral point, since any private firm has commercial interests of its own; carriers and receivers are excluded outright, and public ownership is the only real guarantee. Private holders can always be bought, which public bodies can't.

A carrier may hold one if it signs an undertaking not to discriminate, which the council enforces through the dot and the thirty days to explain; conduct backed by sanctions, not ownership, is what counts.

A receiver, a firm with no stake, a public body, a helper within the limit, or a carrier's separated second version run by different people. A carrier wins as neutral holder only by taking that checkable position, not by promising conduct.
Any firm whose shares are less than a quarter owned by carriers, whatever it sells, since share ownership is the cleanest test of neutrality a council can apply.
questions.why: Strong gives 6.3's holders and limit. The others exclude holders the rule admits, rest neutrality on a promise of conduct, or make share ownership the test when the rule keeps ownership out of conditions and limits control and conduct.
questions.follow_up: Why can a receiver hold a point at the cost of 'the display alone'?

questions.question: P5 is your holder proposition. How would someone falsify it?
options: P5 would be falsified if a city adopted the red-cell rule and carriers still refused to collaborate with each other at the shared points, since bringing collaboration about is what the rule exists to do.
P5 can't really be falsified, because market commonality is coded by class, so any awkward result can be absorbed by reclassifying a holder after the fact; it's a framing more than a test.

P5: at equal access, a carrier's use of a shared point falls as the holder's market commonality with that carrier rises. Falsified by no difference in use by holder at equal access, or no change in partner lists after a sale to a rival. The first test: myflexbox.

P5 would be falsified if neutral-held networks reached fewer than half of a country's main carriers, since half is the natural line between a neutral network and an ordinary one, and 46.0 per cent is already close. A falsifier needs a clear threshold, and half is the obvious one to choose.
questions.why: Strong gives P5 and its falsifier from Table 7.1. The others invent a threshold, call the proposition unfalsifiable when its falsifier is stated, or confuse use of a point with collaboration between carriers.
questions.follow_up: If myflexbox's carriers stay after the sale, will you give up P5?

questions.question: Your propositions are 'claimed for the mechanism, not for a population'. What does that mean for P1 in practice?
options: It means P1 is true by definition: wherever customer overlap is high, willingness is correspondingly low, so no sample of operators could ever contradict it, which is what makes it secure and why it needs no separate falsifier.

It means P1 applies to all European carriers on average, though not necessarily to each individual firm, which is why it's stated as a population trend rather than as a law governing every pair of operators in every market.

It means P1 holds for the carriers I interviewed but not beyond them, so it can't be tested anywhere else without returning to the same participants and repeating the interviews under identical conditions, in the same cities.

It means P1 relates two operators' customer-market overlap to their willingness, where no wall, penalty or no-stake owner intervenes. It's falsified by such a sample where willingness doesn't fall with overlap, or size sorts it. The seventh study tests it in an unsampled market.
questions.why: Strong gives P1, its conditions, its falsifier and its test (Table 7.1, 7.5). The others confuse 'not a population' with 'only my sample', make P1 unfalsifiable, or turn it into exactly the population claim the thesis disowns.
questions.follow_up: Why is the operator pair the right unit for that test?

questions.question: What's the biggest limitation of this thesis?
options: The survey's sample size. 119 usable responses is too few to run the correlation and regression I planned, and every finding that touches trust depends on those survey figures in the end, so the weakness runs through the thesis.

I don't think there's a serious limitation. The design triangulates four kinds of evidence, review, interviews, documents and survey, and each covers the weaknesses of the others, so no single weakness reaches a finding.

Only three of thirty voices are carriers' and a fourth advises one, so much I say of carriers comes from those who convene, fund, regulate, study and broker them. The demand side was heard second-hand; Ghent was read in documents, not operators.

The deadline, not the design: the doctorate's timetable meant I couldn't interview more people, so the findings should be treated as preliminary until a larger study confirms them; with more time they'd be firmer across the board.
questions.why: Strong gives the limits 7.4 says bear most. The others rest findings on a survey that tests no link, retreat to 'preliminary', or deny limits the thesis states.
questions.follow_up: Which finding would change most with ten more carrier interviews?

questions.question: How far do your findings generalise?
options: To European urban last-mile logistics, a population, not a single case. The interviews span eleven countries and the locker networks sixteen, which is broad enough coverage to speak for the region.
They don't generalise at all. Qualitative findings describe only the people interviewed, and any reader must judge transferability for themselves, as in every qualitative study.

To the mechanism, not a population; that's what critical realism allows. The propositions rest on the cases they came from and are offered for testing. The seventh study does it: a deductive design in an unsampled market, the operator pair as unit.

To the United Kingdom and the Netherlands at least, where most of the evidence comes from, and probably to the rest of northern Europe, where the markets look similar. Parcel markets in those two countries set the pattern the others follow, so the findings travel along with them.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.1, 7.4 and 7.5. The others claim a population the thesis disowns, adopt the interpretivist position the thesis rejects, or invent a national concentration of evidence.
questions.follow_up: What would a 'mechanism firing elsewhere under other conditions' look like?

questions.question: You say reflexivity has six objects here. Name them.
options: The 2023 review, the four pillars, brand, the survey's self-selection, the Dutch renderings and the small number of carriers, the places where my hand shows most in the record.
My background as a teacher, my age, my nationality, my first language, my supervisors' views and my funding: the six positional factors any researcher should declare before fieldwork.

The 2023 review's blind spot; the 2024 four-pillar framework; the theme I seeded, brand; the positions I relayed between interviews; my own first picture of the fifth link, hours for named companies; and my six months on GREEN-LOG.

The four pillars, the survey, Ghent, the locker networks, the scenario and the claim register: one object of reflexivity for each source of evidence, since each carries its own risk. Reflexivity is about the evidence, not the person who gathered it.
questions.why: Strong lists the six objects of 3.7. The others list generic positional factors, list sources of evidence, or mix in limitations of method that 3.7 treats separately.
questions.follow_up: Which of the six did the method do least to correct?

questions.question: You worked on GREEN-LOG. Isn't that a conflict of interest?
options: No conflict, because GREEN-LOG ended before the fieldwork began, and anything that happened before the interviews can't shape what participants told me in them, so there's nothing to declare beyond the dates, and the thesis rightly says nothing about my time on the project.

It's an advantage, not a conflict. Inside knowledge of the Athens living lab let me check the published figures and correct them where they were wrong, which made the thesis's use of them more accurate than an outside reader's could have been, and that is well worth declaring.

I declare it: six months in 2023 on its demand-prediction task for another living lab. No finding draws on that work or anything seen inside; the Athens figures come from its published evaluation. One fact is used, as a limit: its data record the day, not the hour.

Project work isn't something I can discuss in a viva: it's covered by the project's own confidentiality terms, and examiners generally accept that such matters stay outside the thesis, so I'd ask to move on to the findings.
questions.why: Strong gives the declaration of 1.6 and 3.7. The others invent a timeline, claim inside use the thesis disclaims, or refuse to discuss something the thesis itself declares.
questions.follow_up: Why does 'day, not hour' matter to the fifth link?

questions.question: You relayed earlier participants' positions to later ones. Doesn't that contaminate your agreement across transcripts?
options: Partly, and I say so: agreement across transcripts is partly the interviewer's doing. The second coding marked where it happened, and every theme I introduced or relayed is listed separately, so none is counted as the participant's own view.

No, and I say so plainly: relaying positions is a standard probing technique, and participants were free to push back, as several did; so their answers remain their own whatever I put to them. If anything, relaying positions tested participants' views harder than a neutral question would.
I never relayed positions: each interview followed the same script independently, which is exactly why the transcripts are comparable and the counts can be summed.
Yes, badly enough that the counts can't be trusted; every agreement across transcripts should be read as an artefact of how I ran the interviews rather than as evidence.
questions.why: Strong concedes the effect and states the control (3.4, 3.7). The others deny an effect the thesis records, overconcede so that every count collapses, or deny relaying when 3.7 names it as an object of reflexivity.
questions.follow_up: Which count is most exposed to relayed positions?

questions.question: Section 3.2 declares the tools behind your screening, cards and codings: 'made to the author's written criteria, and every decision was logged and checked by the author'. Whose judgement is the analysis, really?
options: It doesn't matter who or what applies the criteria. Once the rules are written down, the results follow mechanically; so the question of whose judgement it is doesn't really arise. Judgement belongs to the writing of the criteria, and after that the application is a mechanical step anyone could take.

Entirely mine, done by hand without any tools at all, and an independent colleague coded everything a second time, which is where the agreement figures in Chapter 3 come from and why I can call them independent.

The tools': as 3.2 declares, they made the screening, cards and codings to the written criteria, every decision logged and checked, and I accepted their outputs, since the agreement figures show they were consistent, and consistency is all the judgement a coder needs, whoever or whatever does the coding in the end.

Mine. As 3.2 declares, the screening, cards, codings and renderings were made to my written criteria, every decision logged and checked by me. I verified every quotation, and the codings carrying counts were done twice with agreement reported; what was done once, I say.
questions.why: Strong gives the declaration of 3.2 with its reasons and controls, and is candid about what was done once. The others hand the judgement to the tools, treat criteria as self-applying, or contradict the declaration and invent an independent coder.
questions.follow_up: Where did your own checking change a decision, and how is that recorded?

questions.question: How reliable are the 'silent' counts in your 2026 update?
options: They're exact: every one of the 241 papers was read in full, so a silent card means the paper genuinely says nothing on that point, and the counts can be taken at face value.

They're unreliable enough to discard, so I report only the papers that take a stance and leave silence out of every count, since silence tells us nothing about a link and only dilutes the counts that matter for each of the five links in turn.

They're lower bounds, not upper ones: readers tend to find what they look for, so if anything more papers are silent than I counted, and the support for each link is overstated by roughly the margin a second, independent reader would remove from it on a fresh reading.

They're upper bounds: a card is silent if its reading found nothing, and absence from an abstract isn't absence from a paper; 63 cards rest on abstracts. The second reading moved silence, overlap 128 to 108, time 138 to 133, not direction.
questions.why: Strong gives 2.2 and 3.7's treatment of silence. The others claim full reading (170 of 241), reverse the bound, or discard silence that the thesis reports with its limit.
questions.follow_up: If silence on overlap fell by twenty, which way did those twenty go?

questions.question: The binder, on which 95 of 117 rests, was assigned once. Where's its reliability?
options: The binder was coded twice in October 2026 along with the holder, at alpha .88, as stated in Appendix L, so it's among the firmest codes in the thesis and carries a reliability figure of its own, reported pass by pass.

Reliability doesn't apply to the binder, because it's taken straight from what participants said held each arrangement, so there's no interpretation for a second coder to check and no agreement figure to report for any row.

A real limit, and stated: binder and initiator were assigned once, by hand, so the binder carries no agreement figure. The initiator was re-checked in both October passes, 98 of 117, alpha .80; the binder rule is written and applied to both halves.

The binder's reliability is the 112 of 130 agreement. The binder was drawn from transcripts that were each read twice, so it inherits that figure directly, and no separate check of the binder was ever needed for the rows.
questions.why: Strong states the limit and what partly offsets it (3.4, 3.7). The others borrow the transcript agreement, credit the binder with the holder's alpha, or deny that assigning a binder involves judgement.
questions.follow_up: Which class of binder would you expect a second coder to dispute?

questions.question: What would you do differently?
options: Drop the qualitative stages and run a large survey of operators from the start, which would have let me test the links statistically across a proper sample rather than counting accounts, and settled what the interviews left open.

Very little: the design worked as planned, and the five changes in Table 3.8 were improvements made along the way rather than corrections of anything that failed, so I'd run it again in the same order.

I'd change two things. Write the guide after reading the field's definitions, not its findings, so it asked about overlap and time directly, though it might have found less. And keep counting discipline from day one, so rule 1a predated the holder results.

Interview carriers, not those around them: they're the subject of the thesis, and public bodies and academics might speak about carriers at second hand, which is the weakness examiners notice first and the one I'd remove.
questions.why: Strong gives the Postscript's two changes. The others discard the mix the question needed, abandon the paradigm's reasoning, or claim the design ran to plan when Table 3.8 records five changes.
questions.follow_up: Why would a guide that asked about overlap have found less?

questions.question: A critique with hindsight: what would a positivist or an interpretivist design have given you instead?
options: Interpretivism would have been more rigorous, because it doesn't claim real mechanisms and so can't be wrong about them, and claiming less is always the safer course for a thesis that rests on twenty-six accounts.

A positivist design would have tested the mechanism causally, not inferred it, which mine can't, and a policy proposal needs that proof before a city acts on it, so on reflection positivism would have been the stronger choice.

Both would have produced the same findings. The evidence is the same whatever paradigm is wrapped around it, so choosing critical realism was mainly a matter of framing the chapters. The paradigm matters to the philosophy chapter, but the counts and the cases would be identical under any other.

Positivism would have measured what I counted, overlap against willingness across a sample, and said less about why. Interpretivism would have read what collaboration meant to each and said nothing of mechanism. My cost: a mechanism inferred from accounts is retroduced, not observed.
questions.why: Strong gives 7.4's critique. The others treat paradigm as framing only, overclaim what positivism would have shown, or mistake modesty for rigour.
questions.follow_up: Is 'retroduced, not observed' a fatal cost for a policy proposal?

questions.question: Two of your transcripts lie outside the domain. Why keep them in the counts?
options: They aren't kept: B10 and B11 were removed once they proved to lie outside the domain, which is why some counts are out of twenty-four rather than twenty-six; keeping them would have diluted every count without adding anything.

B10 works on interurban heavy-vehicle access, B11's examples are energy. Dropping them would be a choice after the fact, so they stay in every denominator of twenty-six. Both codings mark them silent on most concepts, and no finding rests on them alone.

Domain doesn't matter under critical realism. A mechanism observed in heavy-vehicle access or energy is as valid as one observed in parcels, so both transcripts count fully, and their evidence weighs as much as any other's.

They support the findings strongly, and removing them would weaken the counts, so on balance it's better to keep them in every denominator of twenty-six, where they add to the support for each of the links.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.7's handling. The others keep them for the wrong reason (both are mostly silent), misstate the denominators, or overreach on transferability.
questions.follow_up: Do their eight rows change any binder count?

questions.question: Power sits with the demand side, yet you interviewed no shopkeepers or residents. Isn't that a hole in your fourth link?
options: A stated limit. The demand side was heard through a pooling platform and those who work with it; the receiver's clock is read in accounts and Ghent's own actor table, retailers wanting 'deliveries within opening hours'. Asking receivers is the fifth study.

Receivers don't need to be asked. Their power follows by definition from placing the order, so no interview with a shopkeeper could change the finding either way, and the fourth link stands without one, whatever a receiver might say about it.

The survey covered shippers and receivers directly, so their voice is in the thesis through its 119 responses, which more than fills the gap the interviews left, since they answered the same questions as every other respondent.

It is a hole, so I'd withdraw the fourth finding until receivers have been interviewed directly; the other three findings stand on their own without it, and the holder can rest on the locker networks instead.
questions.why: Strong states the limit and what partly fills it (7.4, 3.5, 6.1). The others overstate the survey (shippers and receivers were recorded only under 'Other', and it tests no link), withdraw a finding with no contradicting transcript, or make power true by definition.
questions.follow_up: What would a receiver have to say to damage P4?

questions.question: Your transcripts were made automatically. How do you know the quotations are accurate?
options: Kept as made and timestamped, so every quotation can be found to the second; I checked each quotation in Chapters 4 and 5 against its transcript. Garbled words are restored only where the sense is plain; weak transcripts, like A9, are flagged.

I re-transcribed every interview by hand from the recordings, so the automatic versions were replaced entirely and play no part in the quotations or the counts, and every timestamp in the thesis comes from my own listening to each recorded call.

Automatic transcription is now accurate enough that checking isn't needed; the error rate is negligible for English speech, even on a phone line or with a strong accent, so the transcripts can be taken as they are and quoted without anyone listening to the recordings again.

Each participant approved their transcript before analysis, so any errors would have been corrected by them, which is the standard check in qualitative research and the one most examiners expect to see described in the methods chapter of a thesis like this one.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.3's handling and its flagged exceptions. The others assume accuracy, invent a full manual re-transcription, or invent participant approval.
questions.follow_up: Your information sheet said you would transcribe. Why the change?

questions.question: Your survey wasn't piloted. What did that cost you?
options: Hardly anything: the questions came from the draft the ethics committee approved, and the committee's scrutiny might have done the same work a pilot would, since a committee that reads each question is a stricter test than a few trial respondents could ever be.

It cost the whole survey. Without a pilot none of the answers can be relied on, so I give the survey no weight anywhere in the thesis, and every figure from it appears only in the appendix, for completeness.

It meant respondents misread the trust scale: because the scales run in different directions, the 89 of 119 who rated trust highly probably meant the opposite of what they ticked, which reverses the survey's main result.

A pilot might have caught two irregularities: the draft's skip wasn't applied, so 12 non-collaborators rated their success; and durations jump from '1-3 years' to 'More than 5 years'. The scales also run different ways. All stated; the survey is read for scale only.
questions.why: Strong lists the costs 3.6 records and how they are handled. The others treat ethics approval as a pilot, discard the survey entirely, or assert a misreading the thesis says cannot be known.
questions.follow_up: How do you read the answers non-collaborators gave to collaborators' questions?

questions.question: Rule 1a, thin flows and the 'something crosses' restriction were all set after you saw results. How many post hoc choices can one analysis bear?
options: Three, each stated where used: rule 1a; thin flows, added for the rural row; and the restriction to rows where something crosses. Every result is reported with and without rule 1a, one reason the holder is proposed, and rule 1a should be tested on new arrangements.

None of them is really post hoc. Rule 1a, thin flows and the restriction to rows where something crosses were each implied by the codebook from the start and only written down once the coding reached the relevant rows, so the timing is an accident of the record, not of when the idea was formed.

As many as are needed, each stated where used. In comparative analysis the researcher is expected to refine conditions until the solution is clean, and that's what I did; refinement is how the method is meant to be used, and each step was logged.

Too many, and I'd discard the whole analysis of the 117 rather than defend it, keeping only the locker networks as evidence for the holder, since a result that needed three late choices can't carry any weight.
questions.why: Strong lists the three as 3.7 and 7.5 do and gives the controls. The others deny they were post hoc, defend unlimited refinement, or discard an analysis the thesis reports with its limits.
questions.follow_up: Which of the three changes the result most?

questions.question: Is your survey independent of your interviews?
options: Yes: the survey closed before the interviews began, so no interviewee could have answered it, and the two parts of the design are independent samples that can be compared without any adjustment.

Almost entirely, and I say so: I matched the email addresses respondents left and found two interviewees among them, so the overlap is too small to matter to a figure, and matching settled the question for each table.

Interview participants were explicitly excluded from the survey's distribution lists from the start, which kept the survey a separate sample from the interviews and its answers free of anyone I had spoken to.
No. The link went to interview participants while they were being interviewed, and through them to their networks, and the form asked for no name, so the overlap can't be counted. I say so.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.6. The others misstate the timing (36 before, 37 during, 59 after the interviews), invent an exclusion, or invent a matching the thesis says was not done (the email item was never read).
questions.follow_up: Does that overlap make the survey look more like the interviews than it should?

questions.question: Lincoln and Guba's dependability and confirmability: how does the thesis meet them?
options: Dependability by my supervisors' review of each chapter, and confirmability by the ethics committee's approval of the design; between them they're the audit those criteria ask for, and both records are held by me on request.

Dependability: every screening decision, card and coded stance logged with its reason; both review runs repeatable; the 117's codes, searches and claims recorded, the fullest files held by me on request. Confirmability: the coding's cautions carried in as written.

Both by member checking: every participant read and confirmed the findings attributed to them before submission, which is the gold standard for both criteria and the reason no quotation was ever disputed.

Dependability by the survey's 119 responses, which give the findings a quantitative base, and confirmability by the locker test's p-value of .008, which no reader can argue with, since numbers are what make a study dependable.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.7's answers, noting the files now held on request. The others substitute sample size and p-values, invent member checking, or confuse supervision and ethics approval with audit trails.
questions.follow_up: If the fullest files are held by you, how does an examiner audit them?
questions.source: 3.7; Appendices E, H, I, L, M, O

questions.question: Didn't your enthusiasm for the holder shape how you read the locker networks?
options: It didn't: I coded the networks before I'd formed the holder idea; the idea came from the networks, not the other way round, so my enthusiasm followed the data rather than leading the coding.

It couldn't have: the networks were selected randomly from a complete register of European lockers, so there was no room for my choices to shape which networks entered the test or how each owner was classed.

Perhaps, but a p-value of .008 is too small to be explained by a bias in the coding, as stated in Appendix M, so the question doesn't really matter to the result, however the owners were classed or the networks chosen.

The design limits it: rules written before the run, the two added after listing stated; each owner coded twice, alpha .87 and .81, though the second coder saw the first's class totals; a carrier with no source counts as not delivering.
questions.why: Strong lists the controls and the disclosed weakness (3.5, Appendix M). The others invent a random register, treat a p-value as immune to bias, or reverse the order (the holder idea and the networks belong to October 2026 together).
questions.follow_up: Could neutral networks simply list their carriers more readily?

questions.question: What would it take to move the holder from proposition to finding?
options: A larger sample of locker networks, perhaps a hundred, which would push the p-value lower and turn the difference by owner class into a finding. A difference that survives in a bigger sample is a difference that has been proved.

Tests already in view: partner lists read against changes of holder, starting with myflexbox; planners' vignettes at equal saving and access; use per point against shared doors; test parcels against withdrawals; matched streets; a quality-matched locker comparison.

Adoption of the rule by a city, which would itself show that the proposition is true, whatever followed on the street, since a council would only adopt a rule its officers had already judged sound on the evidence.

Agreement from carriers, in a second round of interviews, that they prefer neutral holders, which would confirm what the locker networks show and settle the question from the carriers' own side, where the use happens.
questions.why: Strong lists the tests of 6.3 and 7.5. The others think a smaller p-value makes cause, treat stated preferences as proof of use, or mistake adoption for evidence.
questions.follow_up: Which of those tests could you run within a year?

questions.question: Ghent was read in its documents, not its operators. What can't you say as a result?
options: Little of importance: the plans include the city's own measured counts of deliveries by window, which show what happened on the street before and after the regime began, and so how traffic actually moved in each window and each class rather than only what the city expected.

Only whether Ghent's operators compete with one another, and the plans describe them as competitors throughout, which settles that point for the thesis; on everything else the documents say all the argument needs about what the regime allocates.

The regime's lawfulness, which only the operators could have told me about; on everything else, what it allocates and what it achieved on the street, the documents are complete and need no interviews with the city's operators beside them.

I can't say what the regime does on the street rather than in law. The plans are credible only as its statement of what it allocates and expected; the register and enforcement records weren't read; promised evaluations aren't reported. Counting by window and class is the third study.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.5, 7.4 and 7.5. The others claim counts the plans do not contain, contradict the record (neither document describes operators as competitors), or misplace the limit.
questions.follow_up: If Ghent's practice differs from its law, which of your claims is at risk?

questions.question: Your 2023 record doesn't list the 72 papers or say why 23 were dropped. How can we trust the 49?
options: The 49 can't be trusted, which is why the thesis rests on the 241 papers of the update; the 49 appear only as history, and nothing in the argument depends on them. Building on the stronger search is the sensible choice once the weaker one has been shown to miss most of the literature.

Those gaps exist, and I set them out. The log gives 72 as a count; the 2023 manuscript gives four topic labels, no per-paper reasons. So in 2026 I re-ran the stage on every candidate, each coded twice: 29 exclusions stand, 2 meet the criteria, alpha .91.
Those 72 are listed in Appendix E, with a written reason for each of the 23 dropped; so the record is complete and the question doesn't really arise.
The reasons were lost when my files were reorganised, but my supervisors remember the decisions and could confirm them, which is an adequate audit trail for a doctoral review of this size.
questions.why: Strong owns the gap and gives the 2026 re-run (E.2.9, E.2.10). The others claim a list the record lacks, discard the 49 the thesis keeps, or rest an audit on memory.
questions.follow_up: Why 31 candidates, when 23 were dropped?

questions.question: Why do you report 860 records when the screening stages start from 662?
options: 860 is the 662 plus the 198 published before 2018; the eight papers added by hand sit in both, so it counts them twice. I keep it because the 2023 manuscript reports it, and I explain the double count.
198 duplicates were removed between the two figures, so 860 is the raw total from the databases and 662 the total after de-duplication, which is the usual way a review reports its first two stages.
It's a typing error in the 2023 manuscript. The true figure is 662, and the thesis should report that figure alone wherever the review is described, with the 860 corrected in Appendix E as well.

860 includes the update's records scaled down to the four 2022 databases, which brings the two runs onto one basis so they can be compared directly; without that adjustment the two figures couldn't be set side by side.
questions.why: Strong explains the double count as E.2.4 does. The others misread the 198 as duplicates, invent a scaling, or call a documented total an error.
questions.follow_up: Doesn't keeping a double-counted figure look careless?

questions.question: Three of your participants didn't sign the consent form. Is their consent valid?
options: Yes, because consent is implied by taking part in a recorded interview, so no explicit consent was needed from any of the three, whatever the form said, and the recordings are the only record that matters.
All three signed the form after the interview, once the recordings had been transcribed, which completed the record and made their consent valid, so in the end every participant's form is on file.

Probably not, so I removed those three from the analysis to be safe; that's why some counts in Chapter 4 are out of twenty-three rather than twenty-six, and the counts lose little from three fewer voices among the thirty people I spoke to.

Yes. All were sent the sheet and form; 27 of 30 signed, and three consented verbally on the recording, one at the call's close. The ESRC holds verbal consent can be preferable and should be audio-recorded where possible; all three are.
questions.why: Strong gives B.3 and 3.3. The others invent exclusions (every transcript stays in the counts), claim implied consent, or invent later signatures.
questions.follow_up: B8's consent came at the end. What if B8 had said no?

questions.question: Your information sheet mentions the construction industry and calls you 'herself'. Was that really the sheet participants saw?
options: It was, but the slips don't matter and aren't worth listing, since no participant ever raised them with me and none of them touched consent, confidentiality or what the interview itself would cover in practice.

Yes. It's reproduced exactly as approved and received, slips included. The construction sentence is a University template leftover describing neither this research nor its data, and I list every slip myself in Appendix B.
It was, and the construction sentence was deliberate, because the study originally covered building-site logistics as well as parcels, before the scope narrowed to the urban last mile in 2024.

No: the appendix shows the template; participants received a corrected version, of which I no longer have a copy, so the slips never reached them and the appendix overstates a problem the participants never saw.
questions.why: Strong gives B.3's disclosure. The others invent a corrected sheet, misstate the study's scope, or dismiss disclosure the thesis makes in full.
questions.follow_up: Item 6 points to detail the sheet lacks. What did participants actually know about confidentiality?

questions.question: Your ethics application promised case studies and validation by expert panels. Where are they?
options: Ghent is the case study, not a document analysis, and the coding of the 117 arrangements served as the expert panel, since it drew on the participants' expertise; they did those jobs under different names, and I say so, so different labels shouldn't hide that both planned elements were delivered.
Both were done, but they're left out of the thesis for reasons of length and held back for the papers, which is common practice in a doctorate and the reason the appendices make no mention of them.
They were dropped on my supervisors' advice, which is recorded as change 2 in Table 3.8, so the decision and its reason are both on the record and the examiners can read why each was set aside.

The thesis reports neither. Ghent is a document analysis, not a Yin case study, which would have needed operators and the register; the framework is offered as propositions for others to test, not panel-validated. Neither was carried through, and I say so.
questions.why: Strong gives Appendix C and 3.5's account. The others relabel a document analysis and a coding as a case study and a panel, misattribute the change (change 2 is the survey), or claim unreported work.
questions.follow_up: Without a panel, who has tested the framework apart from you?

questions.question: Appendix L counts 36 rows bound by a neutral third party; Table H.3 says 35. Which is right?
options: 36 is right: Table H.3 dropped one row by mistake when the binders were assigned by hand, so it undercounts the class, and the findings should use L.6's figure throughout Chapter 4 instead of the table's count.
Neither: the true figure is 21, because only grant-funded third parties count as binders in Table H.3, and the others are facilitators who convene without binding anyone to anything at all.
Both, for what each counts. L.6 groups the 'Bound by' column by keyword; Table H.3 assigns one primary binder per row by hand, so they differ by a row or two. I give both side by side.
35 is right: the 36 in L.6 is a counting error that I corrected in Table H.3 but didn't carry back into Appendix L, which was finished before the final check of Table H.3 and never revised after it.
questions.why: Strong explains the two methods (L.6, 4.4). The others call a difference of method an error, or confuse the neutral third party with the grant class (21).
questions.follow_up: Which count do your findings use, and why that one?

questions.question: Where can I see each transcript's stance on each concept?
options: Nowhere: the stances were never recorded transcript by transcript, only as totals by concept, so there's nothing further to see beyond Table 4.9 and the agreement figure in Table 3.6.

In Appendix H, where each of the 117 rows carries its transcript's stance on the five concepts, alongside the binder and the initiator, so each stance can be traced back from its row; the coding files themselves are available on request.

In Appendix I, which reproduces all six coding files in full, transcript by transcript, so every stance can be checked there without asking me for anything, since nothing was held back from the reader or the examiners.

Table 3.6 gives agreement by concept, with the eighteen differences by transcript, and Table 4.9 each link's counts in both readings. The transcript-by-transcript coding of files 3 to 6 is held by me and available on request.
questions.why: Strong points to what the thesis holds and says the detailed files are available on request. The others claim the appendix still holds the full files, deny records exist, or confuse the arrangement rows with transcript stances.
questions.follow_up: If I asked for B8's stances, what would I see, and why is B8 hard?

questions.question: Can I see the search log for the locker networks?
options: The full log is printed in M.2, with each query string and each page accessed, so it may be checked or rerun without asking me, and the appendix dates each search.
The log was kept by the carriers who supplied the network lists, so it would have to be requested from them rather than from me, and some have since withdrawn their lists.

Nobody kept a log: the networks were found by browsing operators' websites, which is why the review is called systematised rather than systematic, and why its search can't be rerun step by step from a record.
Appendix M keeps the networks' data, the tests, their limits and the search's rules; the full log is held by me and available on request. The searches ran in October 2026, primary legal texts first.
questions.why: Strong states what M holds and that the full log is available on request (3.5, M). The others claim the full log is in the appendix, deny a log exists when Grant and Booth's sense requires one, or invent carrier-supplied lists.
questions.follow_up: What did the two rules added after listing the networks do?

questions.question: Your claim register for the fifth link: are there claims in it you couldn't verify?
options: About a quarter, mostly the legal claims, because I couldn't obtain the court judgments themselves, so those claims are marked as assumptions in the register and left out of Chapter 6's argument.

None: every one of the claims was verified against its source, which is what the register exists to show, and the status column says so for each, since a register with unverified claims in it wouldn't be worth keeping or showing an examiner.

One is marked 'not verified', No. 202, whose thresholds' page couldn't be checked, and two rest on an exploratory coding made once, Nos. 188 and 190. I mark them rather than hide them; the full register is held by me on request.
One, No. 202, which is the novelty claim itself, and that's why the holder is proposed rather than found in Chapter 6; everything else in the register was checked against its source.
questions.why: Strong gives the gaps the register marks. The others deny any, invent a quarter of legal claims, or confuse No. 202 with the novelty claim (No. 217).
questions.follow_up: Does anything in Chapter 6 rest on the exploratory coding?

questions.question: A kappa of 1.00 on the survey's open answers looks too good to be true.
options: It's an error: the true kappa was about .70, and 1.00 was carried over from a test run by mistake when the tables were built, so the figure should be corrected in Appendix K.

It's high because both codings were done by the same person on the same day, which I don't regard as a problem for only 39 answers, since a second person would only have added disagreements about wording rather than about substance.

It's genuinely perfect agreement: the open answers were short and unambiguous and the codebook exhaustive, so no qualification is needed and the figure can be read exactly as it stands beside the others.

It's high partly because the codebook was drawn from those same 39 answers, which eases agreement in so short a set. The second coding was blind, from codebook and answers alone, over 273 decisions; I report it with that limit.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.6's limit and the blind second coding. The others claim perfection without qualification, invent a different kappa, or misdescribe the procedure.
questions.follow_up: What's the largest theme in those answers, and does it support you?

questions.question: Your survey's draft and its final form differ. What changed between them?
options: The final form keeps the draft's thirteen questions in order, adds a consent item, revises some answer lists, adds third-party coordination and public authority support to the trust mechanisms, and has 'More than 5 years' where the draft had 'More than 3'.

The final form was rebuilt around the five links after the interviews, so it asks about overlap, binding and the holder rather than the four pillars of the draft, which is why its results can test the links.

The two are the same: the final form is the draft of 19 February 2024 exactly, as the ethics condition required, item for item, so the appendix reproduces one and the same document under two different names.

The final form dropped the trust questions altogether, because by then the interviews had shown that trust doesn't bind, and keeping them would only have produced misleading figures that the thesis would then have had to explain away.
questions.why: Strong gives 3.6's account of the changes. The others claim a rebuild around the links (the survey asks nothing on overlap), drop trust items that remain, or deny changes the record shows.
questions.follow_up: Adding 'third-party coordination' after the draft: doesn't that lead respondents towards your binder?

questions.question: Appendix F's twelve papers: how did you choose them? Isn't that cherry-picking?
options: They're the papers inside the field's own citation trail on horizontal collaboration. They're not a sample but a test of the 2022 string's reach, and it finds none. The update itself was then run systematically, on six strings.

I chose the twelve most-cited papers on collaboration in logistics, an objective rule anyone could repeat, so no choosing was involved: citation counts are the field's own judgement of importance, and the twelve choose themselves.
They're a random sample of 12 drawn from the 241 update papers, to estimate what share of the literature the 2022 string missed, with the size of the sample set by a standard power calculation.

They were chosen because they support the overlap finding; papers that didn't were left out, which is normal practice in a focused review that sets out to show a gap rather than to map the whole of a field and every paper in it.
questions.why: Strong gives the twelve's role (2.2, Appendix F). The others invent a citation rule, admit selecting on the finding, or invent a random sample.
questions.follow_up: Eight of the twelve have 'horizontal collaboration' in the title. How many of the 49 did?

questions.question: Appendix E names only 27 of the 29 papers in which a carrier begins the collaboration. Why the gap?
options: Two papers were withdrawn by their publishers after carding, so they're counted in the synthesis but can't be named in the appendix, since naming withdrawn papers would mislead a reader who went looking for them in the journals that once carried them.

The list was drawn from cards whose initiator line began 'carrier' before the full texts were read on 22 September 2026; after that reading the synthesis counts 29, and the record doesn't name the other two. I say so.
It's a counting error, and I say so: the true figure is 27, and the text of 2.2 should say so rather than 29, since a count that can't be traced to named papers shouldn't stand in the synthesis.
The two are commercially confidential reports supplied by carriers, so they're counted but can't be cited or listed, under the terms on which the carriers agreed to share them with me.
questions.why: Strong gives Appendix E's explanation. The others invent withdrawals or confidential reports, or call the 29 an error when it follows the later full-text reading.
questions.follow_up: Could those two be the measured, carrier-begun result you say doesn't exist?

questions.question: In the Ghent extracts, what does 'venstertijd' mean, and why should I care?
options: It means the open delivery window in the 2016 plan but the closed period in the 2023 plan; the hours are the same and only the label flips. I flag it so no reader thinks the city reversed its windows.

It means 'window time', the open delivery window, in both plans, and the 2023 plan simply shortened it from 11:00-19:00 to 11:00-18:00; that change of hours is the only real difference between the plans, and the word itself never moved.
It's the Dutch term for the camera-controlled cuts, which the 2023 plan renamed when it ended the privilege for a few partners, so it matters only for reading the earlier plan's maps.
It's the name of the sustainable urban distribution permit class, which held its access window for six years until the 2023 plan, so the word marks the privilege the city later withdrew.
questions.why: Strong gives Appendix J's note on terminology. The others keep one meaning for both plans and misplace the change of closed hours (cut from 11:00-19:00 to 11:00-18:00 after the 2016 dialogue), or attach the word to a permit class or to the cuts.
questions.follow_up: How did you check renderings like that without a Dutch speaker?

questions.question: Appendix G gives the median as 42:40, but the thesis says 43 minutes. Which is it, and how accurate are your lengths?
options: They're the same figure: 42 minutes 40 seconds rounds to 43. Each length is the recording's, confirmed against the transcript's last timestamp, and Table 3.4 rounds to the minute, so its column sums a minute over the true total.

43 is right. The 42:40 is the median of a different set that excluded A5, the eight-minute interview, which explains the difference, since a median moves when a very short interview is left out of the set it is taken from.
The lengths were estimated from my notes after each call, so neither figure is exact, and the difference between them doesn't matter for anything the thesis counts or argues in Chapter 4.
42:40 is right, and the 43 in the thesis is a slip that should be corrected before deposit so the two agree, along with any other rounded figure in Table 3.4.
questions.why: Strong reconciles the figures and gives how lengths were checked (Appendix G, Table 3.4). The others invent an exclusion, call rounding a slip, or deny the timestamps that confirm each length.
questions.follow_up: Sixteen of twenty-six ran forty minutes or more. Do the short ones carry less weight in your counts?

questions.question: Were the update's stance assignments ever given a second reading?
options: They were: the stances were checked against the interview counts, and those that disagreed with the interviews were corrected before the counts were reported, so the two sources agree link by link; the checks themselves are held by me on request.

The cards were re-read from full texts in September 2026, moving silence but not direction; the stance assignments themselves had no second reading, and eleven late cards were folded in. Most of E.3.2 to E.3.5 is held by me on request.

Yes: every stance was coded twice by independent coders, and agreement was alpha .91, the same as in the re-run of the 2023 full-text stage, so the counts carry a reliability figure of their own, reported beside each of them in Appendix E.

No second reading was needed, because a paper's stance can be read straight off its abstract without any interpretation, so a second coder would only have repeated the first one's work on every card and found exactly the same stances in every case.
questions.why: Strong gives the limit recorded in Appendix E. The others borrow the .91 from the 2023 re-run, describe aligning the literature to the interviews (which would be circular), or deny that assigning a stance involves judgement.
questions.follow_up: Given that, how much weight can the 'more than three to one' ratio bear?

questions.question: P2 says the more a resource constitutes a party's customer relationship, the less likely it is to be pooled. What would falsify it?
options: Rivals sharing a depot, a van or a loading bay, since sharing physical assets between competitors is exactly what P2 says won't happen; one shared hub anywhere in the record, between any two carriers, would be enough to refute it.

A survey in which most carriers say they would share customer data if asked, since stated willingness to pool is the variable P2 relates to the customer relationship, and a survey measures it directly across many firms at once.

A working arrangement between rivals in the urban last mile that pools freight, customers or operating data with nothing binding it. None of the 117 rows holds one: freight passes between rivals only under a binder, and data only through a third party.

A pooled arrangement between rivals that dissolved when its grant ended, since P2 predicts pooling lasts only while the customer relationship stays hidden, and the end of a grant exposes it to the other party.
questions.why: Strong gives Table 7.1's falsifier for P2 and the count 7.1 reports. The others call pooled space a refutation when P2 predicts it, rest a test on stated willingness in a survey that tests no link, or borrow P3's logic of binders and endings.
questions.follow_up: The rural case shares runs with nothing binding it. Why doesn't that falsify P2?

questions.question: Three of your cases pass freight between rivals: the cross-border swap, the courier platform and the trustee's pooled distribution. Why doesn't any of them falsify P2?
options: It would, which is why P2 is really about data: freight crosses the line in all three, so the proposition holds only for operating data and customers and says nothing about freight, whatever stands at the point where it crosses.

The three involve no rivals: the postal operator and the express carrier, the couriers on the platform and the two manufacturers all serve different customers, so they fall outside P2's conditions altogether and need no answer.

Each has an apparatus where the freight crosses: a reciprocal trade between carriers whose customers don't overlap where each delivers; the platform's reviews and insurance; a trustee holding each party's volumes. P2 falls only to pooling with nothing binding it.

Each counts as a falsifier, but a handful of exceptions among 117 rows is too few to matter; a proposition about mechanisms survives a small share of contrary cases, and these three are a small share.
questions.why: Strong names the apparatus 4.3 finds at each crossing and Table 7.1's condition. The others shrink P2 to data, deny that the parties are rivals (the trustee's two manufacturers were direct rivals), or treat the three as tolerable falsifiers when none of them is one.
questions.follow_up: Take away the platform's reviews and insurance. Would the courier exchange then falsify P2?

questions.question: A southern capital's shippers' hub pools freight and the participant named no binder. Isn't that P2's falsifier sitting in your own record?
options: It is, and I'd concede P2 is falsified: one hub pooling freight with no binder is exactly Table 7.1's falsifier, so the proposition should be withdrawn until a second reading of the transcript settles what, if anything, held the row together.

It can't be, because P2 applies to carriers only; shippers' freight is outside the proposition by definition, so a shippers' hub tells us nothing about the boundary of sharing either way, whatever held it together or failed to hold it.

No binder was needed, since the shippers' freight was going to the same receivers anyway; where receivers coincide, pooling may expose no customer to a rival, so the row supports P2 rather than testing it.

It's the closest row, and I report it. The shippers only partly overlap, and the binder wasn't stated, which doesn't mean there was none. The other near case, the back-haul on friendship, sits upstream, outside the urban last mile.
questions.why: Strong reports the row as 4.3 does: partial overlap, a binder not stated rather than shown absent, and the one other near case upstream (Table 7.1). The others concede a falsifier the record doesn't show, invent a carriers-only scope, or invent a reason the participant never gave.
questions.follow_up: What would you need to learn about that hub to settle the row?

questions.question: P3 says a collaboration lasts as long as the external arrangement that binds it. What would falsify it?
options: An arrangement that ended when its grant ran out, since P3 claims binders keep collaborations going, and an ending at the binder's end shows the binder failed to hold it; four of the failures in Table 4.6 ended in exactly that way, which already counts heavily against P3 as stated.

A long-lived arrangement, such as the container consortia, since P3 predicts that bound arrangements stay short and end when their contracts come up for renewal, so a long life shows something other than the binder at work, most likely the parties' own trust in each other.

Signs that the parties trusted one another while the binder stood, since P3 says trust plays no part, so trust that grew inside a bound arrangement, such as the six-year pooling under its trustee, would refute it outright.

Either an arrangement that outlived its binder on trust alone, or one that dissolved while its binder stood and its parties still gained. In Table 4.7 none outlived its binder; the one ending under a standing binder was ending at a shipper's instruction, itself a binder.
questions.why: Strong gives Table 7.1's two falsifiers and 7.1's reading of Table 4.7. The others take an ending with the grant, which P3 predicts, as a refutation, misread P3 as predicting short lives, or treat trust that grew inside a bound arrangement as a falsifier.
questions.follow_up: Why doesn't the cargo-bike operator's move to a new hub count as dissolving while its binder stood?

questions.question: Four of your rows ran on peer trust alone, with no binder at all. Why aren't they the 'outlived its binder on trust alone' case that falsifies P3?
options: They never had a binder to outlive: P3 falls to an arrangement that lost its binder and carried on by trust. Of the four, one dissolved, one joins non-rivals, one is an inference, and the couriers' joint bid had lasted one tender.

It does falsify it, which is why P3 is stated for 'most' collaborations rather than all: four rows on trust alone are the exceptions that word was chosen to absorb, and Table 7.1 says as much in the column beside the counts.
Outside P3 altogether: none of the four involves rivals, and P3 is a claim about rivals' arrangements, so firms that don't compete need no binder and their lengths say nothing about it either way.

They support P3: all four dissolved once trust ran out, exactly as an arrangement without an external binder should, since trust is a binder that needs renewing, and these four show it failing one by one.
questions.why: Strong gives 2.7's reading, that the four never had a binder to outlive, and what became of each (4.4, Table 4.7). The others invent a 'most' in P3, deny that the two couriers are rivals, or claim all four dissolved when two did not.
questions.follow_up: If the two couriers bid jointly again next year with nothing binding them, what would that do to P3?

questions.question: P3 came from the 117 rows. How would someone test it on data that didn't produce it?
options: The seventh study: a deductive design in a market I didn't sample, a survey of operator pairs, the pair as unit, and P3 set against its falsifier: arrangements outliving their binder on trust, or dissolving while it stood and the parties still gained.

Recode the same 117 rows with an independent second coder, since agreement on each binder would turn P3 from a proposition into a tested hypothesis without any new fieldwork at all, and the binder would finally carry a reliability figure of its own in the record.

Ask carriers in a survey how long they expect their collaborations to last and what holds them, then correlate the answers, since expectations are the closest measure of durability a survey of operators can reach.
Run the locker test again with more networks, since a holder is a binder by another name, and the test already measures how long carriers stay in each network after it is sold to a rival holder.
questions.why: Strong gives 7.5's seventh study and Table 7.1's falsifier for P3. The others recode the rows P3 came from, measure expectations rather than what arrangements did, or merge the holder with the binder, which 2.7 keeps as separate roles.
questions.follow_up: Which class of binder would you sample first, and why?

questions.question: P4 says an instrument aimed at whoever places the order or writes the permit moves flows more than one aimed at the carrier. What would falsify it?
options: A carrier that reorganised its own network or told its subcontractors what to do, since P4 says carriers have no power over flows at all, and any carrier acting as a principal over other firms would refute it outright.
