An instrument aimed at carriers, a price or a rule, that moved flows more than the same one aimed at receivers or cities. Holguín-Veras's tolls point the other way: only 9 per cent of carriers could pass one on.

A city whose permits failed to change behaviour, since P4 says the public side always succeeds; one city that wrote rules carriers ignored would be enough to show the power to reorganise flows sits elsewhere in the chain.
Finding that receivers dislike being asked to change their hours, since P4 rests on receivers' willingness; if they refuse, the instrument aimed at them fails, and the proposition falls with it.
questions.why: Strong gives Table 7.1's falsifier for P4 and the toll evidence of 2.5 and 6.1. The others misread P4 as denying carriers any power (they keep a principal's power over subcontractors, 4.5), as a claim that cities always succeed rather than a comparison, or as resting on receivers' liking.
questions.follow_up: Is there any instrument in your record aimed at carriers that did move flows?

questions.question: Your evidence for P4 is accounts and who began each row. Couldn't a carrier-aimed instrument still beat a receiver-aimed one, and you'd never know?
options: It couldn't: the 42 rows begun by a city against 19 by a carrier settle the comparison, since who begins an arrangement is the instrument P4 refers to, and cities began more than twice as many as carriers.

That's possible, which is why I'd narrow P4 to cities alone; shippers and receivers can't be shown to move flows on present evidence, so the proposition should name the permit and leave the order out of its statement entirely.

Only a comparison I didn't make could show it, so P4 is offered with its falsifier named. But it rests on more than the accounts: the off-hour studies reached the same condition, and Sternberg's facilitated shippers failed partly for want of self-determination.

By definition carriers can't be the target of an instrument, because delivery rates are set at marginal cost, so any instrument aimed at them is void by construction and P4 holds without any comparison being necessary at all.
questions.why: Strong concedes the missing comparison and gives what else P4 rests on (6.1, Table 7.1). The others treat the initiator count as a test of instruments, narrow P4 without cause, or make it true by definition, which a proposition with a falsifier cannot be.
questions.follow_up: What would that comparison look like in a city that prices both carriers and receivers?

questions.question: Holguín-Veras's toll fell on carriers, and only 9 per cent could pass it on. Isn't one New York study the whole of P4?
options: It is the whole of it, and that's sufficient: a toll is the purest available test of an instrument aimed at carriers, so one well-designed study settles P4 for every city and every instrument a council might reasonably consider.

The toll study is from New York, outside Europe, so I set it aside; P4 rests only on the twenty-six interviews, which concerned the European cities the thesis is bounded to, and on nothing the literature reports about instruments.

P4 rests on Ghent instead: its permit windows moved delivery traffic out of the closed hours, which demonstrates that an instrument aimed at cities outperforms one aimed at carriers, which is precisely the comparison P4 requires.

It's one instrument, and P4 doesn't rest on it alone: the fourth finding has 18 transcripts for, none against; the off-hour studies reached the receiver's condition again; and the falsifier stays open, a carrier-aimed instrument moving flows more than one aimed at receivers or cities.
questions.why: Strong sets the toll beside the transcripts and the off-hour studies and keeps the falsifier open (4.5, 6.1, Table 7.1). The others let one study settle every city, discard evidence 2.5 and 6.1 rely on, or credit Ghent with a measured comparison its plans never report.
questions.follow_up: What would a receiver-aimed version of the same toll look like?
